introFa: کتاب «Love and Will» نوشته Rollo May یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Love and Will»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 29 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL Romeo and Juliet, directed by Nancy Meckler for the RSC, Royal Shakespeare Theatre, 20 April 2006, mid stalls. R omeo and Juliet is the inaugural production of the Complete Works Festival which will, in the next twelve months, stage the plays, as well as adapta- tions of the Sonnets and narrative poems, before the Royal Shakespeare Theatre and the Swan next door go dark for extensive rebuilding. The season is ex- pected to attract over two million extra visitors to the town and offers local landladies and others involved in the tourist trade seven fat kine before the closing of the theatres for some considerable time. Such economic and public relations pressure, it might have been hoped, ought to generate only the finest productions, but this Romeo and Juliet was a shocking disappointment. The production represented the very worst excess- es of “directors’ theatre” in which the acting company is straight-jacketed into a “concept” which all but ob- scures the play and demands they attend to the ideas of the director before they may acknowledge those of the script. Apparently we were in 1940s Sicily, where two Mafiosi families had decided to stage Romeo and Juliet as some sort of expurgation of their own internecine feuding — a ritual of atonement. The supposed local atmosphere was underscored by polyphonic songs in a language that turned out to be Sicilian. (None of this was clear from the produc- tion and had to be spelt out to me by colleagues in the Dirty Duck — the pub across the road from the theatres — who had had it explained to them by the assistant director, Rachel Grunwald!) Quite why two feuding clans would collaborate on a bit of amateur- drama was not immediately apparent. Sure enough, before Shakespeare’s play began, we watched two baleful family heads offer their weap- ons for decommissioning. They presented them wrapped in blankets to each other before taking their places on a number of cheap fold-up wooden chairs gathered around a large square dais. One expected the insert play, Romeo and Juliet, to take place on the dais while non-acting members of the company observed the action but the onstage acting seemed to spill into the onstage audience so that the divi- sion was not at all clear, without anything creative emerging from this interaction. (At one point in the evening, a little girl watching the play donned a hat with large bunny ears, though what this could pos- sibly have meant was anyone’s guess — sometimes an onstage audience is more trouble than it is worth.) Around the dais were thousands of red petals: blood or a red carpet (since, at various points, we seemed to be on a film set)? Running diagonally above the dais (upstage left to downstage right) was a gantry made of elaborate scaffolding from which a lighting rig was suspended and upstage centre an operator focussed an enormous lantern. Additionally various stand-mounted lanterns dotted the space and the up- stage wall was filled by the four sides of a rectangular cinema screen. But, if we were on a film set, why was there an exhausted tree upstage right which seemed to have nothing to do with the action of the play or the location of the production? And if we were in a film studio, then why the ambient Mediterranean sound of cicadas? Inevitably and unfortunately, this will become known as the “Gene Kelly Romeo”. Since the Sicilian villagers had disarmed, there were no weapons left to stage the feuding between Capulets and Montagues. Clearly the next best device with which to dramatise the fighting was… elaborate tap-dancing. On the raised dais, with tap-shoes, the aggression of the ad- olescents was figured as an intricate set of dance rou- tines. The opening scene resembled not so much the contretemps between Gregory and Abraham as a se- quence from Singin’ in the Rain. When weapons were used, they were staves which were tapped percus- sively against the stage to enhance the speed and in- tricacy of the steps. As such the fight sequences were a cross between a Hollywood musical and a group of Morris Men. While West Side Story illustrates the ease with which Shakespeare’s play may be successfully translated into another medium, the trouble here was that we were still watching Romeo, not a spin- off of the play. Furthermore, Romeo, like Macbeth, is a play that is dependent for its narrative on the explicit and dramatic nature of violence. Render the violence as (albeit beautifully choreographed) tap-routines and you render Romeo a parody of itself. Tellingly, when Tybalt struck Mercutio, he swapped his staff for a knife — indicating the production’s lack of faith in its own allegorical device. With the volatile atmosphere dissipated, much of the play’s force was also lost. Nicholas Day ranted his way through Capulet’s angry address to his re- calcitrant daughter, and the Queen Mab speech, usu- ally a set piece of eerie darkness, sounded strangely petulant in the mouth of Jamie Ballard’s Mercutio. Perhaps least convincing, though, were the lovers. Rupert Evans overplayed Romeo as though every line needed a physical illustration or action; fine in the theatre of the eighteenth century but unaccept- able in what was attempting to be a fairly naturalistic production (again the onstage audience were on the verge of disappearing). Morven Christie’s Juliet — though more competent — was hampered by some awful staging decisions. Her balcony was a square scaffold tower which re- sembled Nelson’s Column (currently under restora- tion and shrouded in scaffolding) — a column at the top of which branches sprouted. This was another of Meckler’s brainwaves, which worked quite well at times. Standing on a rung at the top of this shaky device, Juliet was at pains to remain stable, and this

30 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 added to her fragility. When she was inside the scaf- folding, she gave the impression of being as physi- cally trapped as she is socially. Unfortunately, the tower was later put to awkward use. It was obviously impossible for the set designer to place a bedroom at the top of the wobbly metal structure which featured the balcony. So in the scene where Romeo and Juliet spend a night together, they lay on the central dais at stage level. The tower had disappeared (only one of the four ladders had been kept) and Romeo had to “descend” from her chamber by climbing up one side of the ladder, over the top, and down the other side into a stage floor trap. Of course, for technical reasons the ladder could not be free-standing and so another member of the company had to brace his shoulder against the vertical and take the strain. Romeo and his brawny mate looked like the Veronan Window Cleaning Company. There were other irritating production decisions. Peter tells Benvolio and Romeo that “if you be not of the house of Montagues, I pray come and crush a cup of wine” (I.3.80) at the Capulet feast. The fact that they were both sporting blue epaulettes (the colour code was blue for Montague and red for Capulet) meant that they clearly were of the enemy house; this Peter was not only illiterate but colour-blind. Perhaps most clumsy and intrusive was the moment when the dead Paris rose zombie-like to take his jack- et off, which was then raised on a pulley to hang high on the gantry overhead. He then had to exit, while dead, without pulling focus from the joint suicide of the play’s climax — clearly an impossible task, since the lovers were still and he the only thing moving. Romeo’s entry to the Capulet monument had been previously accomplished by his pushing the entire dais upstage to reveal a trap. His Herculean effort was followed by his entry into the tomb and his ex- humation of Juliet over his shoulder in fireman-lift style. He then had to lay her on the stage and die, protractedly, Pyramus-like, next to her. All of this was remarkably clumsy and time-consuming but worse was to come. During Laurence’s redundant synopsis, the rest of the company went into slow-motion attitudes of shock and horror with all the histrionics of a silent movie, though what this was supposed to signify was difficult to say. Romeo and Juliet were then res- urrected and folded in each other’s arms, as though the audience needed to know exactly how their stat- ue might look. Then, finally, and totally without ex- planation, Laurence disrobed and put on a peasant’s jacket — this, the only indication that we had moved from the inset play back to 1940s Sicily — but, then again, had I not gone to the Dirty Duck that night, I would have had no idea what was going on. Peter J. Smith with Gaëlle Ginestet * Antony and Cleopatra, directed by Gregory Doran for the RSC, The Swan, 22 June 2006, centre stalls. A ntony and Cleopatra is a notoriously “difficult” play. It offers (at least) three gloriously rich rôles perfectly pitched for mature actors at the height of their powers, some sublime speeches, and a series of magnificent dramatic set-pieces (the drunken carouse on Pompey’s barge, Cleopatra’s berating of the hap- less messenger, and two wonderfully complex death scenes, each partaking dangerously of both farce and tragedy). And yet, and yet… it is also much too long (or it often seems so), too episodic, and too diverse in its narrative strands and emotional textures to al- low for any simple directorial “vision” to be success- fully imposed upon it without savage cuts. Gregory Doran’s new production took these challenges head on and, to his great credit, he gave this monster of a play its due — playing, for example, most if not all of those tiny military scenes set in far flung parts of the empire that are usually cut at an early stage in rehearsals, and playing them straight, skimping neither on the political plotting nor the emotional content. The result, if not an outright victory, was at least a high-scoring draw, the kind of entertaining contest that, fittingly in a World Cup year, seemed designed to send the crowds home happy, convinced that they had seen justice done, without the mockery of a penalty shoot-out. It was greatly to Doran’s advantage that he had at the heart of his team two leading actors who can, and often do, carry a production on their own. Harriet Walter brought to Cleopatra a wonderful, knowing waywardness, a capacity to throw herself seemingly recklessly over an emotional precipice (whether of desire or rage or both at once) and yet somehow stop herself in mid-air halfway down and coast to the ground as if she had always intended it that way. Vulnerable and invulnerable at one and the same moment, her “infinite variety” (II.2.241) was com- pounded of both an enticing authority and an appar- ently instinctive naivety that made Antony’s obses- sive, frustrating dependence upon her wholly expli- cable, as was the loyalty-to-death of all those who served her, however demanding and coquettish her behaviour. In the latter rôles, Golda Rosheuvel was a wonderfully disdainful Charmian, looking with a mixture of pity and contempt upon anyone who was unfortunate enough not to be her beloved queen, while Iras (Emma Jay Thomas) and the Handmaid (Allyson Brown) were more playful companions, who could nonetheless form a protective cordon around their mistress’s throne when danger threat- ened. Even Seleucus, the treasurer (Ewan Cummins), was part of the loyal inner circle. His supposed be- trayal of the queen’s financial sharp-practice to Cae- sar was played as a trick designed between them to win time for the Queen’s suicide. Walter offered him

31 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL the briefest of complicit nods of approval when he completed his speech, and once the Romans had left she settled back with a broad grin of relief that the stratagem had worked. Playing alongside Walter, and matching her ka- leidoscopic subtlety with a commanding, dog-eared nobility, Patrick Stewart enjoyed one very obvious and compelling advantage over most previous Antonys. Unlike other actors, who have to work hard to convey the sense that they had once commanded legions and bestrid the oceans like colossi, but just happen now to look like ageing, slightly overweight thesbians, Stewart brings with him a curriculum vitae that proves the point. We do not have to work hard to imagine him as a martial hero, we have all seen him campaigning in the farthest regions of the universe as Star Trek’s Captain Jean-Luc Picard of the Star Ship Enterprise, boldly going where no one — not even Laurence Olivier — has gone before. So when he talks of swords and victories, we believe him. If he is now the wrong side of three-score, he still has both the physique and the presence to command at- tention, and even the addition of a curly-grey wig to conceal the famous shaven head cannot dispel the as- sociations from a score of films and television series. Indeed, in the tight, confessional space of the Swan, Stewart’s distinctive, rich voice is, if anything, more resonant than on film. He can thus play the military scenes with an almost effortless conviction and trade gesture for gesture, nuance for nuance with Walter in their love scenes. If the two principals were well matched, the sup- porting cast was also thoroughly competent. Ken Bones’s Enobarbus was a grizzled old soldier with a clear, well-modulated delivery. James Hayes brought a poised tremulousness to Lepidus, especially in the drunken carousal scene; while Julian Bleach played the Clown with an engaging intonation reminiscent of a sinister version of Kenneth Williams, an effect made all the more incongruous by its being delivered from beneath a tall red and white striped woolly hat. There were some other interesting directorial choices. Octavius Caesar (John Hopkins) was no shrewd and calculating young politician, but a raging, petulant, thirty-something, who could barely control his emo- tions. In the formal reconciliation scene with Antony (II.2) he was all spleen and barely suppressed anger, having on several occasions to be restrained from storming off after one or other of the older man’s many subtle up-stagings. Yet when Decretas (Ravi Aujla) handed him dead Antony’s sword in Act V Scene 3, his legs spectacularly collapsed from under him and he crashed backwards onto the ground cra- dling the weapon as if it were a lover. The motive behind these excessive gestures (suppressed homo- erotic desire or an outpouring of relief?) was never made clear, however. It was as if they had decided that they wanted an unconventional, passionate, Caesar, but had not quite determined why or how he would be so. Were his rages sexually motivated? His lengthy, very physical kiss of farewell with his sister Octavia (played by Mariah Gale) hinted at in- cest — but this was not pursued further. Was it just emotional immaturity: “He calls me boy!” (IV.1.1)? The issue was not clarified, so we were left with a rather frustrating, emotionally messy performance with nothing productive at its core. All of the calculating, machiavellian “Roman” qualities usually associated with the role of Caesar were devolved upon Maecenas (Edmund Kingsley), who appeared an ever-present fixer and spin-doctor at Caesar’s elbow, a clipboard-like leather-bound volume forever in his hand. Here, it seemed, was the real brain behind the Empire, the man to whom everyone deferred. When, after his initial victory, Caesar issued the order to “feast the army. We have store to do’t, / And they have earned the waste.” (IV.1.15-16), it was more a suggestion to Maecenas than a command, the last clause spoken almost as a question. Kingsley’s slight nod in return suggested that such extravagance was indeed appropriate and might, just this once, be indulged. Where Caesar was all passion and little thought, Maecenas was the reverse. His lack of access to the deeper wells of human emotion was brought out in a splendidly nuanced version of the description of Cleopatra’s infinite variety in the “The barge she sat in” speech (II.2.197ff). While Ken Bones, playing Enobarbus, sat centre stage and spoke the lines softly, using gesture only sparingly, Agrippa (Keith Osborn), who had initially been standing upstage, arms sternly folded, was gradually drawn downstage until he was sitting beside him in rapt attention. Meanwhile Maecenas, who clearly had no idea why this description of ec- centric female behaviour should hold any interest to sensible men, watched with increasing incompre- hension the responses of his colleague. At one point he offered a snort of derisive laughter at a seemingly fanciful detail, but, sensing that it was not the cor- rect response, stifled it and looked merely confused instead. When Enobarbus finally announced that Antony could never leave such a Cleopatra, despite his Roman marriage, Maecenas looked on with com- plete astonishment. That a man might turn his back upon a legal contract and a profitable political settle- ment for a mere woman had clearly never occurred to him. The set (designed by Steven Brimson Lewis) was a simple, flexible affair. The rear wall was covered with a net on which a pattern of what looked like badly applied plasterwork had been daubed. Having initially implied an architectural reflection upon Antony’s fall into moral and physical decay, the net was subsequently back-lit with different colours to produce a variety of other effects: during violent scenes the patterns were made to resemble vivid

32 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 splashes of blood or gaudy purple paint thrown over the stage, at other moments they became dull brown smears suggestive of an H-Block dirty protest or sin- ister black daubs that might have been relief maps of a disintegrating empire or decadent abstract art. The stage itself was largely bare, with ropes and nets be- ing flown in for the nautical scenes. The large central trap was employed for the soldiers to break into the monument and to bring up Cleopatra’s throne and two flaming pots for the final death scene. A kind of mechanical compromise governed the notoriously tricky elevation of the dying Antony into the monu- ment at IV.16.38. Cleopatra and her women at first appeared in the upper tier of the balcony above the stage, but as Antony was winched towards them, the central section of the balcony began to descend towards his rising figure, coming to rest at about the height of the Swan’s middle balcony. Antony’s death was thus played out in this separate highly visible mini-balcony, illuminated by golden lighting as if from braziers within. In the absence of the kind of busy, locale-evoking set employed for the current production of Much Ado, much of the work required to establish a sense of place was done by the costumes (designed by Kandis Cook). Antony’s legions wore sand-coloured leather Roman armour over dull red linen, evocative of long- campaigning across North Africa, while Caesar’s soldiers wore newer-looking black, Maecenas and the bureaucrats favouring togas and civilian dress. The Egyptian court was economically suggested by feather fans on poles, throws in pastel shades on the ground, eastern waistcoats and pantaloons, stick-on beards, and eye-shadow. When in Rome, Antony wore his armour, when in Egypt he lolled bare-chest- ed in a silk waistcoat, pyjama trousers, and a pair of curly-toed slippers, while Cleopatra and her ladies wore oatmeal-coloured chiffon. In the first scene the mood of risqué decadence was established by the rather decorous three-thonged flail that Antony car- ried off to Cleopatra’s chamber (recently purchased at the Alexandrian branch of Ann Summers, perhaps?), while the fluidity of their power relationship was im- plied by the fact that, when they returned together, it was she who was wielding the whip and he whose hands were bound in a silk scarf — a coy metonym for “these strong Egyptian fetters” (I.2.109). Such moments reflected the strengths of the pro- duction, and arguably of the play itself. They were memorable episodes in a play that somehow failed to match the sum of its infinitely varied parts. In doing justice to each scene, and on its own terms, as Doran did here, he was able to provide a well- spoken, well-performed production that had much to commend it and little one would criticise. But he did so at the expense of any unifying central theme or idea. What one will remember, I suspect, will be the engaging moments: Antony with his sex-toy and curly-wig, Cleopatra’s sexual gasp as the asp bit into her, or even Lepidus saying farewell to Octavia with a film of milk on his upper lip (awkward remnant of a remedy for “the morning after the night before”). The play as a whole is perhaps simply too large to be remembered “as a whole” and all at once — and for a production to remind us of the fact, while staying true to its many great qualities, is probably no small achievement. Greg Walker * Othello, in German, adaptation by Feridun Zaimoglu and Günter Senkel, directed by Luk Perceval for Münchner Kammerspiele, Royal Shakespeare Theatre, 27 April 2006, front circle. T he RSC’s publicity leaflet identified this pro- duction’s unique selling points as its two-hour “distillation” of the text and its jazz-piano accom- paniment. Both features were indeed striking: the plot was ruthlessly pared down to its essentials, diminishing Shakespeare’s characteristic richness of texture but gaining in pace and immediacy; and the pervasive piano score, going way beyond con- ventional jazz to provide a kind of atonal emotional soundscape, was as much a part of the text as the modern German dialogue, translated into vividly colloquial English surtitles. There was more, though, to both features of the production. This was not simply a précis but an adaptation of Shakespeare’s play. Predictably elimi- nated were Montano and Bianca, while the business of the handkerchief — decorated with “a colour- ful animal print” — was streamlined so much that we never knew how Emilia had acquired it. More radically, Brabantio survived to substitute for both Lodovico and Gratiano at the end of the play, and the murder of Desdemona marked the conclusion of the action: there was no self-realisation nor ostentatious suicide for this Othello, let alone the other tragic ac- coutrements of Shakespeare’s final scene. This was no more Shakespeare than Nahum Tate’s King Lear or the BBC’s 2005 Shakespeare ReTold adaptations. But did it matter? As for the music, it dominated the production both aurally and, if this makes sense, visually. The central feature of the set consisted of two pianos, an upturned white one straddled by a black one in an image of the “beast with two backs” (one of the few phrases to survive from Shakespeare’s text). The pi- anist, Jens Thomas, was hunched permanently over the dominant, black piano, giving an almost continu- ous, virtuoso performance of his own score, some- times leaning over to beat the interior of the instru- ment or pluck its strings, and occasionally launching into an extended vocal riff, living through the emo-

33 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL tional experience of every character. Sometimes the actors, too, became part of the sound score, segue- ing from their spoken text into a repertoire of noises expressive of their emotional state, often accompa- nied by repetitive gestures or wild movements, as in Roderigo’s grotesque dance of enraged sexual frustration. The cavernous grey chamber of the set, with its single chair and its copulatory pianos, the space between them serving as Othello and Desdemona’s bed, evoked a frightening social and moral void in which the dark-suited male characters, contrasted with Julia Jentsch’s white-clad, blonde-haired Desdemona, enacted their drama of envy and ha- tred, their foul language powerfully expressive of the appalling misogyny and racism that are central to Shakespeare’s text. The stark lighting enhanced the production’s expressionist style, throwing tightly- focused shafts of light across this bleak world, creat- ing deep shadows and sharp contrasts. In the senate scene, the back-lit actors played almost entirely in silhouette; for the arrival at Cyprus the stage bright- ened, but it was a harsh, unforgiving illumination of human bitterness and depravity. Though the setting and costumes made no attempt to suggest that we were in a military garrison, the hothouse atmosphere of the barrack-room suffused the powerfully staged scene of Cassio’s drunkenness, beginning in rau- cously obscene singing and ending in name-calling, smashed beer bottles and flying fists. Though Iago carefully swept up the broken glass, the bare-footed Desdemona had to tread carefully — an apt image of her role in this world. There was a powerful sexual charge between vir- tually all the characters, often displaced into hatred and jealousy; Cassio clearly desired Emilia as much as Roderigo did Desdemona, and even Othello and Desdemona’s married sexuality had something earthy and disturbing about it, with her submission to his ritualised domination prior to her death cre- ating a shocking impact. All this was fuel to Iago’s sexual paranoia: “I can do without all that romantic shit”; “Desdemona will soon fuck him over”. The ob- scenity of Iago’s language was shockingly graphic, but no more so than the racist fulminations of Brabantio towards the end of the play, with his omi- nous predictions of imminent ethnic cleansing back in Venice. The play had begun in an extended silence as Werner Rehm’s Brabantio slowly and carefully undressed, evoking some sympathy for him as he was then roused from his bed; by the end, he stood as the representative of a sick and evil society whose bigotry and violence had destroyed lives. The play’s political context was broadened to suggest machina- tions within the Venetian state, so that Othello could speculate on a political motive behind Cassio’s affair with his wife. The performances throughout matched the direc- tor’s bleak vision in their dissection of these obses- sive, dysfunctional characters. The actors’ concentra- tion was relentless: most of them had been working together in this production for four years. Their skill lay in combining the subjectivity of the characters’ emotional states with an objective, almost Brechtian sense of distance from their roles. As Iago, Wolfgang Pregler conveyed a fiercely intense hatred that paint- ed the world in the lurid colours of his own self-dis- gust. Though Othello praised him as “a good man”, there was little sense that he presented to others the “honest Iago” persona of the original: Desdemona objected to his crudity, and Cassio called him an “unpleasant specimen”. His scenes with Thomas Thieme’s Othello were powerfully gripping, striking an authentically Shakespearean note in the careful pacing of Iago’s temptation and the gradual disinte- gration of Othello’s complacent confidence. For parts of the temptation scene, the piano was ominously si- lent, and at other points the dialogue was whispered inaudibly, creating an unbearable tension. Strikingly, Thieme’s Othello was white, not black. That is, the character was black — referred to as “Negro”, “nigger” or “Choco” according to the context — but there was no attempt to match the actor’s appearance to his role. This was a simple, elegant and eminently Shakespearean solution to a notorious casting issue: because the text stressed Othello’s blackness, that was how we saw him in our imaginations. In every respect, Thieme matched up to the requirements of the role, using his age and his physical bulk to good effect, both in conveying his authority and in suggesting his sense of disbelief that Desdemona could possibly have fallen for him. In the senate scene he was still, restrained, almost mo- notonous in recounting the circumstances of his mar- riage, but his emotional range broadened as events slipped from his control. His physical and moral col- lapse was intensely moving, and the production lost little by ending where it did; one sensed that, even as Othello killed Desdemona, he was conscious of the tragic folly of his act. It was Emilia who was played by a black per- former, but little was made of this in a rather dimin- ished version of her role. As in Shakespeare’s play, she was fully aware of her husband’s real character, but here she seemed to know of his actions too. In the programme note the director talked of casting a black Emilia as “a woman who embodies enormous eroticism and beauty, who is not really nasty, who observes, who lets the game play and tries to sur- vive”, but this did not come across strongly in the performance. In listening to (or reading) the racist insults of this text, we were apparently meant to feel “shame and embarrassment” on behalf of the ac- tress, Sheri Hagen, but perhaps this was one level of awareness too much for an audience whose attention was inevitably divided between the stage and the

34 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 rather inconveniently placed surtitles. A production such as this, particularly of a Shakespeare play, would be virtually inconceivable from a British company, and it was a rare privilege to share this one, even though, at times, an insistent, ir- reverent and very English voice in my head muttered the word “pretentious”. The sniggering of adoles- cents in the audience was disconcerting, and it was difficult to pinpoint the reasons for it: embarrassment at the explicit obscenities? Contempt for the alienat- ing production style? Approval of the racist insults and misogynistic jokes? Or sheer incomprehension? There were apparently walkouts, and refunds, some on the basis that the publicity had been misleading and this Othello wasn’t really Shakespeare’s Othello. To answer my earlier question, this did matter. This was serious European theatre, shamefully under-sup- ported by unadventurous British audiences, and a salutary contrast to the more conservative produc- tions of the RSC itself; however, the “real” Othello remained as a yawning absence in a “Complete Works” season that disingenuously claimed to be presenting everything that Shakespeare wrote. Peter Malin * Hamlet, directed by Janet Suzman for the Baxter Theatre Centre, The Swan, 5 May 2006, left stalls. T ragedy attended this production: Brett Goldin, who was to have played Guildenstern, was mur- dered on Easter Sunday. First and foremost, credit is due to the company for persevering under what must have been very difficult circumstances, and to Nicholas Pauling for filling in at such short notice and for such an abhorrent reason. This lamentable backdrop also lent a certain ur- gency to the question of how far the social and politi- cal realities of life in South Africa should be allowed to infuse a Cape Town production of Hamlet. In the programme, director Janet Suzman astutely notes the perils of political didacticism — but it is also possible to exercise too much caution. Essentially, this staging offered a straight and somewhat Anglicised render- ing of the play, and the audience was obliged to read political resonances into the unfolding drama. Prison bars blocked the balconies flanking the stage, and Hamlet’s attempt to escape to Wittenberg was blocked by the ominous presence of taciturn security guards. These features made concrete the image of Denmark as a prison, and evoked the dis- turbing phenomenon of house arrest. However, they were not employed in a systematic and strident man- ner, one that would suffice to create an all-pervasive atmosphere of political menace and paranoia. The motif of imprisonment remained just that, an allu- sive fragment. A comparable sense of an unfulfilled interpreta- tion emerged in the production’s relation to post- colonial theory, in the sense that an interpretation had to be imposed; it did not arise organically from a fully coherent set of dramatic cues. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern were played by white actors, with English accents, adopting the affectations and attire of those who have arrived at university from a pub- lic-school background, and were treated with con- spicuous contempt by Hamlet. Horatio wore tweed and corduroy, having apparently fallen for a clichéd notion of what a scholar should wear. It is tempting to read these figures as vestiges of a colonial regime, but the racially diverse “Rainbow Elsinore”, as Suzman dubs it, seemed to have re- tained the mannerisms of the system it has, appar- ently, supplanted. The putative old order’s values have been inverted rather than subverted. Hamlet alone demurs, retaining his accent and an eclectic dress sense. He does not ape fashion, but rather fashions himself as an ape, his “madness” result- ing in him clattering the prison bars and hooting like a chimp being driven insane in the confines of a zoo. This outburst could be read as a response to a perceived racial vilification, were it not for the fact that it occurs in isolation, in the context of a court whose manifold and manifest troubles seemed not to include that of ethnic integration. An “antic disposition”(I.5.173) seemed to come as something of a relief in this Hamlet’s case: Vaneshran Arumugam’s soliloquies reached the point of frenzy at an early stage, and the performance of mad- ness had a calmative effect, as did the meditative “Ommm…” that punctuated Act II Scene 2’s closing speech. “To be or not to be” (III.1.58) marked the in- trusion of a fevered imagination upon a session of martial arts training. The fact that John Kani doubled as Claudius and the Ghost triggered the interesting notion that it is Hamlet alone who insists upon the radical difference between the new regime and the old. Only he, it was suggested, discerns the betrayal of the spirit that overthrew an apparently colonial ethos — one now being replicated by the new re- gime. It is difficult to judge whether this perspective is unique in its insight or is arbitrarily applied on the basis of personal rancour. Claudius was an utterly inscrutable figure, hiding behind the painstaking exactitude with which he delivers his lines. The audience is denied the usual choice: is Claudius a monster or merely an opportunist? This Claudius vanished beneath waves of enunciatory precision. Just one slip was permitted, as the King’s apparently repentant imprecations segued into the clicks of his South African mother tongue. Elsewhere, anything reminiscent of ethnic be- longing was treated as a joke: the players cavorted clownishly in pseudo-tribal garb, and the gravedig- ger deployed a broad Afrikaaner accent for comic ef-

S ean Holmes’s production of Julius Caesar con- tained many moments of brilliance, although much of these were stilted by an austere setting and slow sense of pace. The backdrop, the RST stage covered over with a black curtain, at moments worked magic. In the opening scene, for example, when the crowd are said to “vanish”, a change in lighting removed them from view. Gradually indi- viduals became visible as they changed costume for the second scene, James Hayes’s cobbler becoming Caesar, a career progression if ever there was one. The crowd’s metamorphosis into Roman nobles was an impressive visual feat. For the most part, how- ever, the darkness produced a world in which Rome and Italy were oddly absent. The only relief from the darkness was an oblong neon sky that hung above the actors’ heads, which looked like a giant postcard. These whereabouts required the actors to work hard against the gloom, and the ramp that extended from the stage into the auditorium forced them to scowl their lines directly to the audience. The production was at its worst during the storm scene, which could have been an advert on behalf of the RSC’s plans to renovate the RST. The theatre’s limitations were highlighted by water that poured out of the neon sky, the sound of which completely drowned out the actors’ words. The acoustic prob- lems of the theatre were further compounded by thunder, lightening, and, less meteorologically, a violin. There was no doubt of the character’s sense of importance, even as he appeared to improvise a persona for himself, an improvisation which took place in public, at home and in the Senate, seeming to weigh up the rhetoric of his language. I n a fascinating programme note Professor Tony Kapcia deftly summarises the historical roots of Fidel Castro’s rise to power from the early 1950s to the fall of Fulgencio Batista on 1 January 1959. Unsurprisingly, nowhere does he mention Much Ado About Nothing. Might this be because the Cuban revolution and the play have very little in common? Much Ado has nothing to do with the struggles against a nearby superpower, nothing to do with the overthrow of a dictatorial state by a guerrilla network whose invasion attempts, Kapcia concedes, were “badly timed, ill-located and easily repulsed”. Much Ado has nothing to do with the savagery or political complexities of régime change: it is more or less a domestic comedy or tragedy, depending on whether you are Beatrice or Hero. Granted, there is an off-stage war from which the soldiers return in the opening scene but we hear little about it and its function is to provide Beatrice with a number of in- sulting barbs at Benedick’s expense about his martial impotence. Elliott’s decision then to stage Much Ado in pre-revolutionary Cuba — was Don Pedro sup- posed to be Batista? Don John, Castro? — was largely irrelevant, and raised more difficulties than it could possibly allay. What next: a Stone Age As You Like It or Henry V on a desert island? Creative transposition of setting — temporal or geographical — ought only to offend the most narrow-minded purist. Irrelevant transposition is simply intrusive, distracting and occludes rather than enhances the play that it is the director’s duty to explicate. As if this were not bad enough, the director and designer singularly failed to utilise what is one of the best performance spaces in the world. The vir- tue of The Swan is its clarity of sight line as well as the intimacy created by proximity of actor and audience. Here, the sight lines were wrecked by Lez Brotherston’s fussy design. Flashing neon signs spelt out “Cuba Bar” (presumably a clumsy prompt for those too parsimonious to purchase the programme) and strings of Christmas lights were festooned around the balconies of the theatre. Upstage centre a decrepit Vespa was waiting, in a conspicuously “Cuban” way, for spare parts, its front axle chocked up on wooden blocks. The stage was crowded with tables, chairs, benches and, overhead, ceiling fans while filigreed wrought-iron work flanked a central entrance upstage centre. Most egregious of all was a lamp-post set downstage right which effectively blocked the aisle entrance onto the stage and masked off the action happening upstage of it. The function of the lamp-post was to support a whole load of dodgy electrical wiring, as though to hint at the du- bious nature of a society which had the gall illegally to tap into the public power supply — truly a sledge- hammer to crack a nut. Not only were these elements in the way but, at points, Elliott had blocked the action so that actors were completely masked by other members of the company; this is itself something of an achievement on such an open stage. For instance, during the ill-fated wedding of Claudio and Hero, the couple faced upstage with two parallel lines of congregation sitting behind them. Not only were all the actors fac- ing upstage so that their expressions were difficult to perceive, but each actor effectively masked those in front. It was like playing the scene with the lights off. As Benedick listened to the confidence tricksters describing the apparently love-sick Beatrice, he hid behind a potted yucca tree. The problem was that we could not see him hiding since his area of the stage was masked by Leonato, Claudio and Don Pedro who lolled full length around a table placed perversely as far downstage as possible. Beatrice had to cower in the audience during part of the parallel eavesdropping scene, since the stage allowed her no space from which we could actually see her. There remained a tendency, however, for him to use outlandish facial expressions to milk easy laughter from the audience but as the role turned serious the performance grew in stature. He resigned his military office and snatched off his metal dog tag, not deigning to hand it to Don Pedro but placing it ostentatiously on a table past which he

Smith * A Midsummer Night’s Dream, directed by Tim Supple for Dash Arts/British Council, The Swan, 12 June 2006, centre ground. T he production began with the strange sound of a singing stone. The curved, rock-like instrument sat at the front of the stage and water in shallow pools on either side of the stone was used to create a reso- nant hum as the stone was rubbed with wet hands. It was fitting that the seeming alchemy from stone to instrument was effected by Ajay Kumar, who played Philostrate and Puck. His presence at the beginning established his characters’ stage-management skills within the court and the forest respectively. Between the singing stone and the central section of the audi- ence was a small platform, slightly lower than the stage and covered in soil. It was here that Philostrate, and later Puck, did “lurk” (II.1.47), observing the action onstage. The potential that the Swan’s stage offered for this onlooker to be both part of the theatre audience and part of the action onstage established a blurring of boundaries which was compounded by the production’s physicality. The acrobatic spirits climbed ropes and silken sheets, moving closer to the audience in the galleries and swinging above those on the ground. Seeing A Midsummer Night’s Dream in the Swan was novel and exciting in itself, since the play’s box-office appeal has meant that it has been performed almost exclusively in the Main House, with the exception of a 1984 production in The Other Place. Tim Supple’s production, supported by Dash Arts and the British Council, also had fresh and exciting claims to make in its own right. The project took over two years to evolve. It pushed at the boundaries of conventional actor/audience relationships, integrating English theatrical culture with Indian and Sri Lankan per- formance traditions. An audience became aware of the cast’s diversity in the first act where Malayalam, Tamil, Bengali, Sinhala, Marathi, Hindi and English were spoken. Hippolyta (Archana Ramaswamy), Hermia (Yuki Ellias) and Helena (Shanaya Rafaat) all spoke in English in the first scene and this helped to establish an implicit bond between them. Hippolyta’s angry silence and decision to exit without Theseus (P. R. Jijoy) registered powerfully. Within such linguistic variety, characters who shared a language were linked, but other nuances of region were inaccessible to the majority of the Swan audience. The different Asian languages sounded broadly the same, and were simply “other” to that which was doubly familiar: in English and with Shakespeare’s rhythms. The use of Tamil by Egeus (J. Jayakumar) highlighted his verbosity and simpli- fied his anger with his daughter. In the forest, both Oberon and Titania spoke Malayalam and English but Titania had proportionally more English (and sounded more fluent) and, as a consequence, she seemed, to the Swan audience, wiser and more in control. Presumably these linguistic shifts had a dif- ferent effect upon the Delhi audience’s impression of character and perhaps the reception altered when the production toured across India. In Stratford, Bottom’s (Joy Fernandes) malapropisms were amus- ing in the context of his shifts between Marathi, Hindi and English. He seemed to be thinking too hard and this challenged a performance tradition of him not thinking enough. In such a physical production it might seem perverse to focus on these choices, yet the sprinkling of English lines did seem to prompt the audience to listen with greater attentiveness than is often the case. Laughter seemed to follow verbal quips quickly and this was underlined by a restraint from visual gags (with the exception of Bottom’s appendage). Bottom’s transformation was simply staged. He gained a pair of straw ears, a cowbell around his neck and a squash-like fruit dangling be- tween his legs. His “mortal grossness” (III.1.152) had been purged with an emphasis on his transformation into an animal. As an ass he was separated from the mortals and from this spirit world. The production’s visual impact was crucial to the way in which the court and the forest were differ-

Puck pulled a silken sheet from the ground to reveal reddish soil covering the perform- ance area. The disruption of the man-made paper and fabric revealed the forest’s more natural envi- ronment. Theseus and Hippolyta followed the now conventional doubling by becoming the fairy king and queen. As the latter they had their hair loose and flowing and wore more revealing costumes. Indeed, all the lovers progressively shed their clothing during their time in the forest and gave increasingly sensual performances. Part of Titania and Oberon’s argu- ment took place with them rolling on the stage, with their bodies locked together, as their power struggle became aggressively physical. The love-juice was a vermillion powder. When Puck pressed the “dye” (III.2.102) on the eyes of Lysander (Chandan Roy Sanyal) and Demetrius (Prasanna Mahagamage) his power was more threatening than playful. Oberon’s application to Titania’s eyes had a sexual aggres- sion which was compounded by the way in which he ripped open her red, silken bower that was both cocoon and vulva-like. The sense of sexual liberation was demonstrated by the lovers taking the confusion a step further than the text indicates. Hermia kissed Demetrius because he drove her “past the bounds / Of maid- en’s patience” (III.2.65-66) and Helena responded in kind to Lysander and then worried “These vows are Hermia’s” (III.2.130). Their lack of self-control in the forest was exploited by the spirits. Puck created a “mazèd world” (II.1.113) around the arguing lov- ers in Act III Scene 2. The reels of elastic that Puck unwound to criss-cross the stage helped exemplify the contradictions of confinement and release in this “forest wild” (II.1.25). The impact of the forest experience was made ap- parent in the subtle shift in the environment at court for the final act. Philostrate set the scene. He sprin- kled a white powder on the forest’s soil to define three areas. These sections were covered with fabric upon which the married couples sat. The mechani- cals took their play seriously. Their rehearsals had been light-hearted but diligent and their profession- alism was apparent here. Flute (Joyraj Bhattacharya) wore a full-length dress and he gave a sincere per- formance as Thisbe, rather than a comic one as Flute- playing-Thisbe. The tragedy of Pyramus and Thisbe was emotionally engaging. Bhattacharya’s native language removed the crass rhymes and Thisbe’s lament sounded musically genuine. The theatre audience’s emotional connection with Thisbe was also made possible by the stage audience’s still and focussed attention. Their interruptions were retained but they had been redistributed so that Helena and Hermia joined in with the interjections. Their com- ments seemed to mark their engagement with the drama rather than any tension in their relationships with their husbands. The couples’ attentive body lan- guage (facing the same way as most of the Swan au- dience) ensured that more attention was given to the mechanicals’ play than to the observers’ responses. The Bergomask was energetically performed by all the company and it sealed a supportive relationship between the couples and the mechanicals. Puck literally and symbolically swept away “the dust” (V.2.20) that Philostrate had used to define the division between the court and the mechanicals. Theseus and Hippolyta shed their outer garments onstage to become Oberon and Titania and the merging of their characters reinforced this blurring of boundaries. All the performers gathered “hand in hand” to “sing and bless this place” (V.2.29-30) and the majority of the theatre audience eagerly antici- pated the cue to “give [Puck their] hands” (Epilogue, 15). The uplifting final sequence was followed by an encore which, with a more relaxed body language, elided the distinction between actor and character. The audience’s applause complemented the percus- sive drum-beat which was at the core of this commu- nal celebration where performers and audience were “friends” (Epilogue, 15). The enthusiastic response attested to the energy, humour and commitment of the performances. There are lingering doubts, however, about the ba- sis of that positive reaction. Was Shakespeare’s play interpreted in a new and challenging way, or did the text simply serve a colonial project whereby an audience in Stratford-upon-Avon could admire the physical and emotional performances? Post-per- formance praise seemed to focus on the acrobat- ics, especially those of the athletic Changeling Boy (Ram Pawar). Did the mingling of languages offer a contrast between those who aspired to the “civilised and educated” English-speaking world and the less articulate but physically skilled “natives”? Perhaps. There are rumours that this Dream will return to the Courtyard Theatre next year so there will be another opportunity to decide whether the appreciation is of something “strange and admirable” (V.1.27) or of a “palpable-gross play” (360). This production began by staging its artificiality, although it was rather difficult to pinpoint the begin- ning, as audience members mingled with Roman warriors in the foyer before taking their seats. The stage was initially filled with stagehands, clothes racks, and cast members performing warm-up exer- cises. A grid was projected onto the stark white walls of Rome, a pointed reminder of the fact of orches- tration: the characters had to move and act within coordinates stipulated by theatrical direction and, by extension, the unassailable logic of revenge. This moment was, of course, one of meta-theatricality, but its resonances extended beyond the confines of Western academic discourse: it was also reminiscent of the intrusion of everyday reality that inaugu- rated Ninagawa’s Kabuki staging of Macbeth. The production similarly exploited the Kabuki concept of the hanamichi (literally, “flower path”; a walkway leading through the audience to the left hand side of the stage): speeches were regularly delivered from the aisles, and this gesture effectively countered the spatial restrictions so often imposed by the RST’s proscenium arch. As the stage cleared, an amplified voice com- manded the entrance of the set’s dominant feature: a massive statue of the she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus. Its portentous presence acted as a constant reminder of Rome’s mythic dream of itself, and high- lighted the sense of a violation of its ethos; episodes of violence (notably the rape of Lavinia) were ac- companied by a lupine howl. Like the rest of the set, the wolf was a brilliant white, almost blinding under bright lights. Even the forest’s vegetation — includ- ing a phallic tree trunk which witnessed Lavinia’s violation — was white, as were the costumes of the Romans. By contrast, the Goths were attired in bright colours, which were soon partially covered by the white vestments of Rome as their status was trans- formed. The only exception was Shun Oguri’s sen- suous, insidious Aaron (a perfect companion to Rei Asami’s feline, treacherous Tamora), who retained his red robes. As he draped himself over the pristine wolf, he acquired a stark and savage beauty, like a splash of blood on untouched snow. Blood itself was denoted by spools of red thread spilling from garments, limbs, and Lavinia’s mouth. Cruelty was stylised; the visceral became the aes- thetic. Vermilion cotton was already trailing from Titus (Kotaro Yoshida) as he entered, a residue of his battles, a reminder of their cost. To an even greater extent than usual, Titus emerged as a purely martial figure (a point of reference might be bushido, the Samurai ethos): he seemed utterly to have dehu- manised the Goths, flinging Tamora’s shackled sons to the floor after mock-strangling their pleading mother. There was a proleptic irony at work: Titus’s sons (now performing a ritualised keening for their dead brothers) would appear later in chains, repli- cating precisely the fate of their prisoners. This Titus was at home on the battlefield, and floundered amid political intrigue. He called to mind Nietzsche’s ap- ophthegmatic remark, “Under conditions of peace the warlike man attacks himself” (Beyond Good and Evil, §76), and appeared utterly bewildered by the reversal of fortune enjoyed by his captives. They emerged in archways above the stage, a vantage point previously occupied by senators, and Titus could not understand how this hierarchical inversion had come about: he visibly crumpled. He seemed defeated already, but things had yet to fall apart. The psychopathic homosociality inher- ent in the conspiracy of Chiron and Demetrius was foregrounded, and was savagely consummated as, after desecrating Lavinia (Hitomi Manaka), they emerged embracing, ecstatic, naked, bloody torrents cascading from their genitals. The aftermath featured a carefully composed, almost still tableau, again in- debted to Kabuki theatre with its aesthetics of stasis. Titus cradled Lavinia centre stage, rendering concrete the image of her as his flesh by enveloping her in his robe. Their position on the steps leading down from the stage recalled Michelangelo’s Pietà, while Marcus and Lucius flanked the scene like the wings of a trip- tych, the towering wolf standing in for a metaphysi- cal point of reference. Distilled in this scene was the essence of the production. Bloodshed and revenge were staged in tableaux of austere beauty, and the dissonance thereby created seemed utterly appropri- ate to the play’s abattoir classicism. Conventional wisdom says that the audience must choke on Lucius’s invocation of the sense of an end- ing just as Tamora does on her sons’ baked flesh. In this version, the sometimes intrusive post-minimal- ist score saturated the final scene, offering a series of resolving chords whose very repetition militated against their ostensible function. As the victims and survivors were dragged or drawn away from the

T he Chicago Shakespeare Theater’s acclaimed pro- duction of the two parts of Henry IV, directed by the company’s founder Barbara Gaines, is a welcome contribution to the RSC’s Complete Works season. The company has a reputation for “authentic” but not necessarily reverential treatments of the canon, and this approach was evident in the current produc- tion (although, if anything, a little more irreverence would have been still more welcome). Any lengthy or overly rhetorical speeches were brutally pruned: Vernon’s admiring description of Hal rising into his saddle like feathered Mercury (Part I: IV.1.97-111), for example, was halted in mid-flow by Hotspur after “I saw young Harry with his beaver on” (105). Scenes were trimmed to their narrative essentials: Hal’s humiliation of Francis the drawer (I: II.5.25-82) lost about half of its lines. And any potentially obscure allusion was either excised or explicated with ges- tures. The result was a brisk, straightforward, often boisterous production that ran through each part of the play in approximately two and a half hours. If there were few shocks or surprises, there was also lit- tle seriously to disappoint, and one came away with the sense of a workmanlike, entertaining romp that dwelt on the more colourful scenes and confronta- tions, but left the cultural background largely to fend for itself. The lack of a clearly defined historical context was a distinct disadvantage to this approach. The sense that the Percies and their rebellious allies spoke for an older, northern, warrior aristocracy against the up- start “politician” Henry IV, was occasionally implicit in the production — the “rebel” nobles wore a kind of clannish, lived-in, linen body armour reminiscent of the rebel forces in Star Wars episode IV, for exam- ple, while the royal party and their allies sported im- maculate, black leather in the style of Darth Vader (costumes were designed by Virgil C. Johnson) — but this was not drawn out consistently. As a result the grievances and motivation of Hotspur in particular remained somewhat under-developed. This was an opportunity lost in a play which invites audiences to consider the merits of two competing world-views personified by the two young Henries. The focus throughout this production was on the individuals at the heart of the conflict (King Henry, Hal, Hotspur, Falstaff), rather than the values they stood for, in a version of History retold as an engag- ing soap opera or US TV Home Box Office mini-se- ries. The symmetrical patterning to the play, with Hal poised between two potential “fathers” and two pos- sible futures, was evident only sporadically. There was a neat visual parallelism between the first tavern and court scenes, for example. As Hal and Falstaff argued over their respective accounts of the events at Gadshill, the latter tried to pursue the young Prince around the large inn table, seeking unsuccessfully to head-off his nimbler adversary first one way then the other. When, subsequently, Hal confronted the King around the same property table, he was again pursued by the older man, but this time he could not escape, either physically or morally, and was finally thrown against the table by the angry sovereign. Such moments hinted at the wider substructures of the narrative, but again, the sense that they were part of an overarching directorial vision, a design that was more than the sum of the play’s various parts, was lacking. The production was at its most memorable when it was least reverential to the text. Part I began, for example, with King Henry (David Lively) lying in a large bed, centre stage, while amplified screams and shouting filled the auditorium. He woke up and turned to see the crown, resting on the pillow beside him, seeping blood across the white linen. He held his hands to his ears (a pose he would reprise at the end of Part I) and yelled “Richard”; at which point there was a blackout. When the lights rose again the pillow was unstained and the noise had ceased. With sure-footed economy the production showed us a king troubled by bad dreams and guilt as an effective prelude to his opening line, “So shaken as we are, so wan with care”. These productions are revivals from the Swan thea- tre 2000-2001 season, and Peter J. Smith and Greg Walker’s comprehensive review of the originals [Cahiers Élisabéthains, 59 (2001), 108-13] can be read alongside this one for an accurate and incisive sum- mary of action. I have therefore decided that this review should function partly as a chronicle of the choices and textures particular to this incarnation, and partly as a reflection on the way the trilogy works and how it fits in both with the evolving RSC and as part of its Complete Works Festival. Nevertheless, I was lucky enough to see Michael Boyd’s Henry VI trilogy the first time round, and its extraordinary at- mosphere does deserve a second visit in print. Entering the theatre to get going on Part I, we sit down to a forbidding sight: a chrome-black coffin hangs above the (thrust) stage, which recedes back into a monolithic, concave, rusty metal wall. At the wall’s centre an equally rusty, cylindrical, industrial- looking tower consisting of three vertical sections (in ascending order: double doors, a platform, and a spiral staircase) stretches skywards. The ambience is bathed in a fittingly dull ferric-oxide glow and punctuated by erratic, doomy kettledrum beats and the noise of ghostly, metallic whines. In short, the vista that Boyd and his designers have created seems about as inviting as the gateway to hell. And indeed the production quickly makes it plain that what we are looking at actually is the gateway to hell — which means that they’ve got it about right. The first figure to enter is a king. He is dressed in white as he de- scends the spiral staircase high above the stage floor. He is statuesque yet burdened, as though the weight of the crown were pulling him down to our level. He stops when he gets to the platform but he doesn’t look at us. After a momentary pause he disappears. The doors open and weeping women process more or less in unison onto the stage although they seem isolated from each other and from the world in their grief. Through the backlight and dry-ice that pour through the doorway the silhouetted figure of the king comes into view. He walks through the women towards us but nobody seems to see one another. He is pallid and leaden-footed. He is noble, sad, alone, careworn and pitiful. He is also dead. As he approaches the stage front a trapdoor opens to the deafening scream of the battlefield ghosts who are now snatching at his robes. A shaft of brilliant light shoots upwards while clouds of dry-ice billow from the hell-mouth towards which he is now being in- eluctably drawn. He falls to his knees, vomits blood into the pit in an agonised convulsion as even his ghost gives up the ghost. He is seized upon by the spectral revengers and dragged from view. The play begins. As the real-world characters enter, the coffin con- taining Henry V’s body follows his ghost into the pit,

44 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 now merely an earthly sepulchre, and Gloucester’s (Richard Cordery) eulogising, “What should I say? His deeds exceed all speech; / He ne’er lift up his hand but conquerèd” (I.1.15-16), apparently straight- faced on the page, has here a dire, ironic emptiness, although the character doesn’t intend it. The nether- world is a constant presence throughout the three productions; the souls of the dead mingle and collide with the bodies of the living present, and, despite the latter group’s rhetoric and their confidence in the functioning of the institutions of temporal power, they are being watched, controlled and waited for by those who died in vain. Antony Bunsee plays a character listed throughout as “The Keeper”, liter- ally a warder of the Tower of London when one is required, but more frequently the keeper of the aforementioned hell-gate, Satanesque in appearance in long scarlet cassock, who is sent out to usher in the dead. Given the body count over the three plays he certainly has “old turning the key” (Macbeth, II.3.2), and thus becomes not so much a conceptual add-on to the plays as one of their central figures. In this respect, Boyd’s trilogy is of course looking ahead to Richard III, in which the idea of the revenging dead was Shakespeare’s own. In developing this thematic link with Richard III so early on, Part I is clearly inviting us to imagine a coherent sequence. Yet the Henry VI plays are less about a king than they are about families. This is ini- tially raised in the scene between York (Clive Wood) and Mortimer (Roger Watkins), the latter wearing the paper crown that the former will be made to wear as he is murdered in Part III, and fully realised in York’s inheritance-claim scene in Part II, brilliantly illustrated with the use of stones to make the stage an ad-hoc genealogical map. The sequence culmi- nates in the dominance of the individual, realised in the one-man-show that is Richard III, and Richard’s (Jonathan Slinger) growing influence on the audience in Part III hints at this, mirroring York’s role in Part II, although in York’s case the motivational force is the greatening of the family name. Family ties bind him, keep him human, feed his ambition, and the plays honour this impulse in their structural distribution of character. Rutland’s (Alexia Healy) death in Part III, here the most painfully horror-steeped depiction of an infanticide I can imagine, proves the limit of the moral terror the father can endure, while part of the horror of his son Richard’s plans is that they are divorced from any allegiance, even, ultimately, to himself: “And if I die, no soul will pity me. / And wherefore should they, since that I myself / Find in myself no pity to myself” (Richard III, V.5.155-57). Richard’s isolationism in Richard III means not only that his power cannot sustain itself, but also that the play functions in an entirely different way from the tribal conflicts of its antecedents. Boyd describes the trilogy as being like The Sopranos in his programme notes, drawing a not entirely fanciful parallel with the Mafia and its complex and ruthless family-centric behavioural codes. If that’s the case, then Richard III is Scarface, displaying the same will to power of an individual who perceives himself to be (in Tony Montana’s impoverished, immigrant mentality as in Richard’s recognition of his deformity) “scarce half made up” (I.1.21). I remember leaving the theatre in 2001 exhilarated by the company’s realisation of Richard III, but unconvinced that it could be made, as a simple result of its structure, to function as Henry VI Part IV. However, then as now, Richard’s move solus into the spotlight with the parting shot “Now” at the end of Part III confirms the intention. If Richard III needs some cajolement to behave as a continuation of the Henry VI saga, Part I likewise needs to be somewhat bent into the shape of its opening chapter. Considered by many scholars to be a collaborative prequel to what we now know as Parts II and III, it certainly bears some of the hallmarks of being both an afterthought and the product of a different imagination. It is something of a portmanteau affair; part political back-story to the family blood-feud that will dominate the sequel parts, and part historical fantasy and hymn to plain- spoken English heroism. As Talbot (Keith Bartlett) and his son (the fittingly named Lex Shrapnel) are depicted carving their way through northern France towards Joan of Arc (here played by a spirited Katy Stephens, who doubles as Margaret) without the slightest sense of irony or ethical complication, you feel not only that whoever wrote it wanted its audi- ence to whoop and cheer in jingoistic unity, but also that such monochrome elbow-jogging is antithetical to the designs of Shakespeare’s other histories, and certainly to those of Parts II and III (Nashe’s asser- tion that 10,000 spectators wept to see the death of Talbot, “the terror of the French”, may well in fact suggest his authorship). Part I is also, again in con- trast to the other parts, and, indeed, with the rest of Shakespeare’s plays to my mind, partly comprised of disconnected episodes, like the dramatic non-se- quitur that is Talbot’s effortless subordination of his murderous hostess, the Countess of Auvergne (Ann Ogbomo) in Act II Scene 3, a hollow scene that seems to do little more than suggest Talbot as a sort of proto- medieval James Bond figure. Jarringly, it is followed on the heels by the Temple Garden scene (II.4) and the transition is almost schizophrenic; the play’s lan- guage and narrative coherence shift up several gears as the growingly factious nobles (Clive Wood as York, Patrice Naiambana as Warwick, Geoffrey Streatfield as Suffolk, and Nicholas Asbury as Somerset) circle each other around a totemic rose-covered metal lad- der; history becomes a glass through which we see darkly, a family struggle, a mesh of complex private reasons that are unavailable for simplification, dis- entanglement, or, as Shakespeare’s audience would

The production, while frequently employing extra-textual action to darken the mood and make the play behave a bit more like the other two, also realises that its crude impulse to trade in national stereotypes is ripe for satire. Boyd thus adorns his French courtiers (John Mackay, Jonathan Slinger, Forbes Masson and James Tucker) in flowing silks, pearl earrings, and Duran Duran-style wigs as a check rather than an act of corroboration. Apologists and anti-collaborationists prefer to view Part I as an apprentice piece, with Shakespeare on a vertiginous learning curve as the trilogy progressed. If it was indeed a prequel, its lengthy sojourn in France (20 out of 27 scenes) was either a strategy to heighten the pathos of Part II’s la- ments at the loss of English power in France, or as a salve to its (and Part III’s) bitter and unredeemed es- say on decentred English factionalism (the redemp- tion, of course, comes in the shape of Richmond at the end of the then not-written Richard III). Whatever view we take on this play, it is an undeniable rarity to see it produced in full by a major company. In the parts where it fails to talk politics in the fractured, polyvalent voice of the others, it is the production which seeks to complicate matters, and while the bipolar employment of light and dark to knock the play into line does result in an uncertain dramatic direction at times, it is a credit to Boyd that he holds firm on his commitment to the project and does not choose to elide. The first half of Part II has a relative sense of stasis after the Boy’s Own exploits of Part I, with the stage bathed in harsh, bright, light, and character move- ment kept to a minimum, yet the post-interval Cade rebellion fills the senses with its horror-circus frivol- ity, with Cade (John Mackay) lowered on a trapeze to halt the execution of an audience-member dragged onto the stage by two demonic clowns (Jonathan Slinger and Forbes Masson) to the strains of a calyp- so tune. Indeed, just about anything and everything that can be lowered or dropped from a ceiling makes an appearance at some point in the trilogy: red and white feathers, ropes, ladders, trapezes, cages, lights, steel platforms, people, and gilt picture frames (also containing people, in a brilliantly witty take on the painted miniatures that were sent in advance of ar- ranged royal weddings). Talbot and his son are also brought back from the dead, and given a grave and devastating dramatic and symbolic function. Gone are the noble English heroes of Part I; Boyd, in Parts II and III, uses them to oversee the narratives the way Kyd used Don Andrea and Revenge in The Spanish Tragedy, making them malign symbols of waste and regret, spectral pariahs caught between worlds, and, at times, physical arbiters over the affairs of the living. This is most keenly realised when they act as Suffolk’s (Geoffrey Streatfield) executioners in Part II, the culmination of an astonishing conceptual realisation of the play’s action. It begins with Beaufort’s death, his failure to lift his hand as a sign of mute repentance explained by the fact that his arms are being pinned to his deathbed by Gloucester’s ghost. As he expires he is hoisted up to the ceiling on a rope while the bed breaks open and lets out a blast of brilliant light and the Charon figures of the Talbots, who use it as the Stygian ferry upon which they murder Suffolk. The sequence is truly alarming, and provides a potent prequel to their reappearance in Part III as the interchangeable son who has killed his father and the father who has killed his son, again, a metaphysical motif which neatly sidesteps the clunking, improbable literalism of the play, works strongly to make the trilogy cohere as a sequence, and lends a semi-religious quality to Henry’s vision. In fact, barely an entrance, exit, or rudimentary piece of stage business goes by without it being turned into a thoughtful, symbolic tableau of some sort (as in Part III when time and place fall mo- mentarily away to allow Richmond — also played by Lex Shrapnel in a fertile echo of Young Talbot — and Richard, dressed in white and black respectively, to stand face-to-face while the former exits and the lat- ter enters). The 2000-2001 company has been largely replaced, although certain members reprise their original roles. Keith Bartlett exudes indestructibility as he tackles the part of Talbot for the second time in his career (probably the first actor since the 1590s to do so), while Richard Cordery’s magnificent Gloucester makes a welcome return, as does Clive Wood’s ef- fortlessly brilliant York. Chuk Iwuji is drafted in to play the part of Henry, taken by David Oyelowo in the originals. There was much speculation at the time about the casting of Oyelowo, a black actor, as the king in a predominantly white court. The popular consensus seemed to be that given the astonishing power of his performance the choice was colour- blind. The casting of Iwuji here however seems to imply that it was conceptual, though it is hard to say what the concept is. Patrice Naiambana is also draft- ed in to play Warwick, a role taken by Geff Francis in the original staging, another black actor of a similar physical stature. Is this an attempt to re-emphasise an idea, a refusal to compromise on a vision, or a way of trying to ensure a second success through a meticulous recreation of the original blueprint? If a verisimilitude is being suggested it is a strained reading as Warwick and Henry’s characters could not be more different. Iwuji brings a disarming, pain- ful dignity to his portrayal of Henry as sacrificial lamb of God, moving between childlike innocence and explosive pathos as he immaculately steers his character through the difficult journey of three dis- parate plays’ worth of suffering, while Naiambana rarely, if ever, steps outside the narcissistic mindset of his character as all-action hero, as impervious to

Jonathan Slinger, a performer natu- rally inclined to mischief, who cannot help himself from emphatically knocking back his scenes in one go as the Bastard of Orleans and Cade’s lackey, in Parts I and II respectively, brings tremendous nu- ance to his Richard. I had predicted him having a field-day when he finally got to don the prosthetic hump, but in the event, through sheer layering of motive, detailing of insecurity, naïve, wounded reac- tions to insults, and the borderline psychosis of his “Ay, Edward will use women honourably” soliloquy (III.2.124-95), he bravely and successfully rebuked the tempting idea that every aside and set piece that Shakespeare bowled the character’s way was an un- derarm delivery. So, why the revival (something the RSC have only rarely done before with Shakespeare productions)? In the context of a festival it is straightforward enough to begin with a pragmatic reason: if you’re going to do everything Shakespeare wrote then you’re going to need to do the Henry VI plays at some point. If you really want to assert the strength of the enterprise as a whole then you don’t want any token renderings that imply that there are dark recesses in the canon which, frankly, are as unrewarding to watch as to perform. If you also happen to have had astronomical success with these unfamiliar plays in the recent past, in an uncut rendering of all three that just happen to be the brainchild of the current Artistic Director, then why on earth would you even consider a re-design? So rare is it that all three parts are done in full at the same time that the fact they are the centrepiece of this leg of the Festival seems to place more faith in them as famous productions than as great plays. But Boyd’s initial triumph was as much about an avowal of policy as it was an artistic achievement. His first tetralogy came at the fulcrum of Adrian Noble’s reign as Artistic Director, when he decided to overhaul the company, do away with the repertory system, shrink the staff, and bring in star actors for West End-type blockbusters. It came to be wistfully remembered as the last great gasp of an ensemble company at its most successful, as a coda to the principles upon which the RSC was founded. To place this revival so much at the forefront of this historic festival must surely be read as a statement of future intent. Boyd is not just cashing in on past success, or saving the company the thankless bother of producing these obscure plays afresh; he is show- ing the way, leading by example, making good on his promises of a return to company spirit and ensemble casts, and in taking the financial risk of backing these plays to fill a house the size of the Courtyard he is putting his money where his mouth is. In its continuing engagement with the histories, the RSC’s work has been at its most distinctive; and it is where the original aims and aspirations of the RSC, as originally formulated by Peter Hall in the early 1960s, have been most clearly articulated.1 That is Robert Shaughnessy in Representing Shakespeare. Alan Sinfield, in Political Shakespeare, describes these original aims as “Shakespeare-plus- relevance”, and quotes Trevor Nunn on Peter Hall, who “insisted on one simple rule: that whenever the Company did a play by Shakespeare, they should do it because the play was relevant, because the play made some demand upon our current attention”.2 The first big move Boyd is planning for the RSC after this festival is to produce all of Shakespeare’s histories himself, including this cycle. Looking at his Henry VI trilogy, one cannot help feeling that the search for “relevance” does not necessarily stretch out into the wider political world. These produc- tions are not crude parallels of Iraq, or New Labour, or whatever, but focussed explorations of the pos- sibilities of theatre more broadly, and of a particular company specifically. Steadfastly medieval in its aes- thetic, with the fourth wall down — although in this case it is the wall that leads to the fifth dimension; anything that is imported into this world certainly doesn’t come from ours — Boyd’s trilogy is a magnif- icent achievement, as much now as it was five years ago.
