S etting The Tempest, not in some tropical paradise but in a frosty outpost in the Arctic Ocean is a brave move by any standards. Literalist critics will no doubt object to the way Rupert Goold’s produc- tion plays fast and loose with the text (“marmosets” and “scammels” in the frozen north?); but the play’s sense of its own natural history is already rather shaky to begin with (marmosets and scammels on the same island as bears and tortoises, and all within plausible drifting distance of Naples?). What is gained by this unexpected paradigmatic shift more than outweighs the occasional awkwardness that it creates. The move to the ice-fields enables Goold to evoke a whole new mythology for the play, com- pounded in equal parts of Inuit mysticism and the later scenes of Frankenstein, which is every bit as relevant to its themes as the more conventional al- lusions to colonial exploitation of the West Indies. When Prospero (Patrick Stewart) evoked the aid of his servitor spirits, he did so in the manner of the Inuit shaman, chanting over a brazier, dressed in a coat of furs with a high collar made from the skull of some bizarre sea-creature. When Ariel (Julian Bleach) disturbed the courtier’s impromptu banquet (III.3) in the guise of a Harpy, he did so by erupting, keening and covered in gore, like the monster in Alien from the stomach of a slaughtered elephant seal that the spirits had dragged onstage on a primitive sledge. The atmosphere evoked by such moments, and reinforced by Giles Cadle’s often breathtaking sets (of which more in a moment), turned watching the play into a wholly new theatrical experience. (And, literalists might note, the new setting also made much more obvious sense of the need for all that chopping and carrying of wood, which can appear strangely moribund and fetishistic in more temper- ate settings.) Central to the most successful aspects of the pro- duction were Cadle’s stunning sets, which were, from first to last, innovative and eye-catching with- out being either fussy or intrusive. Indeed, during some of the production’s not-infrequent longueurs they offered the eye welcome relief from the slow moving action on stage. The opening image set the scene for what was to follow. A screen bearing a giant sketch of a short-wave radio covered the stage. As an amplified weather forecaster’s voice announced a warning of imminent “severe storms”, the radio- dial became the rotating arm of a green radar screen plotting the storm-clouds’ approach, and then just as quickly became a transparent porthole through which the opening scene was played as if within the cabin of a ship. Meanwhile the rest of the screen filled with a projection of heaving waves and billows. The same device, covered with images of a swirling snowstorm in which vague figures could occasion- ally be made out, was used to mark the transition between subsequent scenes. The “indoor” exchanges between Miranda and Prospero were set in a ramshackle wooden cabin, in which the walls were jarringly misaligned as if contorted by the movements of the ice. In the final Act, set near Prospero and Miranda’s cabin, the most impressive of the sets represented the building as if shown from the outside, a huge shell of planks and logs balanced at a precarious angle against a central promontory of ice as if it had been flung there by the gale. The combination of the promontory upstage centre and various levels of raised ice-sheet, also upstage, with the back-lit screen and subtle effects of white and blue lighting (by Paul Anderson) effec- tively conveyed the idea of vast expanses of ice and sea against which the action was played out. Had the performances matched the invention and innovation of the design, this would almost cer- tainly have been the most exhilarating Tempest seen in Stratford for a long time. Unfortunately they did not. It was almost as if, having lavished such thought and effort on the look of the production, Goold and his team had no energy left to expend on the acting. Consequently many scenes were merely ponderous, static read-throughs of the relevant lines without either compelling characterisation or engaging ac- tion. The first scene was perhaps the best example of the mismatch between design and performance. The idea of the “porthole view” of the crew during the storm made for an engaging spectacle, but the actors gave little sense of either danger or excitement

When she asked a question she put her hand in the air, and when referring to something in the physical world she frequently pointed directly at it with outstretched arm as if identifying it for the dimmer children at the back of the class. Such a young woman might plausibly have lived almost all of her conscious life with only her father’s example upon which to model herself. Her courtship with Ferdinand was conducted in a crisp, matter-of-fact manner that frequently left the young prince, played by Nick Court, bewildered. When she offered him her hand, “with my heart in’t” (III.1.91-92), she grabbed his and shook it with businesslike brusque- ness, throwing the remainder of the line (“And now farewell / Till half an hour hence”) over her shoul- der as she strode purposefully offstage. In the final scene she was so taken with the “brave new world” (V.1.186) of the Italian courtiers, that she could not refrain from stroking and hugging each of them in turn, returning repeatedly to caress the discomforted Antonio (Ken Bones) as he tried to deal with the re- alisation of his brother’s survival. Bleach’s Ariel was a splendidly unearthly, icy spir- it in keeping with the polar setting. With whitened face, spiked hair, and a greatcoat that stretched to the floor, he stalked about the stage at a funereal pace and slid unnervingly through doors and along walls like a cross between Shockheaded Peter and Max Shreck’s vampire in Murnau’s Nosferatu. When the latter final- ly released him from his bondage, he stalked slowly away into the shell of the cabin, leaving Prospero, unaware that he had already left, to deliver his final “fare you well” (V.1.322) to an empty stage. Stewart delivered the final request that the audi- ence’s applause should set him free from the actor’s obligation to please as a tentative query rather than a command, and gave a rather mannered gesture of relief when, a split-second later, the applause duti- fully rang out. O’Connor * Henry VIII, directed by Gregory Thompson for AandBC, Holy Trinity Church, 26 August 2006. T here is a reason Henry VIII, also known as All is True during Shakespeare’s lifetime, does not stand amidst the luminous company of Shakespeare’s better known/studied/performed texts. While there are several memorable speeches throughout the play, there is a distinct lack of a gripping central character to drive the play onwards. Due to the lack of a strong central figure, the play’s scenes feel loosely connect- ed by the sequence of events. Writing in collaboration with John Fletcher, Shakespeare was treading on dangerous ground when approaching the subject of monarchs in England’s recent past. The prudence needed for this situation could have forced the playwrights’ hands to err on the side of caution, henceforth delivering a play that does not delve into the more intriguing elements of the historical figures. Anne Bullen’s fall from grace and eventual execution does not get a mention, nor does the eventuality of Henry’s many more wives. Such is the play’s lack of prominence that the most famous event in its performance history does not come from an amazing production, or an intriguing characterisation, but the mishap of 20 June, 1613, when a cannon shot set fire to the thatched roof of the Globe and destroyed the building. Yet, in spite of the play’s inherent flaws, director Gregory Thompson’s production combines clever staging, good acting, and an amazing setting in Holy Trinity Church. The audience sits on either side of the nave on risers while the action takes place in the narrow space that runs between. The audience’s proximity to the acting space serves the play well as audience members are literally drawn into the action by being selected to hold props and serve as members of the jury. The only complaint against the traverse staging is the sprain in my neck gained from the ping-pong effect of watching action on either side of my pe- ripheral vision. But the production is an outstanding example of site-specific work where the content of the play, staging, acting, and surroundings harmoni- ously blend together. The execution of Derek Hutch- inson’s Buckingham and the pitiful death of Corinne Jaber’s Katherine of Aragon resonate with the nearby tombs that silently witness the action. Most fitting of all, the history behind the large stones of the church acts as a witness to the outcomes of the religious bat- tle being waged in the play. Thompson’s sumptuous staging makes much of the drama’s central structure. Henry VIII dramatises the descent of three central personalities of the Tudor court and the narrowly escaped descent of a fourth. The play’s language and content deal conspicuously with the traditional Elizabethan cyclical image of Fortune: whatever goes up eventually comes down. The dramatisation of each of these falls plays out in a similar fashion: each character is tried and given time to articulate their defence. Each demise is em- bellished by a scene of pageantry and courtly drama that is greatly aided by the grandeur of the space. It is due to this emphasis on spectacle and display that Henry VIII found favour on the lavish Victorian stage. Thompson makes much of the spectacle writ- ten in the play. Fireworks interrupt Wolsey’s feast as Henry’s disguised revellers swarm into the church. During their entrance, one of the merry company memorably performs a lewd dance with one of the female audience members in the front row. The pag-

Byrne’s Henry VIII delightfully battles unsuccessfully with his violent nature: roughly bursting out lines and jos- tling Katherine. Corrine Jaber, playing the doomed Queen Katherine, carries off a dignity and grace that adds gravitas to her defence of the legality of her marriage. Anthony O’Donnell deliciously plays the malignant Cardinal Wolsey, carefully navigat- ing the high rhetoric that constantly spills from his mouth. Jem Wall as Cranmer, Derek Hutchinson as Buckingham, and Cara Kelly round out the excellent cast of actors. The one ill-advised casting choice is the casting of a real, wiggling, infant Elizabeth, played by a very young Alice Wood. During the scene where the Arch- bishop of Canterbury delivers an obsequious nod to Queen Elizabeth, the baby girl is held preciously within the arms of her glowing mother. While the in- fant was sweet and adorable, the presence of a child on stage so mesmerised the audience that they were distracted from the speech which completes a good staging of a faulty play. Liisa Spink * The Two Gentlemen of Verona, directed by Guti Fraga for Nós do Morro and Deborah Shaw for Gallery 37, The Courtyard Theatre, 27 August 2006. F or one night only the Courtyard Theatre was host to a fascinating international collabora- tion. The RSC’s Complete Works Festival brought together groups of young people from the drug- ridden favela, or shantytown, of Vidigal, Brazil, and from Birmingham’s Gallery 37, to present possibly Shakespeare’s earliest play. This was a production inspired by Cicely Berry’s long-standing involve- ment with Nós do Morro (Us from the Hillside), a theatre group started by Guti Fraga in the mid-1980s, which has since developed into a well-respected professional company sponsored by the Brazilian Ministry of Culture and the national oil company, Petrobras. Gallery 37 also assists young people who have had a challenging start in life to realise their artistic potential — offering the opportunity to work as Apprentice Artists alongside professionals. As Deborah Shaw emphasised in her programme notes: “It takes a hormone-fuelled group of young people making their way in a difficult world to re- veal the themes of friendship, love and forgiveness at the heart of Shakespeare’s early — possibly first — play”. With a limited joint rehearsal time of only two weeks, members of the Brazilian troupe had welcomed Gallery 37 actors into their midst to pro- duce a bi-lingual “work in progress” of great energy, verve and musicality. The young and energetic cast really put their hearts and souls into it. The large Chorus became walls and statues around which the main action took place, Crab (a human actor) threw himself around the stage, the young Birmingham actors rapped and sang from the balconies and the whole production was over in two hours without an interval. This was a very musical adaptation, with song and dance numbers bridging the gaps and replacing some of the dialogue — Valentine and Thurio’s spar- ring of wit, for example, became a sing-off in a make- shift ring. The Brazilian actors spoke Portuguese while the Midlanders sang in English, but the two languages meshed well. Where this play suffered — and this is by no means their fault — was in the setting. In many ways, we would have rather seen this in the Dell, or an out- door space, as we think it would have worked better in the less formal atmosphere, where the actors (who interacted with the audience throughout) could have really let themselves go. On the Courtyard stage, on the set of the Henry VI trilogy, it almost seemed to reinforce the lack of rehearsal time and budget. There were a few negatives: the Gallery 37 singing couldn’t be heard over the maturer voices of Nós do Morro (even when right next to them, as we were in the front row) and some of the movement pieces, while very nice to look at, did not seem to have much purpose and thus served as a distraction. This company had come from one of the rough- est shantytowns in Brazil, teamed up with a few Birmingham youths in an outreach theatre group and created something in just a couple of weeks that stood up against many of the Festival’s better-funded professional productions. In the post-show talk, the Birmingham teenagers expressed their appreciation and admiration for the Brazilians, a respect that was built despite the fact that neither group spoke the other’s language. As a community project, even for the actors, this had clearly achieved its purpose, and the audience equally enjoyed themselves. Kath Bradley and Peter Kirwan

53 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL * Troilus and Cressida, directed by Peter Stein for the Edinburgh International Festival in association with the RSC, Royal Shakespeare Theatre, 4 and 5 September 2006, back and front stalls. P eter Stein had assembled an excellent cast for his production of Troilus and Cressida, including Shakespearean veterans Paul Jesson (Pandarus) and Ian Hughes (Thersites), both of whom have won ac- claim for their intelligent handling of Shakespearean text. However, rather than allowing actors of this calibre to be creative and thus discover nuances through the synergy between performer and text, Stein delivered a production that, through the direc- tor’s ineptitude, left the actors floundering and un- able to produce their best work. The reason for this was Stein’s obsession with recreating John Barton’s 1968 production of the play, a fact he willingly ad- mitted in an interview in The Times published just prior to the production’s opening at the Edinburgh Festival: “In 1968”, Stein stated, “I saw his [Barton’s] version of Troilus in Zurich and was deeply im- pressed, and certain elements I have now copied”.1 Clearly, Stein has not learned that what is created by a specific group of actors and leads to a successful, if controversial, production cannot be recreated by a completely different group of actors, particularly not in a different era. Instead, he stripped away the lay- ers of anti-war and feminist readings that have been part of recent performance history and left a vacuum in their place. Stein’s main focus seemed intent on objectifying bodies. Rather than fleshing out characters, Stein and his costume designer (Anna Maria Heinreich), often left both Trojan and Greek in identical pseudo-Greek warrior apparel, the design of which seemed influ- enced by the decorations on extant classical pottery. The actors were, therefore, left showing acres of arti- ficially bronzed flesh, which had the effect of making them look like young Greek gods. Stein stated in the interview that “If you modernize the war, you kill the play”. However, the idealization of the actors by dousing them in bronze body paint, creating the appearance of male beauty, had the opposite effect — it glorified war by putting those men doing the fighting on a pedestal and suppressing the reality of bloodshed. It made nonsense of the anti-war debate that is a critical part of Shakespeare’s play. How can you give enough weight to lines such as “…there’s many a Greek and Trojan dead” (IV.7.97) or “The fall of every Phrigian stone will cost / A drop of Grecian blood” (IV.7.106­–07) when the soldiers themselves have been walking around near-naked in battle with- out a splatter of blood on them? Whereas Stein’s objectification of the male form was frequently camp — as when a half-naked Paris leapt onto the stage during the battle scenes in Act V, pausing centre stage to shoot an arrow from his Cupid bow, eliciting titters from the audience — the objectification of Cressida’s body had an altogether different emphasis. While the men — as well as the other women — were attired in ancient Greek-de- rived costuming, Cressida (Annabel Scholey) was dressed in a contemporary pink dress, which clung to her figure, emphasising her obviously unfettered breasts and giving a glimpse of her thigh as she moved. Cressida’s body language was one of seduc- tion: combined with her costuming, there was little doubt that the angle the director had chosen was that of the “wanton” of the pre-Juliet Stevenson era, rather than a victim caught in a war and having no control over her fate.2 This was particularly evident in Stein’s staging of Act III Scene 2, especially in the early part of the scene. On “the will is infinite and the execution confined” (78-79), Cressida and Troilus (Henry Pettigrew) took a step towards each other and, as they were about to embrace, Cressida broke coyly away, playing games with Troilus’ desire for her. When Pandarus re-entered (95), he brought with him a mattress, which he laid centre stage. Stein placed Troilus and Cressida facing each other, with the mattress separating them for the next portion of the scene and on “Boldness comes to me now, and brings me heart” (109), Cressida knelt on the bed, dragging Troilus to the foot of the bed on “Prince Troilus, I have loved you night and day / For many weary months” (110-11). Pandarus re-entered again and proceeded to make up the bed, having brought on bedclothes with him this time. On Cressida’s at- tempt to leave the room (135-38), Pandarus stood in the upstage doorway blocking her way. As they re- sumed their positions opposite each other, kneeling on the mattress, Pandarus voyeuristically watched them plight their troth from just outside the door. Cressida grabbed Troilus’ hand and guided it as he let the top of her dress fall to her waist, leaving her breasts exposed. She then undressed Troilus, as they said their lines to each other seductively. Pandarus fully entered the room again on “Go to, a bargain made” (191) and, interrupting the couple’s fondling of each other, he took their hands and completed his speech with “Say ‘Amen!’” (199). The couple fell to the bed and re-commenced foreplay as Pandarus covered them with a sheet on “And Cupid grant all tongue-tied maidens here / Bed, chamber, pander to provide this gear!” (205-06). Stein’s staging of Act IV Scene 5, on the other hand, was a bizarre mix of a wanton Cressida walking seductively into the Greek camp coupled with a shadow of dormant violence directed at Cressida. The violence, exemplified by Menelaus wrenching her coat off her and grabbing her in anger, seemed more of a nod towards the post-1985 stage tradition of Cressida being in dan- ger of being raped by the men in the scene than a

54 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 choice firmly rooted in that tradition, particularly as Cressida seemed to enjoy being kissed, particularly by the virile Patroclus (Oliver Kieran-Jones). Stein seemed to stifle the onstage relationships the characters should have been forming, much to the detriment of the cast and the acting. It felt to this reviewer as though Stein had essentially told his cast where to stand but had not been interested in the in- terpersonal relationships on which theatre is based. In a play that is as filled with dense political argu- ment as Troilus and Cressida, this lack of interpersonal relationships retarded the production. Stein’s staging decisions also hindered the actors. For instance, his blocking had them frequently playing scenes so far upstage that it distanced them from the audience, making the actor-audience relationship almost untenable. An appalling set design (by Ferdinand Wögerbauer) culminated in a moment where two halves of a tent, each on opposite sides of the stage, suddenly glided together to make Calchas’ tent for Act V Scene 2. Unfortunately, the gliding, combined with the salt and pepper pot tops with which both halves of the tent were capped, gave it more than a passing resemblance to a pair of copulating Daleks as they slid together, which the titters of the audience around me at that moment seemed to confirm. Stein’s textual additions bordered on the inexpli- cable. The prologue was spoken by Calchas (Arthur Cox), into whose speech was inserted the name of his character: “An actor in the part of Trojan prophet Calchas”. Having Calchas name himself within the prologue did nothing to illuminate the fact that he is Cressida’s father and that he had her removed from Troy, nor did it mention that he was a traitor to Troy, now living in the Greek camp. The most egregious addition came at the end of the play during Troilus’ final speeches. Cressida was brought on by Pandarus shortly before the lines which end the play in the Quarto began. “Look upon thy love”, Pandarus tells Troilus, pointing to where she was standing. Cressida moved toward Troilus as he told Pandarus, “Hence, broker-lackey” (V.10.33), and she knelt in front of her former lover and pleaded, “Forgive me”. Troilus threw her to the ground and she spent the final few moments of the play sobbing downstage. Troilus’ fate was to be killed by the Myrmidons who had emerged over the top of the upstage rake at the beginning of Pandarus’ final lines. Having Cressida extra-textually beg for forgiveness was an abysmal decision that made a mockery of Shakespeare’s text. While a re-evaluation of the play in performance is not necessarily unwarranted, Stein’s execution made this impossible. Frank Marcus titled his 1969 review of John Barton’s production “A play for our time” and remarked, “Troilus and Cressida (Aldwych) is very much in tune with our times. It is anti-heroic and anti-romantic”.3 What was shocking — and relevant — in the 1960s is not shocking now and this Troilus just looked silly. Stein neither successfully re-created Barton’s production nor gave us his own interpreta- tion by using Barton’s production as a starting point. The theatre programme contains a quotation from Peter Stein: “I dedicate my work on this show to John Barton whose 1968 production influenced my vision of the play and my desire to do it”. Unfortunately for actors and audience, this production demonstrated that Stein should have left Barton’s production well alone and created a Troilus and Cressida for today instead of trying to copy a production from nearly forty years ago. 56 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 Measure for Measure, directed by Peter Hall for the Peter Hall Company, The Courtyard Theatre, 15 September 2006, centre stalls. T here is absolutely nothing to complain about when watching Hall-directed Shakespeare. Equally there is hardly anything to enthuse about. Hall’s Shakespeare is a particular brand which is instantly recognisable by its conspicuous tradition- alism. The iambic pentameter is slavishly observed with aural end-stopping so that a metronomic regu- larity too frequently masks the emotional variety of the speeches (in Measure for Measure this is all but fatal when Angelo is lacerating himself for his inability to overcome temptation), costume and setting are natu- ralistic and usually of the period (here the Viennese court was gorgeously attired in full Jacobean dress), stage blocking is textbook… and tedious (every sin- gle set piece was delivered from down stage centre) and the play’s vivacity is rendered subservient to its weighty matter (though Michael Mears struggled valiantly to infuse his oleaginous Lucio with a comic spirit, he remained imprisoned by the production’s doleful solemnity). Hall excels in eliciting some bril- liant performances, his overall production values are superlative — setting, lighting and playing are con- summately assembled — but one still exits the thea- tre without any sense that he has managed to interro- gate Shakespeare’s writing or, in the case of Measure for Measure, address its dark implications. Hall’s theatre, without any new line readings, emotionally detached and flawlessly assembled, is at once the most capable and the most anodyne in contemporary theatre and this is all the more frustrating because of the quality of the artistic team, the acting company and the tenseness of this, one of Shakespeare’s mean- est and most disturbing plays. James Laurenson’s Duke typified both the achieve- ments and the shortcomings of Hall’s overall ap- proach. He entered (and made his final exit) from the central aisle between the front stalls, the only charac- ter to move among the audience at any time — a la- The women were attired in tops and skirts over which they donned crazy farthingales — the first indication that this was a world turned upside down. The Courtesan also wore a farthingale but over the briefest of one-piece swimsuits. As the action grew increasingly fraught, so the male costumes and the female hair bands became loosened and discarded. The set comprised a pack- ing-trunk (so much of this play is about journeys) togeth- er with a number of wooden palettes arranged around the stage and occasionally upended to form drawbridg- es — one for the front door of Antipholus’ house, the other the entrance to the Abbey. The production, which began with Egeon facing a firing squad, made much use of rifles; at one point nearly everyone onstage was pointing a rifle at everyone else. This, coupled with Emily Bull’s bright sunny lighting and the baggy loose- ness of the clothing, made the production faintly remi- niscent of the Spanish Civil War. Given the internecine feuding between two sets of brothers, this seemed not inappropriate. Two or three of the performances could have done with more polish but generally, the company handled the rapid and farcical elements of the play with assurance. A nice final touch occurred after the re-entry of Antipholus of Syracuse following the exit of the two Dromios. In silence he held his hand out and seemed to catch the water droplet to which he had referred earlier with such pathos: “I to the world am like a drop of wa- ter / That in the ocean seeks another drop” (I.2.35-36). In a near-reprise of his earlier gesture, this time his hand closed confidently round the water drop and the lights faded. We were thus neatly assured of the daft plot’s happy outcome. Peter J. Smith boured symmetry suggesting that the action opened and closed with him. Seated on a gilded throne centre stage, he clenched his fists and grimaced, his roaring sigh and conspicuous gestures making him typical of the age of Garrick. As soon as he began to speak, Laurenson’s cracked voice and nervous com- mand demonstrated his mastery of the role and one could not help but sympathise with him for having to gesture his way through the initial moments: it ill behoves an actor of such subtlety to have to person- ate so crudely his character’s instabilities. One felt here the heavy hand of Hall — pushing lucidity to the point of overemphasis — and one wished that the actors had been given freer rein to hint at rather than explicate the text’s darker corners. Kevin Rigdon’s thrifty design comprised a black curved screen upstage with half a dozen doors let into it. As the Duke discussed the responsibilities of office, six courtiers entered and stood upstage of his throne pondering his every word. Identically bearded and cloaked (costume was by Trish Rigdon), they looked like the delegates at the Somerset House Conference. Power, as the stage picture so forcibly demonstrated, was about ordering the court as well as the state; little wonder that the Duke was feeling the strain. The doors in the screen were left open and shuttered with vertical bars so as to provide a series of secure alcoves. Behind each grille, a whore was seen displaying her wares, not dissimilar to the windowed prostitutes in modern Amsterdam. Later on, in a neat piece of staging, we watched Isabella and Mariana circulate round the back of the screen, appearing and pausing at each opening in turn so that there seemed little to choose between the pro- fessionalisation of sex workers and the cultural and financial security brought to Mariana by the bed trick. For the play’s public scenes — the Duke’s tri- umphal return and Claudio’s being paraded through the streets in sackcloth with the word “fornicator” daubed front and back (“Fellow, why dost thou show me thus to the world?” [I.2.96]) — a further series of doors were opened up on first storey level to reveal

57 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL additional peering populace. But for all its capacities to offer a variety of stage spaces, the set was, for the most part, used with the doors sealed, the only vari- ety being the flying in of three large grilles to effect the prison setting. Moreover, the action of the plot seemed statically rendered as nearly all of the play’s key speeches — Angelo’s tortured soliloquies, the Duke’s final summation, Pompey’s comic set piece on his fellow inmates, Isabella’s appeal for justice — were delivered from the same “hot spot” at the centre of the stage, lit in pyramid beams which then broadened out to take in the rest of the stage (lighting was by Peter Mumford). This was an effective device but by the fifth or sixth time it was used, its power began to fade. Likewise, the exclusive use of black and white costume (at court anyway, the lowlife scenes used shades of brown) readily established the doleful and authoritarian ethos of the court but of- fered the production nowhere to go. It was as though Hall established a convention — colour, stage posi- tion, aural lineation — which then tyrannised the design, blocking, speaking: nothing became remark- able amid this Viennese gloom. The casualties of this unimpassioned but entirely proficient approach included the whole social range of the play. The trial of Froth (Malcolm Ridley) and Pompey (Teddy Kempner) by Escalus (Barry Stanton) felt routine. Even the usually fireproof role of Elbow (played here by an unusually youthful Edward Bennett) came and went without the comic vibrancy usually generated by the hopeless consta- ble’s mangled language. The Duke’s encouragement of Claudio’s contemptus mundi (Claudio was played by Ben Turner) was entirely lucid but without any sense that the Duke was being pained and sincere or hypocritical and manipulative or anything else, come to that. But the greatest casualties of the pro- duction’s unadventurousness were the scenes be- tween Andrea Riseborough’s Isabella and Richard Dormer’s Angelo. These exchanges are capable of arousing the most violent reactions in the audience — outrage at the Deputy’s iniquity, sympathy for the powerless position of Isabella, admiration for her resilience or even a shiver of disbelief when we learn that her brother is of less value to her than her purity: “Then Isabel live chaste, and brother die: / More than our brother is our chastity” (II.4.184-85). It was testament to the analgesic nature of Hall’s direction that none of these moments caused the slightest audience discomfort. Clearly rendered and without any impediment to full comprehension, this was a production which lacked any of the danger of Shakespeare’s menacing text. The final moments of Measure for Measure have become notorious since feminism has taught us that the Duke’s overture to the novice Isabella may be less innocent than a proposal of marriage. Indeed, like the final long speech of Katherine in The Taming of the Shrew, these closing moments often function as a barometer by which we may evaluate the production as a whole. This is certainly a crux in any contempo- rary performance and it offered one of the few really interesting moments of this particular production. Textually, the Duke approaches Isabella twice in the final scene. Following the revelation of the disguised Claudio, the Duke perhaps cynically capitalises on Isabella’s ecstasy: “If he be like your brother for his sake / Is he pardoned; and for your lovely sake / Give me your hand, and say you will be mine. / He is my brother too. But fitter time for that” (V.1.484- 87). About fifty lines later the Duke recapitulates this proposition: “Dear Isabel, / I have a motion much imports your good, / Whereto, if you’ll a willing ear incline, / What’s mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (527-30). The first assignation followed the unmasking of Claudio and the passionate embrace of brother and sister. As the Duke awkwardly, and in the full public eye, rendered his proposal, Isabella clung tightly to the body of her brother, her very fin- gers screwing themselves into the cloth of the loose habit that he wore as security that she would not be separated from him. A long and uncomfortable pause followed while the Duke waited for her re- sponse… none came… and so his “But fitter time for that” followed as an embarrassed change of subject. The Duke busied himself with the perfunctory trial and condemnation of Lucio before returning to the subject of his union with Isabella. Ingeniously, with his reiteration, Hall had Laurenson’s tone change from appealing and indulgent to rigorous and stern. As the Duke declaimed his second approach, the axi- omatic certainty of the chiastic formulation, “What’s mine is yours, and what is yours is mine”, rendered his proposal a fait accompli; there was no room for dissent here — this was the pronouncement of an ab- solute authority, not a request for her assent. Indeed, as he delivered the line, the Duke looked directly in front of him, avoiding her response completely. He didn’t wait for an answer — he didn’t need to. As he exited through the audience, she was left, still clinging to her brother and her eyes narrowed — in resignation? in panic? in hatred? The chilling nature of this closure demonstrated that Hall can still work wonders with Shakespeare’s text. It was all the more disappointing that the only such moment came in the production’s final seconds. Peter J. Bloody complicated isn’t it — like a Shakespeare play!” The text’s “Fidele” (Imogen’s sobriquet) became “Ian”. Cloten attempt- ed to grope Imogen: “’Gis a feel of yer arse, yer dirty little moo!” and as Posthumus and Iachimo swapped insults, the former reprimanded the latter: “You can’t say ‘cock’; this is Stratford-upon-Avon”. The RSC’s booklet for the Complete Works Festival describes the production unmistakably as “a new adaptation”; yet, in spite of the warning that this was to flout expectations, I overheard a patron at the interval demanding his money back: “This simply is not Shakespeare”. And yet, peculiarly, it was. Russell Jackson has claimed recently that Throne of Blood by Kurosawa is his favourite cinema Shakespeare; it “has no lines of Shakespeare in it at all, but is one of the great films since it finds its own language and could only have done this starting from Shakespeare”. 2 Similarly, Kneehigh’s perform- ance text eschewed Shakespeare’s (except in a couple of places) and yet, in its narrative thrust, its adroit ex- ploration of the range of emotions in Shakespeare’s play and its reckless mixing of genres (which caused Dr Johnson to condemn Cymbeline as “unresisting imbecility”), it was immediately and unmistakably Shakespeare. What really distinguished this produc- tion was its constant inventiveness, much, though not all, comic. With eight actors (Cymbeline has over thirty speaking parts) and a single set, Kneehigh told Shakespeare’s epic story with clarity and good humour. Michael Vale’s set comprised a large cage constructed from scaffolding within which a set of stairs ran up to a musicians’ gallery. The cage was festooned at the beginning with flowers, children’s toys and Xeroxed photos of the young princes and a spray-painted cardboard sheet which read “REMEMBER”. This impromptu shrine was assem- bled by a number of hooded youths who pegged the mementos to the cage bars on what we learnt was the anniversary of the princes’ kidnapping. A dis- traught Cymbeline (Shepherd) entered to tear down the pointed reminders of his missing sons before re- turning to the inside of the cage to receive a calming injection from his queen (Emma Rice) who wore a nurse’s watch-brooch pinned to her dress. The cage signified the withdrawn, grief-stricken Cymbeline at the same time as it functioned physically to im- prison Imogen (Hayley Carmichael) and exclude the banished Posthumus (Carl Grose). As the couple swapped tokens of remembrance, she gave him her ring. Posthumus, non-plussed, felt into his jacket to see what he could give her in return. Finding his pockets empty he considered his watch, reluctantly undoing its metal bracelet while casting his eyes heavenwards as though to say, “I really didn’t want to part with this but…”. It was a fine example of the company’s resourcefulness and a demonstration of the way they injected the poignant narrative with wit. A similar moment followed when, sailing away from Britain in banishment, Posthumus’ voyage was enacted by having him step into the bows of a small clinker-built hull which was then suspended on braces from his shoulders. He was thus able to walk around the stage rocking the boat up and down as though upon the waves. For good measure he was given a bowler hat from which sprouted seagulls on the end of wires. Fish, similarly, were attached to wires which protruded from the hull and appeared to swim alongside it. For the scenes set in Rome the downstage wall of the cage was hinged open. What in Britain was claustrophobic and closed was wantonly exposed in Italy. Lights flashed and pounding club music set the scene in one of the capital’s brothels. Iachimo (Róbert Lučkay) entered as a caricatured Mediterranean spiv — deckchair-striped shirt undone to reveal hairy chest and crucifix, tight white chinos, handlebar moustache and huge sunglasses. As the hopelessly lost and self-deprecating Posthumus entered, puz- zling over an Italian phrasebook, Iachimo offered him a selection of whores in tiny dressing gowns and long black wigs, each of whom promised in broken English a particular perverted specialism: “You want me to turn you round? You want boy? Girl? Piggie — oink oink?” Posthumus was shocked by this ap- parent degeneracy and we subsequently saw him providing English lessons to the whores with them singing in unison, the kiddies’ ditty, “The wheels on the bus go round and round…”: this was a company with a well-honed sense of humour. Iachimo’s visit to the English court necessitated that he be accompanied by his trunk. In order to manage this, he pulled a female member of the au- dience up on to the stage and, following her assist- ance, he was able to kiss her, give her chocolate and present her with his card — “it has my mobile. You

59 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL call me, OK?” Later on, as Pisanio and Imogen made their way to Milford Haven, they struggled between the stalls of the theatre, forcing audience members to make way. There was a constant sense of the pres- ence of the audience and their participatory role in the humour of the production. As the gross Cloten (Craig Johnson) lolled against the bars of the cage in his jacket, shirt, tie, shoes and socks, but no trousers, his splayed legs and tight under-pants offered a clear prospect of his manhood — “Get a load of that, Mrs”, he called up to the gallery. As Iachimo offered Imogen the letter from Posthumus, he teased her with it, holding it out of her reach and then thrusting it between his legs so that she was forced to approach his crotch in order to retrieve it. Kirsty Woodward’s gangly Pisanio in maid’s outfit and jam-jar glasses was all but overwhelmed by this Italian stallion and visibly panted and fluttered in his presence. As he attempted to wrest the watch from the sleeping Imogen, he stood her on the bed and shook her up and down so that it slid from her arm. Resting her back on the bed, he realised that he had put her body on top of the watch so that all seemed to have been in vain. These kinds of comic touches, constantly inventive, were self-consciously designed to appeal to the audience’s understanding that what they were seeing was something situated between the fiction of Shakespeare’s story and the technical know-how of improvised comic performance. One of the most explicit examples of this ludic quality was the representation of Lucius. An illu- minated screen with the face of Caesar was wheeled on. A member of the company stood upstage of it and pushed his hands through two holes in the screen. While a voice-over sought the outstanding instalments of the tribute, these arms expressed, in gestures, the increasing impatience of the ambassa- dor. But as Cymbeline (and then Cloten) defied the Roman, the screen was swivelled through a hundred and eighty degrees to reveal an image of Caesar’s face contorted with rage. The arms reappeared and the gestures became obscene! The knowing comedy of the sequence typified the company’s deft irony. Perhaps most outrageously, as Imogen received the letter in which Posthumus had instructed Pisanio to kill her, she read out an imperfect copy: “‘Thy mistress, Pisanio, hath played the trumpet in my bed’ [pause… looks bewildered…] but I can’t even play the trumpet!” Pisanio hastily corrected her, “STRUMPET!” The latter half of the play is considerably darker — Cloten is murdered, Imogen wakes next to a head- less corpse, the Roman army invades, the queen dies. For all its knockabout elements, the production managed to shift to this more sombre tone without undercutting the pathos of the play. In particular, the funeral of Fidele (Ian) was accompanied by the sing- ing of “Fear no more the heat o’th’ sun” (IV.2.259). As Dominic Lawton’s Brother (the princes were not separately identified) wailed the lyrics of the song he became increasingly loud until he was howling while the others around him maintained the melody. This was a powerful rendition of the lament and intensely moving. The battle between Britons and Romans was played out on a board game with counters of yellow and red signifying the opposing sides. As Cymbeline manipulated the troops with his walking stick in the manner of a general’s battle plan, ordnance flashed around him. Finally the weird spectacle of the play was also represented. The appearance of Jupiter had Lučkay hoisted to the top of the cage in full military uniform. His feet were passed into stirrups from which was suspended a huge white sheet. This was gathered up behind him so that he appeared against a white backcloth which served to mask the set up- stage. Yet, fittingly, the final moments reverted to the familiar comedy to which the company was so ac- customed. The panto dame entered again remark- ing that she had long been in possession of a mys- terious key. This just happened to fit the box which Posthumus had received following the descent of Jupiter and it was opened to reveal a number of se- pia photographs of children and parents. There was much cooing and ahhing as the characters identified siblings and parents. As Cymbeline’s children were reunited, two double beds were trucked downstage. Into one climbed Posthumus and Imogen. Into the other climbed the two brothers. As they snuggled down, a quilt was hoisted upstage. Embroidered onto it were the words “Good Night” — a fitting conclusion which signalled the restoration of family harmony within the play and the company’s polite farewell to those of us beyond it.
