Lynette Hunter and Peter Lichtenfels, eds, Shakespeare, Language and the Stage (London: Arden, 2005), 105. * Timon of Athens, directed by Adrian Jackson for Cardboard Citizens, Shakespeare Centre, 27 October 2006. T he Royal Shakespeare Company invited London- based Cardboard Citizens to Stratford to present their distinctive brand of socially and politically minded theatre as part of the RSC’s Complete Works Festival. Founded in 1991, Cardboard Citizens has acquired a reputation for producing innovative, site- specific, forum theatre. The company works with, and partly consists of, homeless people, refugees and asylum seekers. No surprise therefore that Adri-

60 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 an Jackson chose Timon of Athens and its tale of debt and despair to highlight issues surrounding social exclusion and dispossession. Writing about his per- formers’ personal experiences of homelessness and enforced exile, Jackson explained in a programme note that “in this constituency, more than one Timon is to be found, with his or her own variations of the story, all in their own way tales of surviving (or not) the wafting hand of Lady Fortune”. This produc- tion presented extremes of social experience, and the interjection of real-life stories of misfortune and fallibility helped to inject Shakespeare’s play with an engaging emotional quality, which it has often been judged to lack. The company chose to open their production with an interactive induction; spectators passed through a mock-corporate conference registration procedure before entering the first of two performance spaces within the building of The Shakespeare Centre. Spectators were asked to fill in lapel badges with their names, job titles and salaries. Emblazoned with the conference logo — “Quick blows of fortune: where there’s Will there’s a way” — the badges served, in the corporate style, to “consolidate” as well as isolate members of the audience, whilst in a theatrical spirit they suggested the power that Shakespeare’s plays can have on the social conscience of societies. The first of the two performance spaces was deco- rated befitting a training event or corporate gather- ing; actors dressed in business suits mingled among the crowd, initiating introductions, creating an at- mosphere of professional networking. The hum of the crowd was silenced as one of the performers took to the stage, microphone in hand, and asked: “Who is the most powerful person in the room?” Actors volunteered the names of a number of spectators, until eventually Shakespeare’s name was suggested. Shakespeare’s power to motivate and speak to us all was elaborated upon via a flip chart whereby Henry V was declared “a work about leadership”; 2 Henry IV “about managing teams”; King Lear “about family management and inheritance guidance”; The Tempest “about working with multicultural teams”. This list of plays ended with Timon of Athens, which was de- scribed as “a play about life from the perspective of someone with no wealth and no friends”. As if to verify this claim performers began to present the opening dialogue between painter, poet, merchant and jeweller. After the poet’s allegory upon Fortune the audience was told that “change is a body blow”, and should any audience member have the misfortune of being mugged on their journey home, then their lives (like Timon’s) would be overturned in an instant. Contextualising frame complete, the audience was ushered into a larger performance space, under the fatuous instruction “we need to get out of here” — “we need to change” — “we need to move!” This second room contained a thrust stage adorned with two television screens, a flip chart, a table and some chairs; sitting by the side of the stage, the performers remained visible at all times, often mak- ing entrances and exits through the audience. The conference atmosphere was maintained throughout the production; scenes from Timon of Athens were performed and then playfully discussed with actors making references to Marx and the stock market with the use of flip charts and power-point presentations. In the spirit of this innovative approach, the interval was termed a “breakout” session, allowing the audi- ence “20 minutes networking time”. The performance style was simple, rough, direct and involving. Timon’s first entrance was made through the audience, with Simeon Moore’s suited Timon shaking hands with spectators as he made his way to the stage. Moore presented a balanced por- trayal of Timon in the opening scenes, resisting the temptation to oversimplify Shakespeare’s depiction of this enigmatic character. While Moore strove to present a plausible character rather than a caricature, Timon’s extreme vanity and naivety were gradually exposed through satirical stage-business; for exam- ple, when he was confronted with his own portrait, Timon’s exclamation that “The painting is almost the natural man” (I.1.157) was granted a wonderful comic irony as he delivered this line standing before a glassless picture frame. Despite Timon’s obvious prodigality, humanitarian sentiments such as “’Tis not enough to help the feeble up, / But to support them after” (I.1.107-08) were emphasised in this pro- duction, which focussed audience sympathy upon unaccommodated man at every turn. Timon’s two feasts were contrasted successfully both in design and performance. At the first banquet, lines of Ferrero Rocher chocolates piled pyramid high were positioned around the borders of the stage, whereas at the second banquet the guests were only presented with plastic bottles of water. As his rage built Moore’s Timon removed the cap from one of the bottles, and holding the bottle to his groin, splashed water over his guests as though urinating upon them. From Timon’s vengeful second banquet onwards, Moore was joined in the portrayal of Timon by two other actors. As Moore tore off his clothes and raged through Timon’s tirade, Albanian born Agron Biba gave a foreign-tongued performance which accen- tuated Timon’s frenzied passion. Dividing Timon’s hymns of hatred between two actors emphasised that such feelings of bitterness and despair are common. The blending of languages and voices at this point helped convey the universality of Shakespeare’s themes, and this notion was reiterated when Mahdad Majdian became the production’s third Timon. Dividing the role between three performers brought variety to a part that has often been labelled

61 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL monotonous and uninspiring. In the theatre, Timon’s sudden shift from philanthropy to misanthropy can bewilder audiences and lead to a lack of engagement with the protagonist’s plight; presenting Timon’s extreme transformation in this innovative manner discouraged audiences from searching for credible characterisation, and focussed attention upon an unbridled outpouring of emotion. While three performers spoke Timon’s lines, the production also presented numerous other Timon figures. Video diaries by two homeless men were screened to break up the scenes of Timon’s self-exile in the woods and at intervals throughout the pro- duction performers related their own personal ex- periences of a harsh and heartless money-obsessed society. As a parallel to the scenes in which Timon’s servants look to raise loans from his friends, one of the performers spoke of his personal misfortunes and the complete lack of support from his friends when he fell upon hard times. Tales of this kind served to stamp this company’s sense of ownership on the play, and also served to smooth over some of the rough presentation of Shakespeare’s scenes. Technological effects featured alongside the com- pany’s style of unsophisticated theatrical presenta- tion. The company used tables and chairs to create the different locations required in the play. The neat tableaux of the opening scenes gave way to a chaotic design for Timon’s scenes of self-exile; tables and chairs were overturned and stacked upon one anoth- er, giving the impression of a rundown squat. Titles for the scenes, analogous to media headlines, were written large upon two television screens upstage: Timon’s lavish banquet in Act I Scene 2 was titled “corporate entertainment”; the trial scene in Act III Scene 5 was titled “Governance”; and Flavius’s la- ment in Act IV Scene 2 was titled “Redundancy”. Pro- jection was used inventively and helpfully at various other points: Timon’s debts rolled down the screen as they were detailed in the conversation between the senator and Caphis in Act II Scene 1, and then in Act IV Scene 3, Timon’s tirade appeared in type on the screen, exploding into bold capitalisation as he declared “Therefore be ABHORRED / All feasts, societies, and throngs of men” (IV.3.20-21). Writ large on the television screen, Timon’s words assumed the significance of a misanthropic manifesto, rather than the wild ramblings of fortune’s fallen darling. The sound of waves underscored the final scenes and at the production’s finale the performers looked out to the audience as video footage of a man walk- ing into the sea, and finally disappearing underneath the waves, played on the screen upstage. The final image suggested a modern moral tale told not by an idiot, but by a drowning man; a fate we are all born into, it seemed to be suggested, if society does not offer a helping hand. Nick Walton * The Winter’s Tale, directed by Dominic Cooke for the RSC, The Swan, 4 December 2006, first gallery, left. A s we entered the auditorium, the haut monde was enjoying champagne as the five-piece dance band played A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square and, ominously, Let’s Face the Music and Dance (“There may be trouble ahead…”); the glitter balls glittered and the spangles spangled. It is a new year party for 1953. The sixty or so members of the promenade au- dience, many of them very young, wandered among the suavely tail-coated gentlemen and their immacu- lately made-up and coutured ladies with those taut, frozen smiles which aristocrats are seemingly trained to adopt shortly after birth. Reflecting the austerity of the period, and in spite of the party trappings, the scene is near monochrome, with subtle use of light and shade and, hanging spotlit above the centre of the stage, a clock: time — as John Barton once said — the most important word in Shakespeare. Dominic Cooke had said in a pre-show discus- sion that his decision to perform the play in prom- enade was based upon the idea that the trial and the sheep-shearing festival scenes could incorporate the audience as participants who would then watch the consequences of these episodes on the upper stage. Cooke’s idea succeeded only partially. The prom- enade audience, of which at least a quarter on the evening which I attended comprised uniformly clad pre-teens, was something of a distraction to those in the galleries, especially when the actors were stand- ing at gallery level on the enormous, curving ramp which swooped from high stage-left, around and down to floor level in the centre of the auditorium. My notes made at the time mention the “bewildered up-turned faces of the little yellow T-shirted army” and the “confusion of the prommers” as actors ap- peared from unexpected places. It may be, of course, that Cooke was seeking confusion and bewilder- ment, in which case he succeeded. The upper stage was not so much proscenium arch as a letter-box, a place for tableaux and set-piece ex- planation, eschewing the promenade device. It was placed high and remote, an interesting counterpoint to the intimacy which the groundlings enjoyed with the cast, but it served mainly as a welcome break for the gallery audience to focus undistracted upon the words and the fine cast. Starting the play first in the austerity and Cold War paranoia of the early fifties and then moving forward sixteen years to the “summer of love” of the late sixties was a device which worked well. The Winter’s Tale is a play about time: a cycle of life, death and resurrection, which in this production is placed in a context which is easily recognised. Changes in mood and time were expertly judged and manipu- lated throughout the play by Chris Davey’s light-

62 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 ing design, which not only directed the audience but also managed partly to obscure the rather ram- shackle look of the over-large aforementioned ramp. The lighting was at no point tricked-up or gimmicky but was subtle and dramatic as the story demanded. The cast wore the clothes of the periods, with some exceptions, and the effect was to impress rather than to distract. Here again, the care which had gone into the costume design and supervision was contrasted by the careless set. The apparel certainly proclaimed the man in the case of Richard Moore’s Old Shepherd who looked as if he had walked on stage straight from one of the local south Warwickshire village pubs. Similarly, Paulina, played magnificently by Linda Bassett, looked as though she had arrived on stage after giving the departmental managers at Fortnum and Mason a hard time for missing the quail’s eggs off her last order. As the mounting paranoia of Leontes began to leak like acid into the confident and satisfied court, and as the alarm and bewilderment of Polixenes and Hermione took hold and the atmosphere became colder, the tension was palpable. Speeches began to be muttered into dark corners and eyes began to fail to meet eyes. Anton Lesser’s Leontes became dis- turbingly Hitleresque as he spat out his words and hissed and stamped and terrified the groundlings at his transformation. Kate Fleetwood, as Hermione, every inch the Emperor of Russia’s daughter, carried off the role of the noble heroine with a soft-spoken mesmerising calm which the Swan Theatre’s excel- lent acoustics enabled all to hear. Nigel Cooke added a third temperament to the mix with well-judged Polixenes, a role which is meat and drink to an actor of his capabilities. Cooke plays both wronged guest and stern parent with the square-jawed tenacity ex- pected of a public school royal whose ordered world has suddenly taken a turn for the worse. There is great sadness as Paulina brings the babe to Leontes with the intention of calming his rage, only to find that he commands her husband Antigonus to abandon the “bastard by Polixenes” (III.2.81). Ben Onwukwe’s voice (I wrote “baritone bell”) was magnificent, and it was a sad moment when we saw the last of him as he exited pursued by the most fear- somely realistic bear ever seen on a stage. Sixteen years later the world is much changed. The band is now playing Catch A Falling Star and California Dreamin’ ; there is an abundance of colour as the flowered idyll of Bohemia becomes flower- power and the summer of love of the late sixties. We meet a psychedelic Autolycus, cleverly interpreted by Richard Katz as a mock-serious and mercurial chancer, possibly under the influence of some highly illegal substances, but who comes good eventually. The young promenaders at last were quiet and hyp- notised by his funny and sometimes almost sinister presence and his West Yorkshire vowels which sin- gled him out as someone from another world. Katz dominated on stage and was a fine and memorable Autolycus. In this, the second “phase” of the play, there were some marvellous exchanges between Florizel and Perdita (Simon Harrison and Michelle Terry), who lilted their way with a touching naïveté and an unfailing determination never to take their eyes off each other. In the tender moments the poignancy was captured brilliantly by the delicate verse-speak- ing which produced a total silence in the auditorium only noticed previously in the court scene. The sheep-shearing feast started with a truly novel and exciting entry of all the revellers, a barrage of sound and colour and some memorable dancing, in- cluding an African tribal rhythm which had the audi- ence roaring and clapping. This part of the play was, however, dominated by Polixenes in some memora- ble exchanges, particularly with Perdita after she had greeted him and Camillo “with rosemary and rue”. There followed a haunting discussion of art and na- ture which ended with a gift of flowers from Perdita to Polixenes, where the passing of time is again em- phasised as she says “…these are flowers / Of mid- dle summer, and I think they are given / To men of middle age. Y’are very welcome.” (IV.4. 106-08.) In the last act of The Winter’s Tale it is notoriously difficult to pitch the various forgivenesses, reconcili- ations, resurrection and contrition at an appropriate emotional level. In this production it was something of a mixed result but, judging by the tears in the audience at the end of the play, an objective was accomplished. The recognition of Autolycus by the gentlemen in the penultimate scene of the play was as comforting as his own acceptance of his basic good nature, as he greets the entrance of the Old Shepherd and the Clown with “Here come those I have done good to against my will” (V.2.123). The final scene would have worked perfectly on the Swan’s traditional apron but seemed rather awkward with the promenade configuration. There was little joy and warmth here, but rather a taut and formal, disciplined renaissance of Hermione. Nevertheless, her “You gods, look down…” (V.3.123). was so touchingly spoken that it was impossible not to be affected. Leontes finally realises the waste of sixteen years and the great value of the dependable Paulina, redoubtable to the end. This production can be seen as a triumph of ex- emplary acting, lighting and music over the restric- tions and distractions of the promenade auditorium especially when there is no way of pre-selecting the promenaders to exclude school parties of youngsters who have no idea what is going on. It was able to succeed on the basis that there is no substitute for good actors who are well directed and at home in their roles — proven beyond doubt here. David Hill

63 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL * Hamlet, directed by Dov Weinstein for Tiny Ninja Theater, The Cube in the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, 31 October 2006, rear. W ithin the auditorium of the Royal Shakespeare Theatre is a box-like studio constructed out of scaffolding with a plain black floor and simple lighting rig. The RST’s seating capacity of nearly two thousand is thus reduced to a mere one hundred. Scaling down is the Cube’s keynote and so there was something particularly appropriate about a version of Shakespeare’s most weighty play reduced to fifty- five minutes and “performed” by a cast of plastic Ninja figures each measuring about fifty millimetres in height. The principal mode of presentation involved Dov Weinstein playing all the roles with a variety of in- tonations — Laertes was a lisping New Englander, Fortinbras Sylvester Stallone, Ophelia a piping teen- ager and so on: he “do the [play] in different voices”. While performing each role, Weinstein moved a plastic figure across his hand, or manipulated them within two white box sets with the aid of a pointer. These box sets were projected via a pair of endoscop- ic cameras onto two large screens above Weinstein’s head. The tiny Ninjas were thus rendered, if not life- size, then at least visible! It took about five minutes for the novelty to wear off but, that said, there were a number of innovative and illuminating produc- tion choices. For instance, the part of the player king was taken by a plastic ear; Ophelia’s drowning was staged by having her upended in a glass of water, and, eerily, the Ghost of Old Hamlet was a close-up of Weinstein’s mouth. As he opened his lips to speak, he revealed a tiny black Ninja clamped between his teeth. When the ghost reappeared in the closet scene, it was a drawing of a Ninja on a piece of transparent plastic sheet, so that we could see the other figures through it. But the most effective moments were when the dolls apparently addressed us — as Gertrude and Claudius attempted to persuade Hamlet to “cast [his] nightly colour off” (I.2.68), they looked directly into the camera so that we were cast as the prince and saw Denmark through his eyes. Hamlet’s racked emotions were conveyed by having the camera trem- ble or turn away. The device was repeated as we hid behind the arras along with Corambis (in the post- show discussion, Weinstein mentioned that Q1 was the easiest version to cut down since it was the short- est text in the first place). By placing the camera be- hind a hole in the curtain, we peeped through to see Hamlet and his mother arguing. Suddenly the sharp pointer came through the tear and the camera angle suddenly shifted through ninety degrees as though we had sustained a fatal injury and fallen to the floor. These novel moments provided the production with a sense of comedy deriving from seeing a familiar play in a fresh light. The friendly and informal post-show discussion confirmed the sense that this was a comedic diver- sion rather than theatre which was taking itself too seriously. When one audience member enquired which non-Shakespeare plays Weinstein would like to tackle, various suggestions were put forward — Waiting for Godot or, perhaps even more outra- geously, Oklahoma. We’ll have to wait and see… Peter J. Smith * Pericles, directed by Dominic Cooke for the RSC, The Swan, 23 November 2006, right circle. H ow does a director accommodate the notorious implausibilities and textual challenges of a play like Pericles? The tribal robes worn by Gower as he introduced the action indicated this production’s solution: he was portrayed as a type of griot, a tradi- tional storyteller who would relate the play’s fairy- tale dimensions in an oral tradition. This allusion perhaps served also as an apology for the text’s cor- ruption; authorship is inevitably obfuscated in a cul- ture of rhapsodic performance. There were overtones of Prospero, too, in Joseph Mydell’s Gower: thumps of his staff inaugurated the action at the close of each of his speeches. The African cadences of his voice meshed perfectly with the verse, and were beauti- fully attuned to the archaisms and understated wit of his narratorial interventions. The audience thronged in promenade around him — the ground floor seat- ing having been removed — and this elision of the boundary between actor and audience reinforced the sense of a story engaging an impromptu assembly. The extensive redesign of the Swan’s interior was highly effective; the ground floor audience was an ambiguous, apprehensive component of each scene, and a wooden, crescent-shaped ramp leading up the gallery (its sinuous geometry recalling Berthold Lubetkin’s famous penguin enclosure at London Zoo) allowed characters to address circle spectators with unnerving directness. The attire and accent of Pericles (Lucian Msamati) echoed those of Gower, and were complemented by the haunting West African lullaby he sang at night in Pentapolis, framed by a doorway, bathed in a warm ochre glow. The melody clearly functioned as a salve; it recurred when Thaisa lay moribund in her husband’s arms. It expressed the yearning of a prince exiled from the home which yet sings within him, and indeed the production strove to relate the play to both the political vicissitudes of Africa and the fate of its exiles. The former part of this process was accomplished

64 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 with great skill, as contemporary resonances were invoked without being imposed. The corrupt Antiochus (Clarence Smith) was visibly modelled on Robert Mugabe; his desperate attempts to conceal the darkness within meant that his only remaining cur- rency was death. The starving people of Tarsus called to mind all-too-familiar images of famine. The throb of helicopters delivering food parcels deftly bridged the gulf between seventeenth-century drama and the present day, even if it did raise the question of why Pericles persisted in perilous sea voyages, given that air travel was a viable alternative. This nautical recklessness took Pericles to Pentapolis, where the production’s careful conjuring of cultural contexts seemed to dissipate somewhat. Pericles was discovered by fishermen whose voices hailed variously from Yorkshire and Wales; the later introduction of a Liverpudlian sailor suggested that a slightly lazy vocal shorthand for proletarian char- acters was in operation. The only indications that the scenes were set in Greece were the use of “Yamas!” as a toast and the presence at the banquet of an Orthodox priest. Simonides was played by Richard Moore, not as a Mediterranean patriarch, but rather with the timbre and aura of an ageing English roué, more Pandarus than Priam. The scenes set at his court were domi- nated by an extended staging of the contest in which Pericles wins Thaisa’s heart and hand. It was ren- dered as a pentathlon, and a succession of tableaux charted the stranger’s triumph over the clownish competition. Virtuoso use was made of the theatre’s reconfigured space, although it provoked the suspi- cion that it was these new spatial possibilities, rather than dramatic imperatives, that suggested the comic extrapolation. This passage of the production was hi- larious, but did threaten to drown the complex voice of tragicomedy in the hubbub of broad farce. The aftermath of the ensuing marine catastrophe saw Thaisa being resuscitated by Linda Bassett’s Cerimon, envisaged as a New Age alternative thera- pist rather than the traditional healer who might have been more appropriate to the production’s evo- cation of Africa. If the staging chose to stray from its initial cultural moorings, Marina did so against her will, and found herself in a lapdancing club appar- ently located in London. The production’s updat- ing of the action again felt uncontrived and highly effective during these brothel scenes, as it posited a continuity of piracy and today’s trafficking of sex workers or slaves. This uncomfortable suggestion constantly qualified the comic effects of Marina’s defiant morality. Her elevation of baboon over pimp (19, 203) acquired a new poignancy in the light of this reading; a yearning for her homeland was infecting her discourse. The geographical and cultural remoteness of the bawdyhouse scenes tended to isolate them from the rest of the production, and therefore to reinforce an awareness of the length of Pericles’ absence from the drama. The eventual reunion of father and daughter carried the usual, moving echoes of King Lear, with Marina’s height advantage over Pericles being a reification of the reversal of authority. It was, however, interrupted by Nigel Cooke’s rak- ish, jokey Lysimachus asking for Marina’s hand in marriage. Pericles’ consent provoked the apparition of the other father figures of the play — Antiochus, Simonides and Cleon. This intervention was both enigmatic and suggestive; it certainly added new emphasis to the exchange of women by and between men as a theme knitting together the play’s disparate episodes. Claude Lévi-Strauss famously regarded the incest taboo as amounting less to a prohibition than a promotion of marriage as a system of exchange in traditional cultures; Pericles was perhaps read here as staging a series of deformations of this foundational cultural practice, moving from Antioch’s deceitful riddle, masking incest, to sex trafficking as the ob- scene double of the marriage contract. The fact that Ony Uhiara doubled as Antioch’s daughter and Marina (and appeared as a silent, spectral presence in the tempest’s aftermath) evoked the mysterious idea that Pericles had perhaps found what he had originally sought, the object of his desire (and, perhaps, the desire itself) having undergone a perplexing metamorphosis in the interim. His poten- tial spouse came to be recast in the role of a daughter only for her to be assigned again to the role of wife for Lysimachus, the wheel having come full circle. While this interpretation is based on mere hints and hunches, it does perhaps reintroduce a sense of consistency that had become attenuated as the play’s episodic structure had drawn the production away from its initial grounding in a carefully realised Africa. This marital economy is fundamentally homo- social, with women being more or less objectified or fetishised. It is to a female goddess, however, that Pericles has to turn for the restoration of his wife, no longer a commodity but a miraculous gift. Diana’s lines were cut, and she was symbolised by an Egyptian statue. She represented less a celestial intervention than a return to Africa, and an end to ex- ile and wandering. The production, too, was restored to its founding locale and rationale, its geographical and stylistic meanderings — which were perhaps inevitable given the peripatetic narrative — having reached an end. This obtuse play had undergone a powerful reworking, driven by commanding central performances. It was suffused by a palpable sense of the inner song of loss and yearning that belongs to the stranger in a strange land. Neil Allan *

65 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL The Taming of the Shrew, directed by Edward Hall for Propeller Theatre Company, The Courtyard Theatre, 9 November 2006, front stalls, centre. I n the recent mockumentary, Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan, Sacha Baron Cohen, in his guise as the sexist, homophobic and anti-Semitic journalist, Borat, meets three New York feminists to ask them about the role of women in contemporary America. As he goads them with increasingly outrageous questions — should women be educated, should women have jobs, particularly in the light of the fact that a Kazakh government scientist has proved human females and squirrels have brains of a similar size? — we watch them bridle with po-faced expressions: one gets up to leave. As their frustrated attempts to explain the idiocy of Borat’s position are met with his laughter and scorn, they retreat into an exasperated annoy- ance which demonstrates both the contemptibility of Borat’s misogyny and their own dour self-seri- ousness. This is difficult comedy indeed; while the position articulated by the feminists is unassailable, one is deflated by their sour humourlessness. One simply cringes as Cohen goes in for the kill with predatory instinct: “Give me a smile, pussy cat!” In his direct challenge to accepted norms of political correctness, Cohen’s film asks larger questions about whom we can laugh at (at one point he deliberately mishears a dinner guest who is “retired” and refers to him as a “retard”). For too long, productions of The Taming of the Shrew have sentimentalised the rela- tionship between Katherine and Petruchio, allowing them to fall in love or at least come to a domestic understanding for their mutual benefit. With an all- male cast, Edward Hall bravely jettisoned any such mawkishness; this was a world in which women were no more than what this savage play depicts them as being — vehicles for the accumulation of money, land or political power. If Kate is not able to take her place in such a patriarchal order, then she will be beaten and starved until she complies. Impressive though this courageous reading was, the production repeatedly compromised itself; it was as though it kept losing its nerve and needed to show us that it did not really mean it. Given the severity of the feminists’ angry responses, Cohen deserves, if nothing else, a reward for bravery; Hall seemed to bottle out at the last minute, worried perhaps that a mainstream Stratford audience would not be able to accept such horror or darkness in the work of the town’s most famous son. Though this became a superbly cruel production, we started off on the wrong foot. Greeted by mem- bers of the cast as wedding ushers as we entered the theatre, we were handed the order of service and assured that “The bride’s on her way”. A group of ushers posed for a photograph which they asked a member of the front row to take for them, officiously instructing him on how to point the camera. Sly (Dugald Bruce Lockhart) sat stage centre in front of a tiered wedding cake, nipping at a hip flask to increase his Dutch courage. The bride entered: the inebriated Sly collapsed at the altar; howling, she rushed off. We had to get from this point of marital disruption through the lords’ proposed deception — persuading Sly he is an aristocrat — to the entry of the players, to Sly becoming Petruchio and the play proper begin- ning. This was something of a mêlée involving the entry of a company of commedia performers, several mirrored Narnia wardrobes and self-conscious and hackneyed consultation of the New Penguin edition of The Taming of the Shrew. This sequence was labori- ous and distracting and by the time we had reached Padua, the interrupted wedding and the screaming bride were distant memories. However, once we were under way, this rapidly developed into a striking (in all senses) production. Lockhart’s Petruchio was a good-looking, arrogant arsehole. In cowboy boots, tight red jeans and open red leather jacket, festooned with chains like some- thing from a Michael Jackson video, under which he wore only a chunky gold necklace, he was a swag- gering, macho, hairy-chested sexist bastard — slap- ping backs, swigging bottles, blowing fountains of white wine through his teeth, and conscientiously assaulting anyone within range. His wedding suit comprised cowboy boots, stetson hat (into which he relieved himself before putting it back on his head), a brown fringed jacket and a leopard-skin thong. Unashamed of his conspicuous wedding tackle, this was a cocksure groom. But as he took possession of his bride, the tone suddenly darkened. At “She is my goods, my chattels […] / And here she stands, touch her whoever dare” (III.3.101-04), Petruchio lashed out with his boots and kicked over the wooden seats around him. On the night I saw the play, one of the chair backs gave way and sent splinters of wood into the audience — there was nothing simulated about this violence. Petruchio grabbed Katherine (Simon Scardifield) by the face so that her expression was distorted by the force of his grip and led her pain- fully offstage. But in spite of the brutality of the script and the excellent central performances, the produc- tion, even at the points of greatest violence, such as this, generated huge audience laughter and for this, it only had itself to blame. The problem was that while the direction seemed convinced of the oppression and injustice of the play (in their programme note, Hall, and textual editor, Roger Warren, write: “Cruelty is built into the play: the abuse has to be taken seriously — and even the self-abuse”), this commitment to registering the des- potic patriarchy of Padua was undermined chiefly by the design. With the exception of Petruchio’s cos- tume which concisely hinted at his shallow macho

66 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 ego, the rest of the costumes were randomly comic. We were in a world of clowns and madcaps. Jack Tarlton’s Hortensio wore pink and purple trousers, a loud red striped tie over a blue-and-white spotted shirt. Tranio (Tony Bell) wore black drainpipe jeans, a white t-shirt, braces, a small leather cap and one studded leather glove. Tam Williams’s Lucentio was costumed in a stylised matador’s outfit — not quite the full suit of lights, but a large shoulder-padded cloak replete with tassels and braid. Every time he stepped forward, a blast of flamenco underlined his Iberian identity (though of course, according to the text, he is from Pisa). His later disguise as a scholar in subfusc included a spinning mortarboard straight out of a joke shop. The crazy variety of costumes, the mixture of styles and the weird setting (the action taking place beneath a highly wrought and multi- coloured chandelier), gave the appearance of a farce: the facetious gimmickry belonged to a set for The Comedy of Errors. Of course, Shrew can be directed as a farce, but the gravity of the domestic violence is then undermined; indeed, in such a setting, it is entirely out of place. Given this counterproductive tension between di- rection and design, the most successful scenes were those between Petruchio and Katherine. Scardifield’s Kate had the stuffing rapidly beaten out of her. The scenes involving Petruchio’s condemnation of the tailor’s efforts to make her a cap and gown dem- onstrated the darkness of Hall’s direction. Usually in performance, it is the tailor who is the butt of Petruchio’s ranting or thumps. Here, however, the tailor (Dominic Tighe) got off pretty lightly. As Petruchio attacked the gown and the cap, Katherine still wore them, so that his blows and rough handling were directed against her physical frame as much as the garments: her body was the object of Petruchio’s misogynistic rage. During these outbursts, Scardifield simply went limp: there was no fighting back; she submitted totally to his brutality. As Petruchio sat back at his dining table, his boot muddying the white table cloth, Katherina stood obediently at the other end, clutching the rags of her dress protectively to her body and trembling with cold and fear. Any displays of shrewishness, the banging of her sister’s nose in a cupboard door or the smashing of the lute over her tutor’s head, were consigned firmly to the past. Her brittle submission was total and irrevoca- ble. Yet, around this vicious domination, were wo- ven moments of oddly inappropriate comic business. Jason Baughan’s drunken Pedant, pretending to be Vincentio, sat aloft one of the wardrobes attempting to eat a take-away tray of noodles with chop-sticks; there were several Chaplinesque pratfalls and comic catches. Baughan’s Grumio got a buttock laugh by turning his back on the audience to reveal his trou- sers cut away and his legs swathed in fishnet stock- ings, his arse hanging out of a purple thong — but this all seemed ill-calculated and redundant, given the sombre tones of the central plot. Of course it is the long submission speech of Katherine, in the play’s final scene, that is the deci- sive test of any production and this was the finest moment. As the play makes clear, the verbs are im- portant here. Bianca is “bid[den]” (V.2.80) to come and the Widow is “entreat[ed]” (l. 91). Katherine, on the other hand, is “command[ed]” (l. 100). She entered and with a quiet humility asked Petruchio’s wish. He responded, “Go fetch them [Bianca and the Widow] hither” (l. 107). Just for a moment, Katherine hesitated but this was enough immediately to arouse Petruchio’s ire: “Away, I say, and bring them hither straight” (l. 109). The threat was clear: if she tarried, she would be beaten up. In the wake of this disturb- ingly public brutality, her submission speech was perfectly played. She delivered the speech into the middle distance, not daring to cast her eyes upon anyone, not daring to put a foot wrong. In utter obeisance to the thinly veiled threat of her husband’s fist, she larded on details of masculine superiority as though to defer her next beating. At Petruchio’s sick- ening “Why, there’s a wench! Come on, and kiss me, Kate” (l. 184), she looked to her father to intervene on her behalf; this was her last, pathetic attempt to seek the protection of another man. But the heart- less Baptista (Bob Barrett) simply cut away from her glance and looked approvingly to his new son-in-law who had taken this time-consuming daughter off his hands and she recognised, at the same moment as we did, that she was utterly lost. Given the power of this final scene, the closing frame once again blunted the force of the production. Sly was baffled to be told that this was but a play and his panicked expression to the audience as the light faded on him seemed little more than an attempt to compensate for the earlier brutality. Perhaps this was the “self-abuse” mentioned in the programme note but however we were meant to react to the prospect of Sly’s own insecurity, it felt like too little too late — an attempt to dilute the production’s courageous re- fusal to lighten one of Shakespeare’s darkest plays. Peter J. Smith * The Phoenix and Turtle, edited and staged by Deborah Shaw for the RSC, Holy Trinity Church, 5 November 2006. A dead phoenix is a contradiction in terms, yet that is what Shakespeare offered his readers in his contribution to a collection of poems published by Robert Chester in 1601 called Love’s Martyr, Allegorically shadowing the truth of love in the constant fate of the Phoenix and Turtle. His untitled poem be- ginning “Let the bird of loudest lay” (first given the

67 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL title of The Phoenix and Turtle in 1807) has long been defined for literary critics by its impenetrability, John Middleton Murry calling it “obscure, mystical and strictly unintelligible”, and I. A. Richards, “the most mysterious poem in English”. Undaunted by such views, the RSC began the evening of their presentation of the poem with a talk given at the Courtyard Theatre by Michael Wood, broadcaster and historian, whose informal, enthusiastic approach created a sense of adventure and exploration; questions and theories about the poem were presented, not as difficulties, but as clues in a fascinating treasure hunt. He pointed out the unique nature of the occasion: since the poems ac- companying Shakespeare’s are not in print, this was a historic opportunity to hear The Phoenix and Turtle in the literary setting of its original publication, and the physical setting of the church where Shakespeare worshipped and is buried. Chester’s anthology, to which Chapman, Marston, Jonson and Ignoto (believed to be John Donne) also contribute, is dedicated to his patron, “the worthily honor’d Knight”, Sir John Salisburie, and probably commemorates the conferring of his knighthood in June 1601. The choice of phoenix imagery may have been intended as a compliment to Sir John’s mother who was descended from an illegitimate son of Henry VII and was described in her epitaph in 1591 as “brittanica Phoenix”. The need to flatter a patron meant that commis- sioned verses needed to be both new and also ca- pable of being applied to differing circumstances. Jonson subsequently re-cycled his Ode Enthusiastic from Love’s Martyr as a tribute to Lucy, Countess of Bedford. Shakespeare shows no sign of such compro- mise. Indeed, as Salisburie needed to avoid any taint of Catholic sympathies, since his brother had been executed for taking part in the Babington plot, it seems all the more strange that Shakespeare’s poem, in which phoenix and dove are mourned by Catholic rituals of requiem and prayer for the dead, should be acceptable in Chester’s anthology. Michael Wood offered varying theories, includ- ing those relating the poem to Elizabeth and Essex, or to the Catholic martyr Ann Line, in a lively and impartial way, skilfully encouraging his audience to speculate for themselves on what they were about to hear, in an admirable attempt to make the poem as accessible as possible. After a dark and wind-swept walk, the audience came into Holy Trinity Church to find it transformed by designer Ruth Hall’s atmospheric setting, the flickering light from hundreds of candles creating a timeless enclosed space in which the appearance of actors and musicians in Elizabethan dress seemed entirely natural. The actors Peter de Jersey, Joanne Pearce and David Troughton spoke the memorised poems with conversational spontaneity, as though the words had just been written, creating an easy, relaxed immediacy, so that the audience could feel themselves to be privileged listeners among a coterie of poets sharing their latest work with us. Music played on spinet and viols was used effectively as a framing device for the work of each poet, the pat- terned richness of musical and verbal harmonies echoing and enhancing each other. The programme began with William Byrd’s motet Deus Venerunt Gentes, sung a capella. Though startling to hear Catholic music heralding poems published during Elizabeth’s persecution of Catholics, and forbidden by Reformers lest its elaborate harmonics prove a distraction from the Word, it was appropri- ate to the coded references in Shakespeare’s poem. It is known to be the motet that Byrd composed for Ann Line’s requiem mass, in February 1601, and it establishes the phoenix theme of death and re-birth in its linking of mourning with the celebration of Christian hope in redemption. The allegorical nature of the Love’s Martyr poems is challenged by diverse authorial treatments of the two protagonists. Ignoto’s phoenix is androgynous and immortal: “The world one phoenix till another burn”. Marston relates the union of phoenix and dove to a spiritual state in which humankind par- ticipates in the Eternal Being and “though men die, humanity itself lives on”. Chapman describes the only constant not devoured by Time and Change to be “Truth eternised in a human heart”. Jonson claims that the love of phoenix and turtle-dove is not “the blind desire” of carnal love, rather, “It is a golden Chaine let down from Heaven”. While Chester, Ignoto and Marston conform to the myth and speak of a new phoenix born, and Jonson and Chapman ad- dress a living phoenix and turtle-dove, Shakespeare declares “death is now the phoenix’ nest”, “leaving no posterity”. His denial of the traditional emblem is one of the unsolved ambiguities of The Phoenix and Turtle. The RSC presentation of Shakespeare’s poem skil- fully displayed its tripartite structure. Peter de Jersey spoke the proem, the calling of birds to the requiem, as an announcement, allowing a pause before clearly structuring the complex metaphysical centre of the poem, with its paradoxes of “Single nature’s double name” and “Love hath reason, reason none / If what parts can so remain”. The threnos was enacted by words, gesture and music, re-creating the dignity of a funeral service. The actor’s slow pacing away, accompanied by viol music, and the long contempla- tive pause which followed, allowed space to reflect on the poem’s unanswered questions. The RSC musical director John Woolf made some inspired choices of music for this presentation, as well as conducting impeccable performances, and one of these was the use of Les Pleurs from Tous les Matins du Monde, by M. de Sainte-Colombe, which empha-

68 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 sised the finality and paradox of the dead phoenix. The continental aesthetic of “tears poetry” reflected Catholic lamentation for heresy. Its influence on English poetry owes much to Robert Southwell, priest and martyr, whose poems have some sig- nificant intertextual links with The Phoenix and Turtle. The use of continental music, such as Pachelbel’s Ciacona, and the French tears music provided an in- teresting subtext to the performance. The RSC musi- cians, whose beautifully judged performances added so much to the evening, were John Woolf on spinet, with David Hatcher and Angela Cranmore on viols. The singers were Gemma Busfield, Hayley Hunt, Philip Jones, Jonathan Stork and Matthew Wright. Some of the devotional poems of Southwell (who was described in a Jesuit tribute as “the ever re-born phoenix”) were set to music by William Byrd, whose name may be punned upon as “the bird of loudest lay” calling the mourners to a requiem in the first line of The Phoenix and Turtle. Perhaps Shakespeare found in the form of the threne, used to mourn the phoenix and dove, an appropriate expression of the grief and distress felt by loyal Catholics living in a Protestant country, as Southwell, Tallis and Byrd did in their poetry and music based on the biblical lamentations of Jeremiah. The classical origin of lamentation lies in antipho- nal singing, and this is the quality Colin Burrow, the Oxford editor of Shakespeare’s poems, discerns in The Phoenix and Turtle: “The poem slips between theological and philosophical registers, and blends voice on voice in a polyphony which has the reso- nance of ritual worship”. This example of form enacting meaning suggests a close affinity between Shakespeare’s poem and the sung lamentations of recusant worship, an affinity given eloquent expres- sion in the words, music and silences of Deborah Shaw’s production. At the discussion on Shakespeare and Faith earlier in the day, Michael Boyd had said that Shakespeare is most at home when the spiritual and cerebral are most closely linked with the tangible. The Phoenix and Turtle presentation was an excellent affirmation of this. In this performance, the aural and visual clues of sixteenth-century music, Elizabethan dress, and red-cassocked choir, in the shadowy candle-lit chancel of Shakespeare’s church, brought us as close as we are likely to come to a poem written at a piv- otal stage in English poetry; a poem which looks to the past in its use of medieval emblem, at the sectar- ian conflict of its present in its reference to proscribed Catholic practices, and to the future of seventeenth- century devotional poetry in its evocation of praise, lamentation and loss. Rosemary Stiles * Richard II, directed by Claus Peymann for the Berliner Ensemble, translated by Thomas Brasch, The Courtyard Theatre, 18 November 2006, left stalls. T his was the second German production to en- croach on Shakespeare’s home turf in this year’s Complete Works Festival with a play, no less, that in this “sceptred isle” (II.1.20) has always been cher- ished for its fervent statement of patriotism: Richard II, the most English of English histories, or as Andrew Gurr tells us (in his new Cambridge edition), “the most extraordinary of all the Shakespearean crown jewels”. Stakes were raised high, the company per se presented a pressing claim to the crown. After all, the Berliner Ensemble, founded in 1949 by Helene Weigel and Bertold Brecht, has been a major role model for the creation of its English cousin, the mod- ern-day Royal Shakespeare Company. Stylistically, the Brechtian pedigree of Claus Peymann’s award-winning production (Friedrich- Luft-Preis 2001) was impossible to miss: for four per- formances, the Courtyard’s thrust stage was trans- formed into a replica of the proscenium construc- tion at the Theater am Schiffbauerdamm in Berlin where Richard II has remained in repertoire since its première on 30 June, 2000. The confrontational set- up is symptomatic of Peymann’s understanding of politically relevant theatre: deliberately refusing to pay lip service to the theatrical Zeitgeist, his carefully concerted production, like the play itself, is all about taking sides, making decisions, whether right or wrong only history can tell. Filing into our seats, we find the stage flooded in a cold white light: not only does it accentuate the stark austerity of Achim Freyer’s abstract set — a triptych arrangement of white walls in an otherwise black room — it also mercilessly throws into relief a bloodied corpse, covered with a nondescript black sheet, lying face-up on the bare stage floor. Add to this another disturbing intrusion: a water tap that with almost indecent expediency protrudes out of the pristine whiteness of the wall to the left. (Its actual functionality provided an incessant source of humour at various points in the production where it was used to revive the oft-fainting queen or, in an ironic comment on Bolingbroke’s symbolic associa- tion with the liquid element, as mains supply for the neurotic “Saubermann”.) This disconcerting visual opening is just as brutally followed by an aural one: the pitch-black darkness into which we are suddenly plunged is filled with the odious sound of buzzing flies. When the noise threatens to become unbear- able, it stops as abruptly as it began, the lights come back on — the corpse has been removed — and the play proper begins. Or rather, it doesn’t. Prefacing the start of Act I with the dialogue between the Duchess of Gloucester and John of Gaunt (usually Act I Scene 2) was Peymann’s

69 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL second rearrangement of Shakespeare’s play, a dram- aturgical decision which helped draw attention to the initial act of injustice, the murder of Gloucester, and the implication of Richard in this crime. It also clearly flags this director’s line of approach: his Richard II is to be a lesson in power politics rather than a portrayal of the poetic fall of a tragic hero. Didactic clarity is the formula that reigns supreme in this production, and it is impressively underscored by every trick in the (theatrical) book: bold sym- bolic use of space, light and colour gives each scene a sharp sense of focus and creates distance. There is no music; props are used sparingly. Whereas place and time remain undefined, opposing factions are clearly marked: the colour of Bolingbroke’s camp is black, those in support of Richard, like Richard himself, are dressed in white. Actors are white-faced, emo- tions hidden behind expressionistic make-up (Ulrike Heinemann) or relativised by mannerist delivery. Throughout, the brisk narrative is held together by Freyer’s highly functional white box of a set which, with its “unfurnish’d walls” (I.2.68), presents a con- vincing symbolic correlative of a political/historical deadlock. That Peymann’s treatment of the play subscribes to the ideological thrust inspired by Polish critic Jan Kott is expressively demonstrated in the deposi- tion scene, a simple but powerful affair: one prop, a black ladder of outsize proportions, and one ges- tus, Richard’s painfully prolonged slide down the “grand staircase of history”1 from an elevated kingly position at the upper rear of the stage into the “base court” (III.3.180) towards the front, sufficed to evoke a moment of political if not tragic eclipse. Such conceptional stringency leaves little room for subtleties or surprises. It does not leave much room for heroes, either. In a scene that collates scenes 1 and 3 of Shakespeare’s opening act, receding white lines on the stage floor find their vanishing point in Michael Maertens’s charismatic Richard, a mesmer- ising but erratic actor-king equally adept at playing billiards with his dandyish acolytes as he is at play- ing power games with his political opponents, or indeed, language games with whoever cares to lis- ten. In this, as in all other aspects, he is the opposite of Veit Schubert’s Bolingbroke, a burly man, who is troubled by a stutter and seems to be permanently ill at ease (except when smashing Richard’s billiard ta- ble). King in ambition only, this repressed bureaucrat was more comfortable with his bowler hat than with the crown. It is Northumberland, played with great vindictive aplomb by a Murnauesque Axel Werner (despite his costume, a mismatched combo of army boots and a codpiece), who is the true Machiavel of this piece. For him, Bolingbroke is the politically expedient alternative to Richard and must therefore be put on the throne at all costs, even if it means manhandling the amiably avuncular York (Manfred Karge) who consequently (if somewhat surprisingly) turns into an overeager champion of Bolingbroke’s cause and Richard’s swashbuckling nemesis. This radical re-adjustment of York’s role discomfits but it is obviously meant to flaunt the central theme: in a ruthless world of power politics none remain un- scathed, least of all those who attempt to “remain as neuter” (II.3.159). Far from being dead serious, however, this politi- cal theatre, this theatre of politics at times has all the makings of a show-booth burlesque: bad news in- evitably causes a dopey and teary-eyed Queen Isabel (played by Hanna Jürgens) to collapse in a fainting fit. With the help of a wheelbarrow, clownish gar- deners (Alexander Doering and Michael Rothmann, who doubled as Green and Mowbray) spread the royal dirt, while Aumerle (Dirk Ossig) somewhat belatedly spreads the word, assessing his rebellious defiance of the new regime with graffiti that reads: “Richard II Forever”. Perspectives change, and in this production of- ten spectacularly so. After the interval, as if bored by its own dogmatism, the production literally re- lieves itself in a cathartic act of inspired iconoclasm. Unkinged, Richard’s re-appearance on stage is accompanied by an explosion of dirt: thrown by invisible hands — a reference to London’s citizens — sods of what looks suspiciously like excrement turn Freyer’s immaculate set (and by implication: Richard’s realm) into a quagmire. While such a hu- miliating showdown has a humanising if not invig- orating effect on Richard and his queen (their white make-up progressively disappears), politically and dramatically it is now up to Henry IV, armed with a hosepipe, to rise phoenix-like from the ashes. And those who know their histories know where that will end. For this Richard II it ends as it began. With a bloody corpse. And a buzzing of flies. The wheel has come full circle. All this is aesthetically clever; it is intellectually stimulating, and grotesquely funny, very Brecht cum Kott, but where does it leave Shakespeare? It leaves him, or rather his poetry, in the hands of Thomas Brasch, the German playwright and poet responsible for the translation of this production, and remarkably capable hands they are. Unfortunately, Brasch’s poet- ry does not translate well. None of its directness and simplicity, its daring conceits and laconic humour, made it to the flickering trio of surtitle boxes. The English audience had to make do with a truncated version of Shakespeare’s text instead; and more is the loss. In his review of Luk Perceval’s Othello, the other German production that visited Stratford, Michael Billington expressed the view that “Translation often liberates Shakespeare”.2 Brasch’s imagina- tive adaptation, written specifically for the Berliner Ensemble, certainly did the trick for me. Following Shakespeare’s text closely, it nevertheless generates

70 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 its original poetic insights in a language both ancient and modern. And it finds its perfect mouthpiece in the expressive range of Maertens’s Richard, who effortlessly makes the layered language his own. Adding his own off-the-cuff verbal interjections, Maertens’s delivery catches that curious blend of the matter-of-fact and the rhetorical that lets us hear Richard’s progress from player-king to poet, though never quite to tragic greatness. As an artistic Gesamtkunstwerk, this highly politi- cised production is essentially an ensemble achieve- ment that provided a more than adequate take on Shakespeare’s “crown jewel”. Theatre, Peymann believes, “should be used for political and moral ac- tion”, but it should also give “free reign to a playful and adventurous imagination”.3 This imaginative and thought-provoking appropriation of Richard II was visually and aurally enthralling: a real royal treat and a definite rival for the (company) crown.
