Press, 1998), 334. * Merry Wives: The Musical, adapted and directed by Gregory Doran for the RSC, Royal Shakespeare Theatre, 14 December 2006 (mid-stalls) and 18 January 2007 (rear stalls). T hirty years ago, Trevor Nunn turned The Comedy of Errors into a witty musical, featuring Judi Dench in the role of Adriana. This time it was Gregory Doran’s turn to transform another Shakespearean comedy into a musical romp, with Dench again in a leading part. Those who had noted in advance her casting as Mistress Quickly must have wondered how so eminent an actress had been persuaded to take on such a minor role. The answer lies in Doran’s canny upgrading of Quickly’s function in the play, giving her a back-story based on her previous rela- tionship with Falstaff, established in the Henry IV plays, and anticipating her ultimate marriage to Pistol, made explicit at the start of Henry V. Thus, Doran also contributed to the debate on the intertex- tuality of the Falstaff plays, placing the fat knight’s Windsor humiliations, like Giorgio Melchiori in his Arden edition, between his rejection by the newly- crowned Henry V and his subsequent offstage death at the start of the King’s French campaign. However, it took some textual wrenching and amplification, in- cluding interpolations from 2 Henry IV and Henry V, to achieve a coherence about which Shakespeare pre- sumably cared little. But who can complain when the result was to restore Dame Judi so triumphantly to the RSC’s main stage? Dench’s Quickly was in many ways the produc- tion’s raison d’être. Crowned by an auburn fright wig and getting full value out of the character’s malapropisms, she managed to be both comic and touching, her good heart leading her to favour all three of Anne Page’s suitors simultaneously. For someone who cannot really sing, Dench’s ability to “put over” a song has long been unparalleled, whether in Cabaret or A Little Night Music. Here, she grasped all her singing opportunities with infectious relish, and her famous cracked voice was employed to particularly good effect in her last solo number, the oxymoronic “Honeysuckle Villain”, which put the final touches to her previous history with Falstaff and had her deciding to abandon him in favour of Brendan O’Hea’s Pistol — a leather-clad roarer with a mop of unruly black hair and a droopy moustache. In this song, Dench achieved the only emotional depth in the entire production, tapping into a genu- ine pain that is completely absent from the character in Shakespeare’s play. Though Melchiori agonises over Quickly’s incarnation as Fairy Queen in the concluding masque, here it was entirely fitting that Dench, appearing as a spangly Eastcheap version of her Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love, should domi- nate the humiliation of Falstaff and the celebratory finale. The elevation of Mistress Quickly as portrayed by Dench was out of key with the tone of the rest of the production, which was essentially musical pan- tomime, a festive romp designed to cheer the spirits without sacrificing the Complete Works project to a non-Shakespearean alternative. That it singularly failed to cheer this spectator’s spirits can be ascribed to a number of causes, not least its failure to trust Shakespeare’s play, which is surprisingly witty and subtle (Oh no it isn’t! Oh yes it is!). Shakespeare’s precise delineation of the Windsor community, with its social striations and linguistic quirks, was sacri- ficed to a chocolate-boxy, Toytown setting, enclosed in a series of white picture frames like emblematic quotation marks, with characters exaggeratedly cos- tumed from a variety of periods. These encompassed the visual ethos of the RSC’s two most famous productions of the play, Terry Hands’s Elizabethan staging, first seen in 1967, and Bill Alexander’s 1950s Windsor, evoked in his 1985 production. This eclec- tic range succeeded merely in locating the action in a cloying, twee, sentimentally nostalgic notion of Englishness. It was hardly surprising that the production’s title song characterised the wives as consisting of “sugar and spice and honeydew”, since the entire presentation oozed the sickly sweetness of a surfeit of Christmas confectionery.

71 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL If the settings and costumes were eclectic, Paul Englishby’s music was simply all over the place, ranging from cod Lloyd Webber to Hollywood musi- cal, and comic operetta to Country and Western. It did, at least occasionally, benefit from some witty lyrics by Ranjit Bolt, but these were scant compensa- tion for the frenzied effort to offer so much variety that, surely, everyone in the audience would find something to enjoy. Particularly cringe-making were a supposedly jolly laughing chorus for the wives and a thigh-slapping music-hall turn from Evans and Caius as they settled their differences after their abortive duel — though at least this was enlivened by some bawdy, politically incorrect jokes directed at the dubious sexual predilections of the Welsh. The show’s opening number, “Let’s Cast Away Care”, offered a Technicolor vision of singing and dancing milkmaids and market traders, as the play’s central characters went busily about their morning activi- ties, and Falstaff arrived with his cronies on a kind of Elizabethan motorbike-with-sidecar that emitted a loud explosion, soon to be echoed by an equally unfunny exploding musket and an inexplicably exploding skeleton in Dr Caius’s chamber. The at- tempt to be all-inclusive is perhaps best illustrated by the wives’ chorus, which began as a hoedown, was briefly interrupted by an Elizabethan pavane, and concluded as a raucous celebration of female emancipation, with the whole company beating out its powerful rhythms on an extensive collection of kitchen equipment — like the show, throwing in everything but the kitchen sink. This was great fun, and superbly rendered — but it was typical of the production’s eclecticism that it was largely borrowed from Doran’s own 2003 staging of Fletcher’s The Tamer Tamed, also with music by Englishby, with its militant chorus of clog-dancing, pot-banging women railroading the audience into believing that that play is a feminist manifesto. Maria, the rebellious wife of The Tamer, was played by Alexandra Gilbreath, who reappeared here as Mistress Ford, bringing her familiar seductive huskiness to the job of teaching both Falstaff and her husband a lesson they would never forget. She was partnered by Haydn Gwynne as Mistress Page, looking like the idealised wife and mother from one of those 1950s adverts epitomising domestic bliss. Her portrayal was rather brittle and, though she and Gilbreath played with energy and verve, there was little warmth in their characterisations — perhaps owing to the fact that they were constantly required to burst into song. One yearned for some light and shade in their emotional landscape, rather than such persistently perky brightness. The play has darker tones that were ignored here. Such darker tones were partly explored in Alistair McGowan’s portrayal of the jealous Ford. A sinister stick-insect in dark suit, silver waistcoat and black cravat, he articulated his fermenting suspicions with an intensity that exceeded the melodrama evoked by his songs, creating a neatly understated comic con- trast with his disguise as Brook, in long beige check coat and black trilby, with adjustable sunglasses and a speech impediment. His two manic searches of the house were entertaining enough, though the staging of the first, entirely in operetta mode with no spoken dialogue, rather vitiated Shakespeare’s dramatic ef- fects. Determined to discover Falstaff on the second occasion, though, McGowan’s Ford rooted around in the buck basket like a demented rodent digging a burrow, until he was left kneeling inside it, sur- rounded by discarded washing, to deliver his won- derfully bathetic, puzzled conclusion, “Well, he’s not here I seek for” (IV.2.149). Elsewhere, a strong cast laboured largely in vain to inject some humanity into the lesser roles. Anne Page and her lover, Fenton, were promoted through a series of emotional ballads, powerfully delivered by Scarlett Strallen and Martin Crewes, into the ro- mantic leads that Shakespeare doesn’t really make them, shifting the play rather inappropriately from Windsor to Shaftesbury Avenue. The surrounding gallery of rural eccentrics was presented as an ani- mated cabinet of curiosities, with tics and grimaces, mugging and vocal quirks employed in a desperate attempt to arouse laughter. This inevitably collided with the law of diminishing returns, and rarely can such a talented group of performers have worked so hard to such little effect. As Shallow, Jeffery Dench gave us the wheezing old buffer we have seen from him so many times before; Ian Hughes’s Evans was a mincing, twitchy Welsh grotesque, partnered by a Doctor Caius from Paul Chahidi so overburdened with comic invention that he was in danger of im- ploding; and the talented Simon Trinder as a lilac- clad Slender was reduced to remorselessly unfunny semaphore and hair-tossing. It was a relief to enjoy the apple-munching stillness of Tobias Beer’s Simple, and the refreshing normality of Rob Edwards, wast- ed in the thankless role of Master Page. The title page of the 1602 quarto prioritises Falstaff over the merry wives as the centre of attention and, despite the play’s ensemble qualities, any produc- tion will stand or fall largely on the performance of Sir John. Rotund, bewhiskered and fruity-voiced, Simon Callow provided everything one could ex- pect, embodying the iconic image of Falstaff whether knocking back tankards of sack, composing identical love letters, berating his minions, seducing Mistress Ford, emerging from his watery humiliation like some bedraggled Neptune with a stray fish in his pocket, or steaming naked (in grotesque fatsuit) in a hot tub. Antlered like some mighty rutting stag for his final assignation at Herne’s Oak, Callow’s Falstaff never short-changed us, and any hollowness at the centre of his performance can be ascribed mainly to

72 CAHIERS éLISABéTHAINS SPECIAL ISSUE 2007 Shakespeare’s diminished version of Sir John in this play. Where Callow notably scored his comic hits was in being allowed to relish Shakespeare’s lan- guage. Indeed, most of the genuinely appreciative laughter generated by the production was elicited by Falstaff’s offhand but verbally precise wit, such as his outraged reaction to Bardolph’s suggestion of eggs in his sack, “I’ll no pullet sperm in my brewage” (III.5.29); or his rueful put-down of the Welsh parson, “Have I lived to stand at the taunt of one that makes fritters of English?” (V.5.141). Perhaps the only miss- ing element in Callow’s performance was a sense of desperation: it is, after all, his dire financial straits that drive him into wooing the two wives. In view of the emphasis given to his and Quickly’s past history, it would also have been interesting to see a greater sense of Falstaff’s broken spirits following his rejec- tion by the erstwhile Prince Hal which, according to Quickly in Henry V, has “killed his heart” (Henry V, II.1.84). However, such emotional depth would have been alien to the spirit of this production. At one significant moment, Dench’s Mistress Quickly entered upstage, as tall as the half-timbered cottages that receded in diminishing perspective to the end of the village street. With a delightfully dis- dainful double-take, Dench cast a glance of wither- ing puzzlement at these tiny buildings, as if to say, with Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard, “I’m still big; it’s the pictures that got small”. And herein lay the essence of all that was wrong with this show: in its picturesque quaintness, its strenuous efforts to amuse and its aspirations to full-scale musical status, it merely ended up diminishing both its talented cast and Shakespeare’s underrated play. Peter Malin * Richard III, directed by Michael Boyd for the RSC, The Courtyard Theatre, 25 January 2007, front stalls. R ichard III describes a startling sense of being in which human life occupies a colony on the edge of the vast and disturbingly active hinterland of death. The knowledge that people die, that people have died and will die, informs every breath. And the traffic is not one-way: death breathes upon life, determining how people act in life and the emotional repertoire with which they respond to it. The RSC’s production at the Courtyard Theatre in the Complete Works Festival, a reworking of the Swan production of 2000-2001 [See Peter J. Smith’s review in Cahiers Élisabéthains 60, 106-10], gave visceral presence to these aspects of death. It began where III Henry VI had left off, with Jonathan Slinger’s Richard nursing an empty white cloth folded as though it swaddled a baby, a disqui- eting image. To reinforce the point, his false celebra- tion of the Yorkist victory was addressed directly to a “son of York”, a boy; his departure was cue for Richard’s self-revealing “But I...”. The corpse of King Henry was, of course, the actor (Chuk Iwuji) who had strongly imposed his image on the role over the course of the trilogy. His white robe was now his shroud. The blood that spontaneously flowed from his body when Richard approached it recalled the even more copious blood that painted the stage when Richard dragged his body away at the end of 3 Henry VI. Actors choreographed their movements around the stain, which remained for much of the first half of the play, forming elegant and emblematic stage images when paired with fallen white feathers or dropped weapons. The sense of continuity with the past was there- fore overwhelmingly strong, as it had been in earlier plays in the tetralogy. The play was performed by the same company. An apparently old woman amongst the mourners of Henry VI, swathed in black and car- rying a pack on her back, turned out to be his wife Margaret — a subtle detail, as she was not clearly identified as such in the scene itself, but an effec- tive one. In Act I Scene 3 she returned to horrify the Yorkists by unwrapping a set of bones from her pack, and then ceremoniously assembling it as the frag- mented skeleton of her dead son Rutland. It was a portable ritual kit and memory machine eerily fit for the purpose of cursing her enemies. Katy Stephens was young for the character in Richard III, but the preternatural aging of the one role that is present in all four plays of the tetralogy was all the more effec- tive for that, and she cursed the Yorkist victors with rhetorical nuance and emotional conviction. Continuity with the past was also affirmed by increasing the opportunities for the roles of the Henry VI plays to reappear. Shakespeare wrote the play for such an effect to the extent that he included Henry VI among the ghosts who address Richard and Richmond in the dream sequence before the Battle of Bosworth Field. The production added Warwick (Patrice Naiambana) and Richard’s father Richard Duke of York (Clive Wood) to the number. They had both appeared earlier as courtly guests at Richard’s coronation. Richard reacted to his father’s fierce expressions of denunciation by calling “Stand all apart”, a moment that anticipated his far greater enervation in the ghost scene. This was one aspect of the father-son motif carried through from the trilogy. And at the end of the play, the text was manipulated to suggest that Stanley was Richmond’s father. The actors (Keith Bartlett and Lex Shrapnel) were those who had movingly played Talbot and his son in I Henry VI and had sustained the motif thereafter. In this production Richmond was a strikingly refresh- ing and cleansing figure, whilst having Stanley as his father rooted him in the world of the play and made

73 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL him a more credible salvific figure. Given the burden of past experience, it was a marvellous thing for a father and a son to survive. The set was the same that had served well in the Henry VI trilogy, featuring a rusted round-tower against the centre rear stage wall. The tower doors could clang fatefully. A spiral staircase leading to en- closed upper acting spaces might suggest an outlook, a window, or a rampart. There was less use for the military application in this play, but the production built on the suggestions of other-wordly fatality that had been established in the earlier plays. Antony Bunsee, the red-robed and aquiline-nosed actor who had repeatedly commanded this space in Henry VI in a composite of roles identified as “Keeper”, returned as Brackenbury, the Lieutenant of the Tower. In Richard III the identity of the rusted tower therefore stabilised as the Tower of London itself. One might reflect that all previous locations associated with this structure were prefigurations of this brutal presence in the play’s symbolic geography of London. The Plantagenet past of Henry VI was further re- called in the recurrence of the trilogy’s uncanny stag- ing effects. At key moments white feathers drifted down from above, or there was a harsh noise that sounded like a wet finger vibrating the rim of a glass. The question that might have puzzled audiences watching Henry VI was now answered: why white feathers? They were the feathers from the pillows that smothered the young princes, falling thickly to mark the moment of their deaths as a euphemistic and gentle substitute for spilt red blood. I have emphasized the continuity between Richard III and the trilogy because the prevailing impression was just the opposite. The medieval world of Henry VI had decisively been left behind. Costumes were predominantly twentieth-century in style. Gone, or at least etiolated, were the testoster- one-driven aggression and physicality that made the trilogy memorable. Richard interrupted Henry’s funeral procession with an intimidating gang of SAS troops equipped for modern warfare; the mo- ment was not so much an act of brave effrontery on Richard’s part as a declaration of a new theatrical style. When Richard, Buckingham, and the Mayor of London were rescued from the entirely imaginary coup by “enemies”, Catesby (Julius D’Silva) and his troops were lowered from above to the sound of helicopters whose aerial search-lights swept the stage; the soldiers quickly made the area secure with yellow “police do not enter” tape. This descent on ropes from above was a strong point of intersection between the theatricalisation of medieval war in Michael Boyd’s I Henry VI , with its spectacular ropes and ladders, and the twentieth-century stage tradi- tion of playing Richard III as an allegory of modern political violence. But it was pure theatre: in contrast with both points of reference, there was little really at stake. There was a distinct loss of energy and coherence of style throughout. The play did not belong to the same world: the collectively violent and superstitious medievalism was a heavy residue in conflict with the lived present. Yet it had to be so. The play shows a so- ciety in which the violence of open warfare has been re-routed into other channels. Unmodified, the style of Henry VI would have been a disaster in Richard III. Arguably, the production of this play was stymied by its part in the tetralogy. Yet Boyd and designer Tom Piper were aware of the issue, as is evident in Piper’s comments “In Conversation” in the programme, and the production was cleverly postmodern in its stylis- tic repositioning. As can happen when the play is part of the larger sequence, the established ensemble mode of pro- duction and the sheer weight of the past mean that Richard does not quite steal the show. He is an ab- erration. In her two scenes Margaret puts him in his place as the means towards an end that is not his own. Slinger played the role with intelligence. He had a sharp awareness of verbal nuance, and expressed occasional emotional force, but the range of his performance was narrower than that of the de- finitive actors of the role. The opening soliloquy was a shade understated. Richard’s challenge to a notably spineless Anne (Hannah Barrie) and the arrest of a notably stupid Hastings (Tom Hodgkins) were too easy. So too was the contest with Buckingham, who, despite the effortless mastery of the role by Richard Cordery, proved naive and impotent in opposing Richard. Stephens’s Margaret entirely dominated Act I Scene 3, and Queen Elizabeth (Ann Ogbomo) was a strong and sympathetic adversary in the strenuous verbal tennis of Act IV Scene 4. The appearance of the ghosts at Richard’s coronation had already signified that he was a spent force. Slinger’s was a smart but ultimately childish Richard. The pent-up fury that emerged in his rendition of the soliloquy in Act III Scene 2 of III Henry VI never fully resurfaced until his wild self-interrogation in the final soliloquy after seeing the ghosts. This was an impressive moment of self-torment; it also indicated that Richard was ripe to fall from the stage of history. The Courtyard production highlights the se- vere problems inherent in playing Richard III as IV Henry VI, even when a conscious effort is made to create a suitable artistic distance. The greater and better-known play emerges as a disappointment, its distinctive voice muted by the context in which it is performed. But the production also highlights the ways in which the play can draw strength from its connectedness to the trilogy, acknowledging the im- prisoning and fatal hold that the past can exert even on a revolutionary present. Though not quite estab- lishing itself as a landmark production of Richard III nor as a climax to the tetralogy as resounding as the

John Jowett * Henry V, adapted and directed by Pippo Delbono for the Compagnia Pippo Delbono, The Swan, 2 February 2007, side stalls. “I ’m not interested in reconstructing history”—so says Pippo Delbono in the programme and pub- licity for Henry V, and his company’s performance of the play at the RSC suggested that, if anything, it is deconstruction he’s after. Even more than the German Othello that played at the RST earlier in the Festival, Delbono’s Henry V was only loosely related to its Shakespearean forebear, taking its legacy and text as starting points and interpreting them through experiments in movement, sound and image. Presented on a spare stage, with three core actors and few props, the production stripped the play of any pomp or pageantry left over from the days of Olivier. In contrast to Shakespeare’s original, which invites its audience to picture theatrical verisimili- tude through the magic of language and imagina- tion, Delbono’s version cast off traditional narrative structure, historical representation, and — for the most part — verbal expression in favour of a more conceptual art form. The production opened in darkness, with sounds, rather than images, setting the scene. Around the stage clumsy, frantic stomping could be heard, until a lone voice finally shouted, “I arrest thee of high treason”, several times over in Italian. As the lights went up and the accusations drew to a close, the audience found itself thrust into the heart of the Cambridge, Scroop and Grey treason scene (II.2). Gone were the majestic chorus and his muse of fire; instead an overweight, sweaty Hal (Delbono) began the show by condemning three men to death. More Falstaff than prince, this play’s Harry introduced himself to the audience as a frustrated, betrayed and vengeful old man. The show went on to document Falstaff’s death, Hal’s coronation and his immediate hunger for France, punctuated throughout with swelling music and bemusing, memorable dancing. Henry’s inces- sant, importunate cry for France — “Voglio la Francia!” — at first seemed hasty, but the smug Dauphin/“The French” (Gustavo Giacosa) soon came on and justi- fied Henry’s enmity. With his fine manners, gaggle of friends and exquisitely silly dancing horse, he repre- sented a sophisticated, elitist court culture that stood in stark contrast to Henry’s lonely kingship. The core of the production finally came with the English army’s departure for Agincourt. More of Shakespeare’s original text came out as the play explored the plight of common men, represented by a company of twenty-five amateur actors cast from auditions in Stratford. As Henry screamed out his “Once more unto the breach” speech, now contorted into a shrill, ugly war-cry, the company stomped out a heavy, mechanical dance sequence that seemed to parody military conformity. In these scenes, more innocuous lines from Shakespeare’s original gained new prominence. As the battles began, a common man/”Henry’s friend” (Pepe Robledo) ducked through the fighting, pleading for more soldiers to reinforce the English side. “And for my part, I have not a case of lives”, he cried out, emphasizing the terror and destruction every soldier must feel in the midst of war. When the same man came back at the end of the play to declare England’s victory, he hob- bled on with only one arm and one leg, suggesting that the only thing that is true in war is that no one really wins. While occasionally visually arresting, the produc- tion failed to take flight. A more sympathetic re- viewer would probably wax poetic about Delbono’s clowning and the Italian tradition of commedia dell’arte, or absurdist theatre and the need to unset- tle complacent RSC audiences. A more dismissive critic would lament the play’s rather heavy-handed, anti-war stance and the pretension of the avant- garde. For my part, the show hovered somewhere in the middle, proving an interesting commentary on Shakespeare’s Henry V but not a transformative evening at the theatre. F ormally titled The Baghdad Richard, Sulayman al-Bassam’s Richard III was presented in Arabic with English sur-titles at the Swan as part of the RSC’s Complete Works Festival. Bassam’s work on Shakespeare is familiar to British audiences; this was the second Shakespearean tragedy that he had shown in this country, his first work being the po- liticising of Hamlet in Middle Eastern context, The al-Hamlet Summit in 2004 (English version at the 2002 Edinburgh Festival). Bassam transposed a piece of the Arabian Gulf to Stratford by using actors, musicians and designers from countries across the region and from Britain; these included Iraq, Kuwait, Lebanon and Syria. He took a cameo role as the American ambassador in this multi-cultural multi-lingual production. The different Arabic dialects were distinguishable by the variety of accents in which they were delivered;

75 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL Bassam’s play was written in a combination of al- fu.sha (basic Arabic) as well as local Gulf idioms juxtaposed with French and English. Bassam sets his tragedy in an unnamed oil-rich Gulf state where he lets Richard loose to unleash his tyrannicidal fury against his Arab rivals. Fayez Kazak’s Richard shares many characteristics with Shakespeare’s Earl of Gloucester, in that he is charming, persuasive and blinded by an overpowering compulsion for totali- tarian rule over the kingdom. To call this a political adaptation with contem- porary allusions to the turbulent political situation in the Middle East would be an understatement. Family feuds, blood-revenge and monarchical usur- pations go hand-in-hand with greed, corruption and espionage. In many ways the political grid in the Arabian Peninsula echoes the medieval England Richard of Gloucester was occupying. Demonised by Shakespeare, the Machiavellian Earl seems like a ready-made character for the tyrant Arab Amir won- derfully portrayed by Kazak — who won First Prize for Best Actor at the Cairo International Festival for Experimental Theater for his role in Jawad al- Assadi’s Baghdad Public Bath. Although the Arab Richard has been compared with Saddam Hussein for his autocratic behaviour, the beetle-browed and moustached Kazak resembled the late King Hussein of Jordan, and his eloquence echoed that of Omar Sharif. As Richard moves closer to taking control of the throne, his dress became more Arabicised with each scene. The only visible sign of deformity in the beginning was the neck collar under the military suit. Gradually we got to view the surgical brace that held his body together; but once he let go of it, his whole body fell apart which resulted in a more dra- matic effect than a humped-backed disability might have done. Raymond Hosni was superb as the Arabic-French- and-English-speaking Buckingham; not only did he deliver all three languages clearly, his diction was excellent in each of them. His timing was also superb as he announced that “War on terror” would be his political spin. Buckingham was the Palace Advisor and the traitor from within. “He is used by Richard”, said Hosni, “for his expertise in foreign affairs and his knowledge of worldly political tactics and dip- lomatic espionage”: Buckingham seemed invincible as he went on: “I can change the map of the world with the tip of my finger; I can disintegrate foreign countries with one glance of my eye, I can destroy entire cities with one of my eyelashes”. But in the end the native double-agent received a traitor’s horrific death. It was apparent from the beginning of Bassam’s production that a bloody war had been fought in the unnamed Arab state where the House of York had claimed the throne and Margaret (of an unspecified clan) seemed to be the only survivor of the losing side. Amal Omran was marvellous as the venge- ful Margaret who represented the crying spirit of haunted battlefields; she had crammed her suitcase with the body parts of her slaughtered menfolk and murdered children, which she threw bitterly in the face of her usurpers. Margaret announced in her chilling opening speech that she was on the side of the losers, but she had come back to haunt the House of York and bellow out her pregnant curses. “I would ignore myself if I could”, she said, “but my history will not allow me. We lost”. In this announcement Margaret highlighted that the winners write history. Bassam also plays on writing history when he has Buckingham tell the Crown Prince (also played by Omran) that the English built the tower, instead of Julius Caesar, as in Shakespeare’s play. The balance of power in Bassam’s play hung between male and female characters that played equally important roles in this Arab tragedy. In fact, the Arab tragedy was as much about Richard’s blind ambition for power as it was about Margaret’s blood-thirst for revenge. Bassam sets a big challenge for Amal Omran, which she rose to in her stage pres- ence, her powerful delivery making her curses, at times, all consuming. “I don’t want your reconstruc- tion grants”, Margaret continued in her opening speech, “your loans […] I just ask of you not to ques- tion my thirst for revenge, not because I’m Arab — I have a degree”; thereby confirming that her revenge was a rational act. She not only had the passion for it but she also knew how to execute it. “Revenge-tak- ing”, said Omran (Margaret), “is still a relevant prac- tice today. The responsibility of taking revenge lies with the women in society. As mothers, women keep reminding their children of [the need to] avenge the family honour”. Bassam ingeniously used the scribes mentioned in Shakespeare’s text to caricature modern Arabic me- dia, of which al-Jazeera has become an internation- ally recognisable station. Faisal Al Ameeri read the news on the York television station with an uplifted tone in his voice that is all too familiar to listeners in the region. The media devices were informative but at times distracting. The scenes were short, sharp and speedy, giving the impression of being filmed. Bassam admitted his aspiration to film his adapta- tions for television. As well as live music, Bassam used chanting of Qura’nic verses. It is not surprising that Bassam is often accused of overstretching and cramming a lot of information in the well-known Shakespearean plot-lines, or that his productions lack focus. The complexity of the mate- rial, coupled with the British audience’s alienation from both political and cultural aspects of the region, makes portraying these dimensions a difficult job indeed. However, the audience was bombarded with information thrown at them in this free adaptation: email messages flashing on the screen, four televi-

Yvette K. Khoury * Macbeth, directed by Grzegorz Bral for Teatr Piesn Kozla, The Swan, 21 and 22 February 2007, mid- stalls. T eatr Piesn Kozla (Song of the Goat Theatre) from Wroclaw, Poland brought Macbeth to the Swan Theatre for a limited engagement at the end of February as part of the Complete Works Festival. Billed as a “work-in-progress”, what audiences wit- nessed was theatre-as-evolving-work, “a theatrical experiment”, as Peter Brook calls his own produc- tions. Like Brook, Piesn Kozla is heavily influenced by, and progresses from, the extraordinary work of Jerzy Grotowski, one of the most influential theatre practitioners since Stanislavski and Meyerhold. As a result, the work did not present the story of Macbeth as much as it explored aspects of the interior life of the characters and the milieu of the play. Needless to say, as Grzegorz Bral joked during the presentation, if you came to the theatre to see the story of Macbeth, then perhaps you came to the wrong theatre. For those who left early, and they only averaged two or three people over the two nights I saw the work, they missed what can be described as a struc- tured exhibition of theatrical exercises. Sometimes speaking the text, other times discarding it entirely, the company used movement and vocal techniques

77 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL to present “improvised research”, what Bral called “training […] leading us to performance”. The programme stated that workshops on the project began in April 2006, rehearsals in November, and that the current “presentation […] is the comple- tion of the first stage of the journey towards the final performance […] planned to take place on April 19th, 2008”. Bral also elaborated that productions for the company often take three years in rehearsals before performance, a luxury that English companies can- not afford. Grotowski’s idea was to seek the via negativa, the “eradication of blocks” that are inherent in the body and resist the expression of pure impulse.1 Through extensive physical training, those blocks are eradicat- ed, a breaking down of the body in order to allow it to channel its natural energy. Rather than “building a character”, this approach to acting allows an actor to channel a character that is spontaneous and unpre- dictable. Even the text is subordinate to allowing this “secret motor” — the subconscious — free reign to guide the actor’s responses to situations and condi- tions, a state called “secular holiness” by Grotowski.2 This state is achieved when an actor gives up their body unselfishly and freely to the communal state of theatre, to channel the forces residing within into a state of transparency, to “virtually cease to exist”.3 This Macbeth began with twelve wooden chairs set into a circle on the stage with three more placed in 120º angles in the centre of the circle. The cast en- tered and sat in the chairs, one performer beginning by intoning a pitch. The actors slowly joined her pitch and continued to align their voices, achiev- ing a harmony. Once this had been attained over a period of a minute, two or three of the voices began to establish their own individual melody within the stream of intonation. One sounded like keening, another like Gregorian chant. The intervals between the base pitch and the intervening voices opened up the audience’s ears to the variety of sounds we were to experience, as well as attuning the actor’s ears to each other’s rhythms. Within this framework, amid continuing intonation, one actor recited the report of the battle that begins “Doubtful it stood, / Like two spent swimmers” (I.2.9-10). Then Lady Macbeth (Anna Zubrzycki) stood, reading the letter from her husband and walking around the circle until she reached Macbeth (Gabriel Paul Gawin), pouring the criticism of his nature — “full o’th’milk of hu- man kindness” (I.5.12) — into his ear. He then stood and delivered the “If it were done” (I.7.1) soliloquy in the centre of the circle. Once these speeches were finished, the company broke off their intonation and pulled the chairs from the stage. Between exercises, Bral explicated aspects of the company’s work. “Polyphony” was an essential term, defined here as many voices joining into one but retaining the individual voices of each performer. He explained that the vibrations which the company employed in the opening exercise were devices to produce synchronous vibrations in other actors and in the audience itself. What they achieved, according to my ears, was a tuning fork quality that opened our ears to the sounds that we were receiving; the result was that the text, when used, was negotiated into new meanings through its aural properties. Their “questions towards how Macbeth could sound” opened new pathways into the physical world of the text and of the play. The next segment was intended to explore the world of the weird sisters through a Siberian funeral song introduced to them in a village where they had performed. In “Cauldron”, the women of the company knelt around a staff tied with multi-col- oured ribbons. Beginning with a keening incanta- tion, the others joined in a chiming reiteration that was passed in-the-round. Within this chiming and swooping aural tapestry, the actresses seemed to be in states of grieving and mourning, one of them with tears streaming down her face. Clearly, the exercise had opened up the actor’s bodies to receptivity of emotions. Another exercise involved Lady Macbeth singing “Come, you spirits”(I.5.38) while being shadowed around the stage by the females of the company; the cast multiplied until she cried “hold” (52), where the polyphony and movement stopped and she continued, speaking the speech. This exer- cise was meant to find the “music hidden inside the performance, expressed though movement”, as Bral explained during the performance. In this way, the music and the frantic movement reflected the state of Lady Macbeth’s mind, the cacophony of discord- ance that accompanies her “mortal thoughts”(39) as she abandons her placid mental state and reaches towards the “direst cruelty”(41) that attends them, here made manifest by the bodies of other perform- ers. Usually played as an intellectual address to her own mind or to invisible spirits, this exercise made them physical forces for Lady Macbeth to interact with, demonstrating, as Bral asserted, that “art doesn’t happen within, it happens between”. Other exercises used the physical in complement with the spoken word. In “Dagger”, that famous soliloquy was spoken with constant movement, accompanied by three of the male performers who maintained an equal spacing from Macbeth as he both grasped at and recoiled from his fatal vision. Spoken with psychological intensity, the move- ments of all four performers amplified the text and physicalized what is often performed as an interior speech. This dance of sorts was a representation of the movements of Macbeth’s mind, still unable firmly to accept the murder until the very end of the speech; he has supped with horrors on the battlefield and now willingly chooses regicide. In “Banquet”, the interaction between characters was represented

Reminiscent of Cicely Berry’s work, itself also derived from Grotowski, the Macbeths moved forward when they felt that their character presented a case for the murder and backwards when they shrunk away from it. Constantly swaying on their feet, their movements eventually synchronized to- wards the end of the scene. They moved towards the back of the stage, watching Banquo present his own suspicions of the Macbeths while moving on changes of phrase. This movement was mirrored by another male member of the company for “Horse and Rider”, the murder scene where Banquo’s lines were met by slashes from his company mate. Accompanied by in- tense rhythmic drums and with each cut of the knife embellished by an exhaled sting from the murderer, Banquo was slowly hounded to death, ritually tor- tured and brought down by sound and movement. The performance continued to offer these same striking movements and sounds in lieu of the play proper. “Family” presented a seated Macbeth la- menting his enslavement to the seeds of Banquo, while several actors presented the family portrait in his mind around his throne. Malcolm and Macduff spoke their English scene while tumbling on wres- tling mats. Their movement paced the scene by ac- centuating turns of phrase and making them physical responses as well as intellectual justifications. But the most striking exercise of the evening was “Queen”, the sleepwalking scene of Lady Macbeth represented by a return to the Cauldron exercise. On a raised platform, the queen responded to the intonations is- suing from the female members of the company by slowly entwining herself in the ribbons from the pole used earlier. Like the strands of a web, she ended up trapped by the ribbons and tried to raise herself with the pole but slipped twice, the second time proving her death fall. The disjointed images of Shakespeare’s text became physical trappings, tangible blocks that brought the character down. This served not only as a metaphor for the murderous couple, but also as an image for the work of the company, the eradication of the blocks that seize upon the body and disallow suppleness of free expression. Teatr Piesn Kozla did not bring a production of Macbeth as much as present experiments based around the psychology and subtext of the play. Rather than an intellectual and textual approach to the play, the exercises evoked the interiority of the characters in a visceral way by using voice and movement to engage the senses. What resulted was always intriguing and often exhilarating. With such subtle differences over two evenings, one longs to see the final product in a year’s time. I t may be fitting for the RSC to bid farewell to its Main House, which closes at the end of the month for major re-development, with Shakespeare’s fare- well to tragedy, but much is lost in its attempt to cele- brate this difficult theatrical space. Richard Hudson’s towering, blood-spattered set, together with the re- lentless use of shades of red in the Roman costuming, dominate the stage, leaving the actors generally un- derpowered and seemingly overawed by their sur- roundings. Corioles and Antium are also represented by overwhelming walls, and their soldiers wear grey equivalents to the Roman battle gear. The gigantic marble porticos that represent Rome close off much of the acting space, whilst wide steps leading down into the auditorium attempt with limited success to draw the audience closer to the action. Doran’s production opens with a non-textual, Corn Riot, with a handful of actors dashing through the audience crying “Corn, corn!” and bearing agri- cultural implements as weapons. Their hoes, spades and scythes jar with the insistently urban setting of a play concerned with the internal class schisms of this most powerful of cities. These unquiet citizens, however, are easily quelled by an unconvincing and strangely melancholic Menenius Agrippa (Timothy West) whose rambling “Fable of the Belly” moves them swiftly from rage to laughter at the expense of the First Citizen (Jonty Stevens) whom Menenius characterises as “the big toe of this assembly” (I.1.153). Calmness and laughter dissipate rap- idly once William Houston’s Caius Martius strides through the auditorium before mounting the steps to take centre stage. Dressed in an odd conflation of Roman and Renaissance dress, with more than a hint of a kilt about his pleated skirt, his rigidly martial stance is aided by a broad studded leather belt from which protrudes his sword at right angles across his back. He relishes the opportunity to display his contempt for the plebeians and his disgust that their riotous behaviour has led to a devolution of patrician power into the hands of popularly elected Tribunes. He is clearly delighted at news that his great en- emy, and soulmate, Tullus Aufidius (Trevor White) is again in arms against Rome and as the citizens “steal away” through the audience and side doors of the auditorium, he strides confidently towards his natural environment — war. The stage is left to the two brown-clothed, slightly sinister, tribunes (Fred Ridgeway and Darren Tunstall), whose machina-

They almost shout their plots across the width of the stage rather than take advantage of the many quiet corners that are revealed as the set’s five doors open to expose rows of columns disappearing into the depth of the stage. This is, however, a production much more con- cerned with familial relationships than the body politic. All Rome may be clothed in shades of red but Martius’ mother, Volumnia (Janet Suzman) is the most strikingly physical symbol of the blood- lust in which she seems to revel. Entering upstage in a vivid scarlet dress and bright red toga, she leads her grandson, young Martius, by the hand, a textual interpolation that emphasises her ongoing centrality in the family drama. Taking her seat in this domestic setting, she and the boy who kneels at her feet are brightly lit, leaving Virgilia, his mother (Eleanor Matsuura), stitching in shadow. Volumnia delights in conjuring visions of Martius on the bat- tlefield and smiles approvingly at her grandson as he demonstrates how well she has taught this second generation by voicing his father’s imagined battle cry “Come on, you cowards, you were got in fear / Though you were born in Rome” (I.2.35-36). As the boy exits, however, she signals awareness of both son’s and grandson’s potential flaws, responding to Valeria’s tale of the boy’s “mammocking” of the butterfly with a sardonic “One on’s father’s moods” (I.3.68). This is no simple Oedipal relationship, how- ever. Although, as Coriolanus, he kneels before his mother presenting to her the garland he earned in Corioli, Houston creates a depth of feeling for his wife and son that is seldom seen in performance. There is a long, heartfelt kiss and embrace of farewell to Virgilia at his banishment, before he turns once more to kneel in submission to his mother. The humour in the text is played most powerfully in the scenes when the newly-crowned Coriolanus, having dressed himself in an ill-fitting linen robe and disdainfully fulfilled the requirement to beg the consulship of the people, learns that their “voices” have been withdrawn. As the Senate meets to ratify the appointment, the Tribunes attempt to take the seats reserved for Coriolanus and the command- ing Cominius (Michael Hadley) and are ignomini- ously re-directed further down the pecking order. Returning home enraged, Coriolanus is bewildered by his mother’s politically astute encouragement to address the population “mildly” whilst handing him not the “bonnet” of humility but an emblem of his martial success — the laurel garland he had earned in battle. Having stormed back into the room in a temper shouting “I will not do’t”, like a sulky child he finally concedes “Mother, I am going to the mar- ket-place / Chide me no more” (III.2.131-32). That he is unlikely to succeed in pacifying his enemies is clear in the contrast between tone and content as he reluctantly acknowledges that “mildly” must indeed be the word. This mildness cannot be sustained, however, and this failure results in a banishment from which Rome initially seems to prosper greatly. Balloon-bearing citizens stroll contentedly across a stage bathed in warm light and the Tribunes enjoy their newfound status. But the peace is soon shattered, as Coriolanus and his new-found ally, Tullus Aufidius, march on the city. For here is a Coriolanus who is much more mild with his enemies than with the plebeians. He may treat Aufidius’ servants with contempt, but he kneels before their master in supplication. Beneath the high marbled walls of Antium there is a strong sense of the homoerotic as a bare-chested Tullus joins him on his knees before embracing and kissing his erstwhile foe. The most moving scenes are also those that dem- onstrate what the RSC will lose by replacing this deep proscenium arch stage with a more intimate thrust space. The overpowering walls are flown out to leave an immense and uncluttered stage. Both Menenius and the women appear to have trudged miles from Rome across this vast empty space to plead for their city. West is finally convincing as he stands unmoved by the mocking of the guards who have witnessed his rejection — a rejection too deep to be affected by the taunting of others. It is not only Suzman’s Volumnia that succeeds in saving the city, as she stage-manages wife, child and neighbours in their pleading. The cost of capitulation, however, is etched in her face as her kneeling son finally breaks his long silence to concede that he cannot ultimately “All bond and privilege of nature break” (V.3.25). She is greeted by a joyous Rome chanting “Vivat Mater” in a triumphal procession that echoes that of her son’s earlier victorious entry; but she cannot speak. Turning her back on the celebrations she de- parts, head bowed, and with her young grandson, no longer held by the hand, but ignored as he chases to catch up. Here is a mother who has learned too late that she has earned her own place in the ranks of “mothers who lack sons” (II.1.176); a lesson that just may save her grandson. Unfortunately, however, this emotional charge is dissipated slightly in the final scene. Coriolanus’ suicide seems at odds with the soldier who has just boasted of his martial prowess, an oddity heightened by it taking place downstage left. Aufidius is left to drag the body centre stage before balancing awk- wardly upon it in contempt. Once his rage is spent, however, he falls to his knees and is spot-lit cradling the body in a masculine pietà as his soldiers desert him. The martial world in which both men found a home has disappeared, and the last word to be spo- ken on the RST stage echoes in the vastness of the auditorium as his command, “Assist”, is ignored. G avin Bryars’s credit in the programme is not as “creator” but as “curator”. The phrase “curated by” makes the project sound like something out of a museum, as though Bryars were presiding over a series of ancient artefacts or precious fossils. In fact, the musical settings of thirteen sonnets — five in the first half, each by a guest composer, and the remain- ing eight of the second half by Bryars himself — were anything but historic or traditional. Bryars, in the words of Richard Clayton is “known for [his] lugu- brious minimalism” (Sunday Times, 18 February 2007) and the second half of the evening was a single piece (lasting about forty minutes) which concentrated on the theme of time and death in the sonnets (60, 123, 128, 94, 102, 146, 55 and 64). In the post-show dis- cussion, Bryars mentioned that he wanted to avoid sonnets about love and indeed the concentration on a single theme gave the second half a uniformity and coherence. Yet herein lay the problem, for this sustained and melancholic concentration on the theme of decay rapidly became ponderous and tedious in its de- spondency. Not only were the musical settings of the first half as various as the number of composers (and Bryars himself spoke of their “massively contrast- ing” styles), but the variety of reading tones which prefaced each musical setting served to emphasise these contrasts. Richard Dillane and Nina Sosanya read each sonnet before its musical rendition. Their readings were the epitome of clarity and in the case of Dillane’s rendering of 130, full of wit and irony. The musical performance — by soprano Anna Maria Friman and tenor John Potter — emphasised the va- riety of moods in Shakespeare’s poem sequence. The first half comprised settings of 73, 43, 130, 40 and 27 — each sonnet was chosen by the composer — re- spectively Natalie Merchant, Alexander Balanescu, Mira Calix, Gavin Friday and Nico Muhly and Antony. In part two, however, each poem was growled into the microphone in a mixture of affected agony and Hollywood horror by Gavin Friday — speaking in a bass drawl somewhere between the voices in the advertisements for Old Spice and Carlsberg Lager. He seemed to be grunting more often than not, both obscuring the musical delicacy of Bryars’s score and flattening the poems into an unvaried univocality. The final sequence involved him barking in conver- sation with the singing voices, which served only to sharpen the sense that his contribution was consider- ably less than theirs. Musicians were as follows: piano and musical director, James Holmes; clarinet and bass clarinet, Colin Honour; guitars, James Woodrow; percussion, Christopher Bradley; first viola, Howard Breakspear; viola, Katie Wilkinson; cello, Judith Burgin and bass, Gavin Bryars. Pippa Nissen had filmed a sequence of objects shown during the second half. They concen- trated on images of decay or death — dead flowers, a smashed light bulb, a smoking match, an extin- guished candle, a glass of wine tumbling in slow mo- tion onto a table cloth — all the sophistication and originality of a final-year graphics student. All in all, the project as a whole, though producing some deli- cate settings, was Nothing Like the Sun(nets), and it may be that this is a text, unusually for Shakespeare, that does better on the page than the stage. Peter J. Smith * Twelfth Night, or What You Will in Russian, directed by Declan Donnellan for Cheek By Jowl and the Chekhov International Festival, The Swan, 1 March 2007, centre stalls. W hy can’t theatre always be like this? An ensemble of men in white shirts, black trousers and braces enter an open space and start to make music with a couple of guitars, a tambourine and other percussion instruments. We hear the sug- gestively flirtatious lilt of a cha-cha-cha. Never shall I forget the sound of the shaker, gently beckoning us in to Cheek by Jowl’s relaxed and sultry Illyria. We are being put at our ease to feel desire, to imagine desire playing and working in different directions. Curiously, “father” is the first word to be spoken, gesturing towards the line “My father had a daugh- ter loved a man” (II.4.107). The word “father” is repeated by the assembled company who then put a skirt around one of the younger actors on the line: “I am all the daughters of my father’s house, / And all the brothers too” (II.4.120-21). For the next two and a half hours he (Andrey Kuzichev) becomes Viola; Olivia is identified and similarly clothed. Orsino emerges from the group and the music turns into his “food of love”. A butch cuteness characterized this production. The disarming spareness of the set and simplicity of the costumes (most characters were linen clad in the second half) were coupled with the uncompro- mising reminders of strong male torsos, large arms and hands. Yet, whilst a constant reminder of male sexuality sat like a veil as humorous as the ones Feste, Maria and Olivia all wore to fool Viola on her entrance in Act I Scene 5, the pervading sense of an openness to desire made it possible for us to imagine female truths and perspectives being inscribed onto and generating from these male bodies. In the very maleness of the ensemble — and especially from

81 COMPLETE WORKS FESTIVAL individual performances — emanated a tenderness and gentleness of movement, pace and rhythm. Here was no less than a lyricism of gender. So, it became fascinating to watch Olivia (played by Alexey Dadonov) sitting, administering her af- fairs quietly at her writing desk. A stillness seemed to exude from the actor which drew the audience in. She was dressed in a figure-hugging black chiffon dress — large biceps, broad shoulders, huge hands — but, in the stillness and the conviction with which the ac- tor playing Olivia fulfilled his action, he became an- drogynous; then he became she — momentarily but utterly female. Simply watching Olivia write became itself an act akin to loving her, desiring her. Through a stillness of focus and concentration in which the performance invited us to participate, we managed to see a figure who was always male and always fe- male, like Orsino’s “master’s mistress” (V.1.323), or the “master mistress” of Sonnet 20. Drawn to Olivia as we were, we were ready to learn one of her secrets. Here was a brilliant touch of interpretation. She was quietly afraid of Malvolio and her stillness became a way of coping. Later we saw this same behaviour become a way of sublimat- ing her own desires for Viola. An old, fading, end-of- the-pier Feste (played by Igor Yashulovich) dressed in motley — pale grey and white checked plus fours — managed to fool her out of it with his brutal cat- echism and the pair of them played and tugged at Olivia’s mourning veil. Malvolio’s look alone sup- pressed both of them and Olivia leant on Feste for a moment of nurture. It took the love of Viola for this Olivia truly to blossom. And when she did, her still apprehension broke into a genuine radiance of affec- tion. Vladimir Vdovichekov’s Orsino brought a con- trasting, virile masculinity onto stage, which made his passion bear-like enough for him to live up to his name. His purple velvet dressing gown was enough — as was Olivia’s bandanna-style head-dress (and in the second half an elegant straw sunhat) — to sug- gest their social status. Orsino was drawn to Cesario by an evident sexual drive that he found difficult to define and strange to place. It was not in anyway a straightforwardly homosexual desire that was being portrayed between the two of them. What we saw instead was Orsino falling for both the femininity in the actor’s performance of Viola and the masculinity in his performance of Cesario. Viola let her disguise drop during their private and intense dialogue in Act II Scene 4 by resting her head against Orsino’s right arm, while the two were sitting on a low platform downstage, facing the audience. Viola’s momentary pang of joy was palpable, but she suddenly shifted her position in case Orsino should see too much be- yond her evident vulnerability. Malvolio’s frustrated restraint in gradually giving in to temptation and reading Maria’s letter — such a sin for him to prise it open, yet delicious to peer inside — culminated in a pervasive mood of mel- ancholy. Dmitry Shcherbina’s steward began to sob with delighted and life-changing surprise when he read the terms in which he was loved. There was no delighted whooping from Maria, Sir Andrew or Sir Toby (played respectively by Ilya Ilin, Dmitry Dyuzhev and Alexander Feklistov). Fabian was cut altogether; Maria spoke his lines in the final scene. The production broke for the interval as Malvolio himself broke down in tears of joy, kneeling on the floor. His yellow stockings could not be seen immedi- ately he entered in Act III Scene 4. Olivia tried po- litely to ignore him while she took tea in her orchard. Malvolio was now dressed in a white tail coat and spoke to her confidentially. He lifted up his trou- ser legs to reveal bright yellow socks: a restrained costume choice but absurd enough in this context of gentility. Maria, Sir Toby and Sir Andrew soon appeared with a strait-jacket in which, by Act IV Scene 2, they had managed to bind him in the dark house. Malvolio’s prison filled the stage; the three other characters appeared in a galleried walkway above. It was strange and enigmatic for Feste to be- come Sir Topaz the surgeon, instead of Sir Topaz the curate. One reason might have been to suggest that Malvolio’s body might be cured, if not his spirit. In Act II Scene 3, Feste was given a Russian folk song to sing to Sir Andrew (dressed in a burgundy velvet, sixties-style suit) and Sir Toby (untidy in a crumpled dinner jacket). Sir Toby’s dangerous drunkenness had him striking Maria when she dared to interrupt his, Feste’s and Sir Andrew’s late night party. This Sir Toby damaged others because he himself was damaged, though his drunkenness amended somewhat during the second half. A bit of silly business had Sir Toby lining up a golf ball on a putting green (III.2.1-50), a tactic aimed at impress- ing Sir Andrew. What it provided was an activity for Sir Toby powerfully to ignore his friend, and to control him at the same time. T he received wisdom regarding the forest of A Midsummer Night’s Dream these days is that it is a murky, mucky arena in which identity becomes malleable while latent, anarchic sexual energies rise to the surface. By contrast, the forest of Arden / Ardenne (this production opted for the former, so explained Charles’s reference to “Robin Hood of England” (I.1.111) by making him Italian) has usu- ally seemed a slightly safer place. This account of the play picked up on the allusion to Eden (II.1.5) by making apples a regular feature of the set. The apple motif is, of course, ambiguous: it can either connote paradise or function as a proleptic image of sin. This polysemy was central to the conception of the forest at work in this staging. It was rendered by designer Katrina Lindsay as a blank white space, a tabula rasa or receptacle for the projections of the characters. It was reminiscent of the dimensionless blanched vista of the “base program” of The Matrix; its objects (a sparse tree, an orb that stood for both sun and moon, a puzzling, oversized bird) had the onto- logical status of simulacra, quite appropriate to the week in which Jean Baudrillard died. This uncoded level, it was suggested, forms a fantastic continuum, reaching beyond the confines of the play: while Celia slept, Little Red Riding Hood darted across the stage, her exit accompanied by the wolf’s ravenous howl. There was a seriousness to the notion of the for- est being “as you like it”: it was a function of sub- jectivity; its denizens could reconfigure their roles and social baggage in whatever way they could conceive. There were conspicuous limits, however, to what the characters were psychologically able to envisage that spoke of the tenacity of socio-political normativity. So some (such as Adam and, it seemed, Corin) were able to perceive the forest only as forbid- ding and privative, whereas Duke Senior styled it as an idyll, though one nonetheless arranged along feudal lines. This staging seemed keen to highlight a political myopia underlying the Duke’s paeans to rustic bounty. His aristocratic sense of entitlement remained unquestioned in exile — “According to the measure of their states” (V.4.173) was heavily stressed, a sort of maxim of his — and he modelled himself as tweed-clad country squire, ignorant of the struggles of his serfs; Corin was left to clear up after the climatic wedding scene. This level of the produc- tion was richly nuanced and made perfect sense of the bewildering multiplicity of evaluations of the forest present in the text. The forest is, of course, pre-eminently a space in which gender becomes more fluid than is possible in a rigid, frigid court. However, a layer of irony is lost when female actors are used, one generated in the past by the audience’s awareness that boys were playing women playing boys. This production seemed to compensate for the loss of a complicating further dimension in two ways. Firstly, we were of- fered a meta-theatrical prologue: there was a chorus of cellphone chirrups (reminding the audience of their potentially intrusive role), followed by a rendi- tion of “All the world’s a stage” (II.7.139), which ac- companied the funeral of Orlando’s father. Secondly, male transvestism was proposed as a counterpoint to Rosalind’s protean gender role. Perhaps this was a nod to Deleuze and Guattari’s insistence that any becoming-man must be accom- panied by a symmetrical becoming-woman, but it was not entirely dramatically fulfilled or fulfilling. Orlando (Sam Troughton) appeared after the in- terval sporting eyeliner and nail polish in addition to Rosalind’s earlier gift of a string of pearls. She remarked on the latter when sarcastically describing his attire as “point-device” (III.2.370), but his accou- trements were not associated with any real androg- yny. Similarly, Jaques tottered in high heels, with a diminutive hat more suited to Ascot than a forest perched precariously on his head. His flamboy- ant appearance threatened the degeneration of the comedy into high camp. However, Daniel Weyman’s performance belied his costume, which in turn ham- pered any attempt to conjure genuine melancholy. Despite the various insinuations of homosexual-

Rosalind delight- ed in dissimulation: as she toyed with Orlando, ad- ministering her own Ars Amatoria, she tapped out the morals of her lesson with a cane. The sexually teasing aspect of her behaviour was rendered explicit, as was the rhythm of her discourse, and indeed careful at- tention to metre was a conspicuous asset of the pro- duction as a whole. As her disingenuous dissertation progressed, Celia shook her head in disapproval, then let it hang in shame at her friend’s audacity. Dillon’s wonderfully expressive face and body lan- guage allowed her to offer a running critique of her companion’s conduct, and she made great comic use of the use of the long periods during which she was an unspeaking presence; her silence typically spoke volumes. The fact that these two women could impose such a forceful presence in the forest was an eloquent testi- mony to their courage and resilience, for they had fled from an intimidating world. While Oliver’s threat to Orlando seemed largely putative and puerile, Duke Frederick (played by Christopher Ravenscroft, who doubled as Duke Senior, Jekyll to Frederick’s Hyde) cut an altogether more malevolent figure. Confined to a wheelchair and wearing dark glasses, he seemed somehow to have escaped from Beckett’s Endgame and to have installed himself as a military dictator. Medals adorned his jacket, a woman who seemed half-nurse and half-dominatrix attended him, a sick- ly green light accompanied him as if he poisoned the air, a sinister echo effect permeated his speech, and his security forces constantly menaced from behind a diaphanous curtain. In an apparent allusion to the atrocities of Abu Ghraib, Oliver was threatened by the Duke as he stood at gunpoint with a sack over his head. All the while, the preceding scene’s “Blow, blow, thou winter wind” (II.7.175-94) kept playing; the already jarring levity of “This life is most jolly” (II.7.184 / 194) became even more dissonant. Frederick’s darkened court, clad in inky cloaks, offered a stark contrast to the bright white sylvan spaces. The latter opened up the abyss of freedom: Rosalind embraced it with open arms, giddy at the prospect of self-reinvention, whereas Duke Senior suffered a certain vertigo and retreated into Sartrean bad faith, replicating the hierarchy of his court with his ersatz rural aristocracy. For all its none-too-subtle colour coding, the production nonetheless succeeded in delineating Rosalind’s ability to hold a torch in ob- scurity, and in qualifying the promise of the woods’ bleached dreamscape. Samuel West compared the forest to an ashram, an ambiguous zone of simulta- neous emancipation and exploitation: “[T]he locals are quite poor and people come to study yoga […] then they go back and say how marvellous it all is […] It’s all rather indulgent”.1 Perhaps, given the menacing nature of Frederick’s regime, a better anal- ogy might be a kibbutz: a space that promises lib- eration even as frightening forces lurk at its borders, awaiting their cue. The metamorphosis of these fig- ures into the eponymous characters of the poem was thus an elegant transformation and implied both the amorous intrigues of the Elizabethan court as well as the inequalities of status between the Virgin Queen and the fair young man — the Goddess of Love and the callow boy. The initial action in the box switched to the introduction of a shell-shape “light chariot” on wheels (line 1192) drawn by “silver doves” (line 1189) and attended by Venus. The theatrics then shifted to the marionettes that appeared on the table platform. The importance of this change (alternating the box, dais and stage) is that the stage space was navigated extremely well considering the production was “peopled” by puppets. The use of space, cou- pled with Robert Jones’s artistic design, attentive to details to the extent of having wardrobe staff sew the miniature costumes, created a spectacle of opulence and beauty. Much of the onstage puppetry was achieved in silhouette such as the hind pursued by hounds or the initial appearances of the boar. These moments were delicate but often a little distant. Far more ef- fective were the moments in which the puppets were articulated on the dais, each being manipulated by two or three puppeteers in black clothes and gloves. Thus, while they were clearly visible at all times, the puppeteers were easy to ignore and the deft- ness with which they manipulated the figures was extraordinary — tapping feet impatiently, brushing hair back, attempting to embrace or elude embrace. The detailed actions allowed this stage interpretation to play up to Venus’ narcissism and sensuousness: “Thou canst not see one wrinkle in my brow”, as she stroked her forehead, and “since I have hemmed thee here”, as she straddled Adonis seductively (lines 139 and 229). In order to intensify the verisimilitude, while their words were spoken by the narrator as part of the larger story, the characters’ sighs, moans, tuts, kisses or grunts were voiced by the puppeteers. Additionally, the puppeteers facilitated subtle mo- ments of stage / space management. For example, Adonis’ exit “So he glides in the night” (line 816) was achieved via the puppeteers gracefully gliding the marionette in a smooth running motion and exiting downstage left. The puppeteers then surrounded the stalls at the rear and whispered across the audito- rium: “’Tis so” (line 851), in response to Walter’s af- firmation of Venus’ isolation. Of course the central narrative sequence — and it is one to which Shakespeare’s readers continue to be most erotically drawn — comprises the failed attempt of Venus to seduce the stubbornly unyield- ing boy. She was the star of the scene and in a moment where she finally receives an eagerly awaited kiss — “Incorporate then they did seem; face grows to face” (line 540) — she was in absolute control and they both floated in the air in a caressing kiss movement which was abruptly halted by the “fall to earth” (line 546). W elcome into the “near future”, as the pro- gramme put it. One might be forgiven for thinking that Stratford’s Swan Theatre had been hired by a culture-conscious company for the launch of its latest range of computers. On the open set were displayed three silver laptops, with the recognizable bitten-apple logo, and overhead screens. The set re- mained virtually unchanged throughout the produc- tion: open, uncluttered, except for the tables upstage on which the computers stood (they disappeared for the scenes in Shylock’s home). The back of the stage was closed off by a tall glass screen with a slick effect of fine, slatted blinds that alternately suggested an office block — Antonio’s world of golden boys of fi- nance — or large windows opening onto the gardens of Belmont. This, at first sight, seemed to be a world that had moved on, with no time for the walls of the ghetto and other community or social divisions. The excep- tion was Shylock’s home, a gloomy, claustrophobic place where, precisely, the clock seemed to have stopped for Jessica (Nicole Lowrance), who pol- ished silver, dressed in a drab pinafore, with her father (F. Murray Abraham), overhead in the gallery, watching. Shifts in setting and atmosphere were in- stilled by the lighting: cool greyish-blue for an office environment, warm golden light for Belmont, harsh clinical glare for the court scene. The overhead com- puter screens indicated stock-exchange results and, in Belmont, became the caskets. Shylock (onstage) spoke to Tubal (Marc Vietor, up in the gallery) over his mobile phone. Contrary to what one might initially have feared, this hi-tech environment did not get in the way, but served instead as a medium for communication. Somehow, Shylock’s ranting about his daughter’s departure sounded more like the kind of excessive language one can get carried away with on the phone, where there is no restraining eye-contact. The chessboard floor, appropriately laid out in three colours — lead, silver and gold — remained unchanged throughout the play. It made ideal, Italian-villa, marble flooring for Belmont — but not only. Throughout the play, as actors moved on the catwalks leading onto the stage and around the stage itself, privileging diagonal and circling movements, facing one other across the width of the stage, or standing and looking outwards at the audience, the chessboard effect subtly underlay the various rap- ports de force at work in the play — those written into the text and others that are potentially present in its margins. Launcelot approached Jessica, leaving a table between them, read to her, sat on a table look- ing towards her. Embarrassed, Jessica moved diago- nally across the stage to Lorenzo, putting her arms around him but looking towards Launcelot, who left abruptly, shoving Lorenzo and thrusting the book into her hand. This thread resurfaced later in the garden, moon- light scene. Lights were turned low and reflections of water rippled across the glass screens at the back of the stage, suggestive of a lit swimming-pool. Lorenzo and Jessica were alone, in bath robes and underwear. Playfulness, as they rolled and em- braced on the floor, seemed to be the mood in which they remembered the lovers of classical mythology whose loves were marred by separation or treachery. Their attempt to inscribe their love in that tradition proved a mistake, however, and the game degener- ated into an outright quarrel, with Jessica breaking away when Lorenzo reminded her how she left her “wealthy Jew” of a father “And with an unthrift love did run from Venice / As far as Belmont” (V.1.20). Raising her voice to a high pitch, Jessica reminded him in turn of his “many vows of faith, / And ne’er a true one” (V.1.24-25). Lorenzo tried to get on with his speech, briefly interrupted by Launcelot who, ignoring him, came on to announce Portia’s return. Jessica left, crying, followed after a while by Lorenzo. Tellingly, Portia and Nerissa arrived on an empty stage, and the allusion to the moon sleeping with Endymion was cut. This is a production for the twenty-first century, moving The Merchant of Venice out of the soul-search- ing debates of the post-Holocaust years, when schol- ars like Pierre Spriet went so far as to consider that its staging “must be abandoned” [“The Merchant of Venice’s Doom”, Cahiers Élisabéthains 34 (October 1988), 53-59] — a debate John Gross expounded on in his book, The Legacy of Shylock. There is no such ago- nizing debate here. Shylock is an authoritarian pater, an urbane, cunning businessman. Quintessentially, he is a believer, whose identity is destroyed when his religion is taken away from him by those who seem to be ruled by hedonism and the lure of gratifica- tion — financial and/or sexual. Take away a man’s religion and you are left with a shell — a disturbing, post-September-11 question-mark at the heart of an elegant, polished production, that suggests that we may, in fact, have already caught up with that “near future”. Janice Valls-Russell * King Lear, directed by Trevor Nunn for the RSC, The Courtyard Theatre, 28 April, 18 May and 18 June 2007, stalls. T revor Nunn’s production of King Lear, with Ian McKellen as the King, came as the grand climax to the Royal Shakespeare Company’s fifteen-month long Complete Works Festival. This ambitious project required the co-operation of numerous native and overseas companies as well as a heavy work-load for the RSC itself. Performances were given in many languages as well as English, and in a variety of ven- ues ranging from the soon-to-be redeveloped Royal Shakespeare Theatre and its Siamese twin the Swan through the newly erected and allegedly temporary Courtyard Theatre to Holy Trinity Church (for All is True, or Henry VIII) and to rooms in the Shakespeare Centre (for Timon of Athens). Productions covered a wide range of styles from the comparatively con- servative mode of Janet Suzman’s Hamlet, from the South African Baxter Theatre Centre, and Gregory Doran’s Coriolanus (in which Suzman played a moving Volumnia), through the RSC’s joyfully up- dated Cuban Much Ado About Nothing and Dominic Cooke’s brilliantly transposed promenade Pericles and The Winter’s Tale (in the Swan) to the brutalist modernisms of an adapted Othello in German from the Münchner Kammerspiele and a Cymbeline in modern English from Kneehigh Theatre. For those fortunate enough to see a wide range, or even all, of the productions, the season — a triumph of logistics — provided a conspectus of contemporary theatri- cal approaches to Shakespeare, proof at once of the
