Though the company that performed King Lear included actors who had taken part in earlier pro- ductions of this and of earlier seasons, and though it was directed by a previous Artistic Director of the RSC, it was assembled specifically to give related productions of King Lear and The Seagull which rep- resented both a culmination and a fresh start as they embarked, after leaving Stratford, on a world tour. Inevitably this raises questions about the RSC’s com- mitment to a company ethos. This was essentially an ad hoc group of actors that might equally well have been brought together under a different manage- ment. And to my mind it was none the worse for that. I saw Trevor Nunn’s production of King Lear three times: once from the back of the stalls, twice from further forward to the left of the auditorium. Its style and mode would have come as no surprise to theatregoers familiar with his work. Textually it was eclectic though with a bias towards the Folio; nevertheless it included Quarto-only episodes such as Lear’s mock-trial (History, Scene 13) of Goneril (Frances Barber) and Regan (Monica Dolan) and the description of Cordelia (played by Romola Garai) on her return from France — “You have seen sunshine and rain at once” (History, Scene 17, “History” being the edited Quarto text and “Tragedy” the edited Folio text). Verbal changes seemed designed to shift the text towards naturalism. Cordelia’s asides in the opening scene were omitted. Adjustments at the end of the hovel scene permitted Lear’s later statement “My poor fool is hanged” (History, Scene 24.300; Tragedy, V.3.281), sometimes held to refer to Cordelia, to look back unequivocally to his Fool (Sylvester McCoy). After Lear had left the stage the Fool stretched him- self out on a bench to sleep; a firing squad of soldiers entered, to ominous musical accompaniment, and marched the Fool to the side of the stage where a gallows was improvised. His Folio-only prophecy (Tragedy, III.2.79-96) was moved forward to form his last words as he was strung up to provide a climax to the first half of the production. The text was fleshed out with much additional business. Gloucester (William Gaunt) read of the “late eclipses” (History, Scene 2.103; Tragedy, I.2.101) from an almanac which he took from his bag. A bevy of nurses with a medicine chest and a drink ministered to Edmund (Philip Winchester) after his self-inflicted wounding (History, Scene 6.34; Tragedy, II.1.34). Cornwall (Guy Williams), Regan and their train entered with suitcases on their arrival at Gloucester’s house (History, Scene 6.85; Tragedy, II.1.184). Real rain fell in the storm scene. A vessel full of “red burning spits” (History, Scene 13.12) was on hand for Lear in the mock trial. In the last scene Goneril dropped poison into a glass of wine that she gave to Regan, and as Kent (Jonathan Hyde) left the stage on “I have a journey, sir, shortly to go” (History, Scene 24.316, Tragedy, V.3.297) he produced a pistol as if he intended to shoot himself. (Was this a conscious parallel to the end of The Seagull?) Sound effects (re- duced in later performances) and off-stage business supplemented the text. Dogs barked before the entry of Lear’s knights (History, Scene 4.6; Tragedy, I.4.7) who (as famously in Peter Brook’s 1962 production) were indeed riotous, shooting off rifles and indulg- ing in rough horse play with the King. An off-stage dance was in progress as Kent taunted Oswald (John Heffernan; History, Scene 7; Tragedy, II.1). Birds twit- tered as we heard of Cordelia’s grief at her father’s plight (History, Scene 17). The basic setting, however — designed by Christo- pher Oram — was symbolic rather than naturalistic. As the audience took their seats they were confront- ed with the sight of a receding Victorian-style theatre balcony with scarlet plush drapes overhanging the boxes. A faint mist drifted across the stage. Organ music thundered out and Lear’s court, elaborately costumed in formal attire suggestive of, perhaps, Imperial Russia entered from afar and advanced slowly forwards, culminating in the entry of the King himself, benevolently if bemusedly bestowing bless- ings on his followers in the manner of a religious patriarch. As the action progressed the drapes fell to reveal crumbling walls, and the setting disintegrated into ruins along with Lear’s mind. Much as critics have emphasized Shakespeare’s abnegation of a Christian frame of reference for the play, Nunn left us in no doubt that this was a society with a profound awe of the supernatural. All the many invocations of pagan gods were taken seriously. Everyone on stage knelt in fear as Lear invoked “the operation of the orbs / From whom we do exist and cease to be” (His- tory, Scene 1.104-05; Tragedy, I.1.111-22) in his banish- ment of Cordelia, and Goneril tottered and collapsed as Lear cursed her (History, Scene 4.267 ff.; Tragedy, I.4.254 ff.). Presentational realism corresponded to a high de- gree of psychological verisimilitude. In the opening scene, Cordelia suggested pent-up hysteria in the way she spoke “Nothing, my lord” (History, Scene 1.81; Tragedy, I.1.87) and was scornful of her sisters’ falsity. She clearly preferred the more glamorous Duke of Burgundy (Peter Hinton) to a studious, in- tense King of France (Ben Addis). Edgar’s statement that he had spoken with his father “Two hours to- gether” (History, Scene 3.149; Tragedy, I.3.145) became a rueful comment on Gloucester’s verbosity. Regan quivered and pranced with orgasmic glee as she watched her husband pluck out Gloucester’s eyes (History, Scene 14; Tragedy, III.7). For me, this reduced the horror of this physically and symbolically climac- tic episode; for once I did not shut my own eyes as it

All this was in keeping with McKellen’s inter- pretation of the King. This was a complex human being, no austere, rigidly authoritarian patriarch but a self-aware humorist, capable of folly, of act- ing the role of despot, but also of recognizing his weaknesses. He had clearly prepared his abdication speech in advance; as he delivered it point by point he let drop the cards on which it was written. (If I had sat only in the further forward seats I should not have known this, as Regan and Cornwall blocked the view throughout the episode. Bad blocking such as this has been a common fault in productions at both the Swan and the Courtyard.) The idea that Lear would “crawl toward death” (Tragedy only, I.1.41) amused him; he spoke jokily, as if it were all part of a premeditated game. By far the most relaxed char- acter on stage, he allowed us entry into the king’s personal feelings by ruefully wiping his lips after ac- cepting Regan’s hypocritical kiss. Goneril and Regan knew the roles they were expected to play, stepping up to deliver their prepared speeches from a lectern. Lear was amused by the disguised Kent’s bluntness, tolerant of the Fool, very much one of the lads with his knights, but rose to true magnificence on “I gave you all” (History, Scene 7.408; Tragedy, II.2.423). The subsequent “O reason not the need” was masterly in its pacing, moving in its shifts of emotion. Like others before him, this Lear failed in his determina- tion not to weep. The grotesque comedy of the hovel scene brought to mind Wilson Knight’s classic essay “King Lear and the Comedy of the Grotesque” (The Wheel of Fire, 1930). There was comedy but pathos too in Lear’s insistence that Edgar’s plight, like his own, must have been brought about by filial in- gratitude. Lear splayed apart the legs of the prone and nearly naked Edgar (Ben Meyjes) as he con- templated “unaccommodated man” (History, Scene 11.97; Tragedy, III.4.100), taking down his trousers to reveal his genitals. This aroused prurient criticism, but is surely justified by the play’s latent Christian iconography. The first time I saw the play McKellen followed this up by pointing to his genitals on “every inch a king” (History, Scene 20.105; Tragedy, IV.5.107) as if to suggest exceptional endowment. Later this was dropped. He boldly sustained his self-irony in the dialogue with the blind Gloucester, blowing his nose as he said he was “not ague-proof” (History, Scene 20.103; Tragedy, IV.5.104-05), and imitating a baby’s cries on “Thou know’st the first time that we smell the air / We waul and cry” (History, Scene 20.168-69; Tragedy, IV.5.125-26). He was tenderly vulnerable in his reunion with Cordelia. In the final scene some actors deliver “Howl, howl, howl, howl” (History, 24.253; Tragedy, V.4.232) purely as an inter- nal cry; others treat it as an imperative address to the onlookers. McKellen affectingly did both, speak- ing the word twice as if to himself as he carried on Cordelia’s body, then to the watchers as he displayed her corpse. His speeches over her body flowed with the inevitability of music. The five “nevers” (Tragedy only, V.3.284), widely spaced, hung on the air like drops of blood from Lear’s heart. This king died as he had lived, every inch a human being. Stanley Wells
